TEEE MAIDS AND THE MAGPIE. Three little maids and a magpie Went out one day for a walk ; The little maids bunted for flowers, The migpie did nothing but talk. " I've three little maidens to care for, Each one from dangers to save— While dogs or runaway horses— What a good thing I am brave I" Soon they were laden with flowers— Bunches of red, white, and blue ; Great ox-eyed, snowy.leaved daisies, Harebells, and bright poppies ton. Then they turned homeward together, Magpie still hopping before, Pasied though the wood and the village. Came to the rectory door. There stood a quiet gray prissy— Magpie flew off in a fright. So, afier all his vain boasting, Proved himself coward—not knight --A Little Folks" Magazlnt for August.
"ARTHUR IN AVALON."

Stricken of man, and sore beset of Fate, He lies amid the groves of Avalon; What c mfort mete ye unto Uther's son, 0 mournful Queens? Wnat styptic to abate Life's eager stream? Alas, not theirs to sate His soul with earthly vision ! he bath done With mortal life, and chivalry's bright sun Is darkeued by the powers of hell and hate. Lo! now, the garden of his agony Is very sweet, though dread the hour, and drear With ntterless spell of horrid potency; The barred east beyond the brightening sea, Thick with portentous wraiths of phantom fear, Is flashed with triumph, stirred with melody.

"Glory of knighthood, that through Lyonesse Was as a lamp, 0 selfless soul and pure, What though thy visionary rule endure So ill the assault of envy? Not the less Thy victory, though failure thee oppress; Not sterile thy example, and most sure The seeded fruit; with might thou shalt allure For evermore through life's embattled press Thy spiritual sons to follow thee ;" The mystic Four their solemn vigil keep Until day break, and eastward silently, Over the kinglesa land and wailing deep, The sacrificial symbol fire the sky; Then they arise, no more to watch and weep. - —J. Arthur Blaikie, in "The Magazine of Art."

div.p: "Yes," she said," I always obey my husband, but I have something to say about what his command shall be." Experience ought to be a head-light which throws its rays on things to come; instead, it is generally a stern-light which throws its rays on what we have already passed through. "John," said the schoolmaster, "von will soon be a man, and will have to do business—what do you suppose you will do when you have to write letters, unless you learn to spell better ?" "Oh, sir," replied John, "I shall put easy words in them." , Recently four brothers whose united ages total up to 346 years, or an average of 86, met in the parish of Debenham, Suffolk. They are members of a well.known family of six- teen, descendants of a venerable resident of Debenham. Their ages were: John, 94 years; Charles, 86; Henry, 83; and Frederick,Bl. It is not many places that can boast of so many octogenarians in one family. SIR Isaac NEWTON.—Newton invited a friend to dinner, and forgot it. The friend arrived, and found the philosopher in a fit of abstraction. Dinner was brought up for 'one." The friend, without disturbing Newton, sat down and de- spatched it. Newton recovered from his reverie, looked at the empty dishes, and said, "Well, really, if it wasn't for the proof before my eyes, I could have sworn that I had not yet dined. BALL PRACTICE FORTY YEARS AGO.—A writer in the Staffordshire Advertiser gives from personal recollection the following account of ball practice with the old "Brown Bess," as it was carried on by the regulars forty years ago. Be says :—ln a large claypit at one corner of a well-known race-coarse an old door was set upright, and thereon was sketched in chalk a rude figure of a French soldier. Over the heart was suspended a wine bottle, and the soldier who hit the bottle received from the officers half a-crown. The men were drawn up in squads at a distance of fifty or sixty yards from the target, and when the practice was very good a dozen or so of bottles would be broken in the course of a summer's afternoon. This was only ten years before the Crimean War. MOZART.—One evening the Empress Maria Theresa gave a grand concert at her palace in Vienna. A young prodigy of an artist, only eight years of age, was to make his first appearance at Court. His success was stupendous, and he was recalled—a very unusual thing in so august an assembly. Unfortunately, as he was stepping forward to bow his thanks, his foot slipped, and he fell. A young lady then rushed forward to pick him up, and inquired, "Have you hurt yourself ?" The little fellow looked at her intently for a few moments, then exclaimed with a face beaming with smiles, "Oh, what a beautiful young lady you are! will you marry me ?" A burst of laughter greeted this ingenu- ous proposal. The amiable young lady Was Marie Antoin- ette, the future wife of Louis XVI. ; and the little boy- musician was no other than Wolfgang Mozart. A STRANGE MEETING.—I bade good-by to a medical friend of mine once in Soho-square. He was going away , to the country to get married and settle down in a mining !district among the Welsh hills. Years flew by. I was out lon the eastern shores of Africa. We were fainting slavers. One rascally old dhow gave us much trouble and a long chase. We ran her at last down to shooting distance, and as she would not stop we brought our big guns to bear on [l2 er ; still she flew on and on, fair and sq .are before the wind, till a lucky shot knocked the mainmast out of her, When we boarded her the very first person seen on deck was 1 the medical friend I had bidden a final adieu to—as I ' thought—in Soho-liquors. There was not much mystery ! about the matter after all. He bad not got married. He had not settled down among the Welsh mountains. Be was on his way to Zanzibar to join a mission, and had taken passage in this dhow for cheapness sake.—Cassell's "Family Magazine." AN ANXIETY or THE HOLIDAYS —However necessary rest may be, work, in itself has a fascination for most people when they are accustomed to it; and no one like.; to leave his affairs if there appears any chance of their suffering by his absence. And however excellent may be the substitute a man leaves at his post, it is difficult for him to believe that this alter ego can exactly fill his place. An explanation of the phenomenon of "The White Lady of Hohenzollern," whose supposed reappearance in Berlin at the time of the German Emperor's recent illness caused such alarm, is given by Mr. Karl Blind in the August num- ber Of Cassell's Magazine. Ben Jonson had a love for his "dear Spenser." Among the books sold at Sotheby's was his own copy of the "Faerie Queen," " Shepheard's Calendar," Sm. The margins of the pages have many notes; not a few of the remarks are pithy, and it is of no little interest to go over the pages and dis- cover what Ben Jonson has to say of his "dear poet." A much-needed step in the right direction has been taken by the establishment in Calcutta of a Zenana library. One of the stock arguments against the education of Indian women is that when educated there is difficulty in providing them with books fit for female reading. The library, it is said, has already been a great success. A them-rum. In the course of the autumn a monument wiil be erected to the late Dr. Moffat, the African missionary, in his native village of Ormiston, near Tranent, in East Lothian. The execution of the memorial has been intrusted to Mr. D. W. Stevenson, A.R.S.A. The obelisk, which is to be of red granite, and 20rt. in height, will be furnished with a bronze relief of the features of the eminent missionary. Two Frenchmen, the brothers Forre, have invented a new kind of harp, made entirely of wood. Instead of strings the inventors use strong strips of American fir. The sound is produced, as in the ordinary harp, by the contact of the fingers; but the player wears leather gloves covered with resin. The tone of the instrument is said by Le Mdgestrel, from which we have obtained these details, to be of remark- able purity. The Moniteur des Arts says that "Les Artistes Japonais" are now collecting in Tokio the materials for a special exhi- bition in Paris. A. society has been formed in Japan, under the presidency of a member of the Imperial family, for the protection and revival of Japanese art. This society com- prises a thousand members. One of its modes of action will be exhibitions, of which the Parisian gathering will be one. An exhibition of pictures is now open at Tokio. Americans are naturally solicitous about preserving the houses and other relics associated with the memory of their great men. An outcry has been raised over the threatened destruction of the house in which Poe lived at Fordham during the most interesting period of his life. The odd thing is that the act. of vandalism was contemplated by a
re ,ent purchaser of the estate, who is described as "a warm admirer" of Poe, and who had resolved to build "a fitting mansion" on the site—for himself.—lthenwitin.

The results of Dr. Schliemann's excavations at Tiryns turn out to be very important. The buildings he has dis- covered consist of a palace and two temples. The arrange- ment, size, and position of these agree in the most remark- able manner with those of the temples and palace of the second prehistoric city at Hissa.rlik, and thus help to settle the date of the latter. In spite of the wall paintings, the remains at Tiryns most be older than those at Mycenm, since, besides the archaic pottery found among them, large numbers of obsidian implements have been disinterred.— Academy. A DISTILLING INSECT.—Livingstone met with a wonder- ful distilling insect in Africa on fig trees. Seven or eight of the insects cluster round a spot on one of the smaller branches, and these keep up a constant distillation of a clear fluid, like water, which, dropping to the ground, forms a little puddle. If a vessel is placed under them in the even- ing, it contains three or four pints of fluid in the morning. To the question, whence is this fluid derived? the natives reply, that the insects suck it out of the tree, and natural- ists give the same answer. But Livingstone never could find any wound in the bark, or any proof whatever that the insect pierced it. Our common frog-hopper, which before it gets its wings is called " cuckocespit," and lives on many plants in a frothy, spittle like-fluid, is like the African in- sect, but is much smaller. Livingstone considers that they derive much of their fluid by absorbing it from the air. He found some of the insects on a castor-oil plant, and he cut away about twenty inches of the bark between the in- sects and the tree, and destroyed all the vegetable tissue which carried the sap from the tree to the place where the insects were distilling. The distillation was then going on at the rate of one drop in every 67 seconds, or about 51 table- spoonfuls every 24 hours. Next morning, although the supplies of sap were stopped, supposing them to come up from the ground, the fluid was increased to one drop every 5 seconds, or one pint in every 24 hours. He then cut the branch so much that it broke, but they still went on at the rate of a drop every 5 seconds, while another colony of the insects on a branch on the same tree gave a drop every 17 seconds—" The. World of Wonders" for August.

THE MANAGEMENT OF PoULTRY. POULTRY KEEPING BY COTTAGERS. In France the great majority of the fowls kept are owned oy small farmers and cottagers. But we fear that in this country there is not sufficient effort made to induce cot- tagers to augment their incomes by poultry keeping. There are rural clergymen and gentlemen who do all they can in this direction, but much more could be done if others would follow in their footsteps. Every plan which proposes to augment the quantity of food, and to increase the comforts of the cottager, is deserving of success. The extent to which this end may be attained by a cottager's wife direct- ing her attention to the management of poultry does not appear to have been accurately investigated; nor is it clearly understood by many whether this branch of cottage economy is advantageous or disadvantageous, owing chiefly to the absence of some useful rules by which to conduct it according to a systematic and uniform method, based on experience and information. Attention has, however, been generally directed to the subject, but information has not been extensively conveyed to those for whom it is specially useful, and the various opinions of different writers have not been compared, so as to deduce rules of undoubted utility. The great William Cobbett, in his useful work entitled "Cottage Economy," has expressed the following opinion on the matter :—" It as," he says, "perhaps seldom that fowls can be kept conveniently about a cottage; but when they can, three, four, or half a dozen hens to lay in winter, when the wife is at home the greater part of the time, are worth attention. They would require but little room; might be bought in November and sold in April, and six of them, with proper care, might be made to clear every week the price of a gallon of flour. If the labour were great I should not think of it, but it is none, and I am for neglect- ing nothing in the way of pains, in order to secure a hot dinner every day in winter when the man comes home from work. . . . Nothing lawfully within our power ought to be neglected in order to secure comfort at home, for without comfort there is no home." The cottage economist of Ireland, Martin Doyle, devoted about fifty years ago in his " Hints to small Holders" some attention to this subject, as this extract from that work will show. He says A few cocks and hens if they be prevented from scratching in the garden, are a usefal and appropriate stock about a cottage, the warmth of which causes them to lay eggs in winter—no trifling advantage to the children when eggs are scarce. The French who are extremely fond of eggs and contrive to have them in great abundance, feed them so well on cards and buckwheat, and keep them so warm that they have plenty of eggs, even in winter. Now in our country, especially in a gentleman's fowl yard, there is not an egg to be had in cold weather; but the warmth of the poor man's cabin ensures him an egg even in the most ungenial season. You constantly want salt (and I hope snap), and candles in winter; now a few eggs taken to the hucksters, procure you these most necessary articles in ex- change. . . . Wherever you are within reach of the steamboats you may calculate on having a demand for fat poultry for the English markets, if those at home should not afford a sufficient price. Many a clever woman in the barony of Forth earns smart sums by rearing and fattening fowl for the Wexford market. In Scotland, that valuable association, the Highland S miety, has given prizes to those cottagers who have been most successful in the rearing and management of poultry ; and a prize has been offered for the best essay on the means of improving the supply of fattened poultry for market towns. In a journal published nearly fifty years ago we find the following :—ln the counties bordering on the Metropolis, particularly in Surrey, Sussex, Essex Cambridge, Norfolk, Suffolk, and Berkshire, the rearing and fattening of poultry for the London market is thought worthy of attention by considerable farmers. At Wokineh am, in Berke, the London dealers sometimes pay £l5O to the poultry feeders in that district in a single market day. Reigate and Dorking are also large poultry markets. The prices are sometimes very high. In 1827 young fowls were sold in London at 18s. a couple; and from Cs. to 10s. is considered a moderate price. The sadden demand which arises during the fashionable sea- son in London will account for these high prices. Twenty dozen of the finest fowls are sometimes required for a single gala; and if the prices were higher, the extravagance of , fashion would perhaps cause the demand to be greater, though ordinarily an increased price at once diminishes the sale. L The present Earl Spencer, who has always warmly inter- • ested himself in any species of rural and domestic improve- : ment, a few years ago instituted a poultry show at Chapel Barmpton, in Northamptonshire. As it is always desirable to have a standard in view, raised as high as the most ap- proved system will carry it, we give the weight of the fowls , which gained the prizes in 1829. The best turkey weighed • 201 b. 4oz ; capon, 71b. 1411 oz. ; pullet, 61b. 3ioz ; goose, 18lb. 2,ioz ; couple of ducks, 15lb. 10oz. L But, perhaps,continues the same paper, the cottager may direct his attention with more advantage to the production of eggs than to the fattening of poultry. The Poland breed will be found most valuable to him. Their colour is a shining black with white feathers on the top of their head. , They are called "everlasting layers," and so seldom are in- clined to sit that their eggs are often set under nens of a different breed. Some very interesting experiments on the , production of eggs have recently been made by Mr. Mowat, of Stoke, near Guildford. Ile received three pullets of the Poland breed on the first of December,lB3s, which had been ' hatched in the Jane previous, and they cemmenced laying on the 15th of December. The number of eggs they laid between the first of December, 1835, and the first of Decem- ber, 1836, was 524, or 174 and 175 each, and only one of them showed a desire to sit. Daring the twelve months ' they consumed three bushels of barley, lithe. of rice, and a small qoantity of barley meal and peas, the cost of which amounted to 16s. 10d. The number of eggs being 524, there were 31 eggs produced for every shilling expended. Asentn- ' ing the weight of each egg to be lioz , there would be 41lbs. of food of the most nutritious kind it is possible to obtain, at a cost of less than 411. per lb.; or, if these eggs, instead of being used for family consumption, had been sold to the huckster, a profit would have accrued of at least 100 per cent., for the trouble of attendieg to so small a stock of poultry scarcely deserves attention. If the barley had been purchased in a larger quantity, it could have been obtained at 49. per bushel instead of 48.9 d., and there would have been 36 eggs for each shilling expended. From the above it will be seen that comparatively little advance has been made in this question of cottage poultry !keeping, and we commend to the notice of our readers these old observations as applicable now as when they were written.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING

CLUBBING.—This is a disease that attacks the cabbage tribe at this season of the year, and judging from the droop- ing foliage of cauliflowers and others, it is unusually preva- lent this season. On pulling up the plants, it will be seen that the small roots and real feeders of the plants have dis- appeared, and are replaced by a number of irregularly. formed tabercules, some of them the bulk of a hen's egg, and which are more numerous in dry weather. May and June last were most favourable to the spread of the disease, and we found traces of it in the seed beds, and the plants were destroyed. The origin of clubbing is supposed to be caused by an insect puncturing the top roots. Whatever it may be, it is evident that circulation is arrested and growth ceases. The best preventives are lime, nitrate of soda, com- mon salt, and soot. We have great faith in good culture, and as the above are manurial, they would have some effect by stimulating growth, as well as being distasteful to Insects. So soon as there are any indications of clubbing, we tread the plants firmly all round, and with the spade we mould the plants up as high as possible. In a fortnight or three weeks the plants will form numbers of fresh roots and be re- established, and this is the only measure we can suggest that is likely to save the crop. DWARF FRUIT TREES.—In gardens of limited area it is of the utmost importance that these should be constantly pruned every summer, in order to maintain them of a size suitable for the dimensions of the garden, as weir as with the view of increasing their fertility. The most vigorous grow- ing tree is not the most productive, and by resorting to summer pruning we weaken its growth and restore the , balance of power, so that the tree is hastened to form fruit bads. When we cat away a vigorous shoot from a tree in a healthy condition, the sap which supported it will go to supply food to other parts, and especially those that have been its nearest neighbours. If the shoot has been cut off at the proper season, the probabilities are that flower buds will be formed and fed at the base of the portion left of the shoot. Should the latter buds push forth and form shoots, they also must be pinched back to two or three eyes. We do not approve of doing the whole tree at one time, but prefer to commence at the top, and shorten the very strongest half way downwards, and in a fortnight after to serve the remainder of the tree the same. By this time the weaker shoots will have increased in strength and, be ready for moving in a week or two later still. Flower buds rarely form at the base of weakly shoots after they are cut, so it is best to encourage them to make all possible growth before being shortened,and when they are numerous we advise that their number be reduced by cutting them clean away. THE FRONT GARDEN.—The Carnation, though a peren- nial, is all the better for being annually propagated, and the labour of doing so is so trifling that it should not be neg- lected for a single year. A long spell of severe weather re- duces the number of old plants, whilst not one layer or young plant will be lost. This is more noticeable in stag- nant soils, and in such it is perilous to leave even all the young ones out during winter. For the purpose of layering which is the best method of propagating these plants: A quantity of moderately fine sandy soil is essential to pack well under the shoots intended for layering, and as these are usually pretty regular round the parent plant, the soil should be arranged in a round flattened cone about 4in. or gin, above the ordinary level. Provided with a sharp knife we trim off the bottom leaves, leaving from six to eight to form the layer, and it is better to dress all in this manner that are intended to be layered at any given time, than to dress one and layer it and so on, because there is the danger when trimming one of disturbing others that are layered. If with the knife an upward incision is made on the under side of the shoot just below the third joint, and drawing the knife through the latter our layer is made, and if pressed quietly on to the soil and held at the same time in a vertical position the tongue will be directed perpendicularly into the 841, into which it should be assisted and then the whole pressed down and secured with a peg or bent piece of willow In the shape of a hairpin. Excellent pegs are also procured from the stem of the bracken or common fern. At the point where the peg is inserted we place quite an inch of soil, so that the peg is entirely hid. Though that is not our object, but rather that the bend in the cutting should be well covered so as to assist root formation below, and when it is completed we like to see our layer as erect as if it were an established plant. The number that may be layered from one parent may vary up to eight, and there is no injury done if some weakly ones are entirely cut off. Water must be withheld from them for a few days after they are layered, and for that reason we prefer to operate on them on a fine day, and when there is a probability of the weather continu- ing so for a few days, but after that the soil must not be allowed to get dry. THE WINDOW.--HYDRANGEAS.--Judging from some window specimens we have seen of this we conclude that it receives treatment most conducive to its flowering at the hands of some cottagers, for on one we counted as many as six respectable heads, whilst others we have seen had only one, and that very inferior. As soon as the flowers become dingy it is best to cut the shoots that bear them to within two or three inches of the starting point. From the por- tion left two or three shoots will push that will produce flowers another year. Shoots that have not flowered this ' season will do so the next lithe plant is placed in a window with a sunny aspect or, better still, out of doors in the full sun. The beat time to pot such plants (that is, those hav- ing shoots that have not flowered) is in the spring, just when the flower buds are visible. Large corymbs are pro- duced by reducing the number of shoots, and by allowing only one we have had them so large as to fill the entrance of the largest hat that ever covered a head.

SHOCKING FA TALTTIES.-THREE PERSONS KILLED. A distressing accident accurred on Saturday afternoon, near Padgate, when a platelayer named Richard Bate, 59 years of age, was run over by a train whilst working on the line in company with some fellow workmen. He appears to have inadvertently stepped in front of a passing train in a moment of forgetfulness or pre-occupation, as be must certainly have been aware of its nearest approach. His body was shock- ingly mutilated, and had literally to be taken up in pieces to be removed to the Stocks Inn at Padgate to await an inquest. The deceased resided at Rixton-with-Glazebrook, and was married. The inquiry respecting the occurrence was held at the Stocks Inn, Padgate, before Mr. Husband, deputy coroner, on Tuesday afternoon. Mr. Jenkins, solicitor, Warrington, watched the inquiry on behalf of the relatives of the de- ceased, and the following evidence was taken:— Catherine Bate, widow of the deceased, said that her late husband was a tailor by trade, but went to work on the rail- way about eleven years ago as a platelayer. On Saturday last he was working for the Cheshire Lines Committee. He was in his seventieth year of age. If he got a little cold he was deaf, but he was not deaf when he left home on Satur- day. He was not often deaf and was not short-sighted, being able to read without glasses. She heard about her husband's death on Saturday afternoon, and had since identified his body.—By Mr. Jenkins: Deceased did not complain of cold on the morning in question, or on the previous day, and she was not aware that he was in any way suffering from cold. William Parsonage, platelayer, Rixton, deposed that he was employed by the Cheshire Lines Committee. He was working on the Cheshire Lines on Saturday, between Pad. gate and Risley box. At one o'clock the men commenced to collect their tools, and for that purpose put a bogy on the up line which they pushed along for about a quarter of a mile in the direction of Manchester. Bites, a , man narnA Timperley, and witness were on the up line when ! the 1-20, which had to pass on the down line, left Glaze- kook. It watt their intention to wait so that they could re- turn by the down line. They were sitting on the bogy on the up line waiting, and the deceased was placed with his back to the direction in which the engine was coming. ' When the traits was approaching deceased got up as if he ' were going to cross the line to fetch a tool, and as the train I was close at band it knocked him over and he was instantaneously killed. The deceased only took two steps before the train caught him and it was impossible for witness and his companions to stop him, or for the driver to blow his whistle, as he walked right in front of the engine. : I.•tie deceased was cut to pieces and witness pick-d him up and wrapped him in some sacks as well as was possible. His ' clothes were stripped from him, even his shirt being torn away. The body was afterwards removed to the Stocks ! Inn in a sheet. Witness re ts examined at length by Mr Jon- ' kiss as to their exact position and movements on the line, ! but nothing transpired to indicate carelessness or neglect of the rules of the railway on that occasion. ! William Timperley, platelayer, Rixton-with-Glazebrook, gave corroborative evidence. "fin:nada feudal', Manchester, engine driver, said that he was in charge of the engine that knocked the deceased down. lie was about 200 yards away when he first observed the deceased and his companions on the I urry. It would take from two to three minutes to reach them at the rate he was driv- ine—from 30 to 35 miles an hour. When the train was two or three yards from them witness saw the deceased step from the side of the lorry right in front of the train. 'En summing up, the Coroner said that the evidence pointed to the fact that in a moment .f pre-occupation the , deceased stepped in front of the train, although he must have known of its' near approach. There was nothing to make them presume that he met his death by his own in- tention, or that it was caused by anyone else. Mr Jenkins ; was present on behalf of the relatives of the deceased, but they were not trying an action at law for damages. If any claim for compensation was raised, it would have to be • made at the proper source. Their verdict would not in the ; slightest degree influence a County Court judge in such , an action.—The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental Death."

A FATAL FALL. On Monday evening, a labourer named Thomas Hedge- cock,aged 42, employed at Howley Quay, and residing at 2, Green's Gate, off Church-street, met with a fatal accident at Howley Quay under singular and distressing circum- stances. The deceased appears to have been engaged in unloading spelter from the flat Hercules until noon on Mon- day, when he went home to dinner. He returned shortly after two o'clock the worse for liquor, and the foreman, William Mason, said in consequence that he should not require him to work. The deceased then went on the fiat, and when there he fell head first into the hold amongst the spelter, cutting his head very severely. He was at once conveyed home on a lorry, and attended by Drs. Joseph and Smith, but he died from hie injuries the same evening. Mr Husband deputy coroner, held an inquiry into the cir- cumstances of the death at the Parade-room at the police- station, Warrington, on Wednesday afternoon, when the fol- lowing evidence was taken :—Joseph fledgecock, Irlam- street, Warrington, said that the deceased was his brother. Witness went to his brother's house on Monday and saw him lying on the sofa; he had been hurt about the head and WAS cut. He was unconscious. Drs Smith and Joseph were in attendincs upon him, and witness remained with him nearly all the time until his death. William Masan, Howley Quay, a foreman under the Bridgewater Navigation Company, deposed that on Monday morning the deceased, who bad worked for him some,years, was work- ing until noon, when he appeared in good health and sober. Deceased went to his dinner and returned a few minutes after two o'clock. He appeared to have had a drop of drink and witness told him that he must not remain to work that afternoon. Deceased loitered about for a while and witness saw him on a flat a few minutes afterwards, but he was only sitting there speaking to some of the men. About twenty minutes afterwards witness was called to the flat and found that the deceased had fallen into the bold of the fiat. He was got out and was conveyed home on a lurry. The de- ceased bled very much from the head. The flat belonged to the Navigation Company.—William Shaw, of Corbett's- buildings, Hulme, Manchester, a labourer on the flat Her- cules, said that on Monday the flat was lying at Howley- quay, being half laden with spelter. Deceased came on board the Hercules about 2-30. The fore hatch was closed, but the remainder of the flat was open. Deceased sat beside witness on the hatches at the fore side of the boat talking for about ten minutia Deceased had had a little to drink but not very much. He knew what he was doing. Witness got up from his seat to go to the cabin to light the fire, leaving deceased sitting near the batches, and directly after- wards heard a fall. Witness looked down the hold and saw deceased lying with his head on the spelter and his legs in an upright position. Witness had no doubt that the fall was accidental. The jury returned a verdict of "accidental death."

div.head: NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, HORTICULTURE, &c.
div.p: NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, HORTI- CULTURE, &c.

Mr. J. A. Perry, of Wilmington, Illinois, has bought a large number of Hereford cattle, males and females, for the States. There is at present quite a run on this breed of cattle, and the prices have consequently advanced consider- ably. YORKSHIRE PIGS FOR THE PESTS! MARKET.—An Aus- trian gentleman, an extensive breeder and importer of pedi- gree stock, has decided to fprm a herd of pure bred York- shire pigs for the purpose of supplying the Penh market with porkers of about 1001bs. weight. There appears to be a great demand for pigs of this weight, possessing a large amount of lean meat.

ADULTERATING Hoerev.--A Bee-keepers' Conference, pro- moted by the British Bee-keepers' Association, and held at the Health Exhibition, has, declared that honey is largely adulterated. It was shown how to distinguish genuine from factory made honey. A curious statement was made by Dr. Otto Helmer. To collect one pound of sugar 62,500 heads of clover would have to be rifled, and 3,750,000 vieits by bees would have to be paid. The expediency was urged of a systematic exposure of adulteration, and of opening markets with published prices of honey produced by British bee-keepers. AN IMMENSE RANCHE SALE—Mr. J. P. Lawson, of Den- ver, has just sold to a syndicate of English and Scotch gentlemen an immense tract of country, in Old Mexico. The price realised was 1,000,000 dole., and the area of the coun- try sold was larger than some of the New England States. The possessions are situated in the States of Chihuahua and Durango, in the Republic of Old Mexico. Among the pur- chasers are—C. Macpherson Grant, Lord Tweedmouth, J. Daziel, and Messrs. Cran, Bruce, and others. The company intend stocking the land with the finest and best breeds of English and Scotch horses and cattle, and the land will be cultivated by skilled workmen with the best modern ma- chinery. HERD-BOOK FOR HIGHLAND CATTLE.-4 meeting of breeders of Highland cattle was held in the show-yard of the Highland and Agricultural Society on Thursday, to consider a proposal for the establishment of a Highland Cattle Herd book. The Earl of Dunmore presided, and urged the necessity for establishing a herd-book for this fine old breed of cattle. On the motion of the Chairman, a Society, to be called the Highland Cattle Society of Scot- land, was formed, its object being to maintain the parity of the breed of Highland cattle and eqabliah a herd-book. 'The following rates of subscrtetion were agreed to :—Life mem- bers—proprietors, £lO .1.05.; and tenant.farmers, £5 55.; ordinary members, 103. ENSILAGE.—Mr. G. Fry; P.L.S., writing on ensilage, says: —"A practical experiment can easily be made to satisfy us that our cattle are aware that as soon as grass is mown a change in its constituents begins to take place. We all , know that, if cattle are grazing a meadow, the spots where manure has previously fallen and where consequently the herbage grows more rank and course than in the other parts of the pasture, are avoided by the cattle ; they will graze bare the other parts and will leave the rank tufts untouched. Now if we send a labourer with a scythe to mow down the rank patches, the cattle will, in a few hours, leave their favourite food and will eagerly devour that which they be- fore despised. The explanation cannot be that they prefer withered or partially-dried toed to the fresh gos.ss. A change has taken place in the mown grass which makes it more palatable then it was before! The silo presents a more favourable means of studying this ferment %Von than the hayfield and the rick, because the complication caused by the drying is avoided." ADULTERATED DAIRY PRODUCTS.—Here is a fact, taken from an American contemporary, which may be useful to Canon Begot in the campaign he has undertaken against the sale of adulterated dairy products:—" Some time ago found one of my fat hogs dying. Did not know what was the matter with it, but I dressed it and rendered it into lard or grease and shipped it to Chicago, and wrote a card to my commission merchant that I had sent him a tub of grease, and did not call it lard. In about two weeks my returns came thus: "One tub butter grease, 60 pounds at 7 cents." Commenting on this disgraceful revelation, The Farm, Field, and Fireside of Chicago says :—" The farmer shipped the grease to Chicago without any intention of selling it as anything else, bat it was purchased as batter grease to enter into the compound of some imitation 'gilt edge,' and to be eaten by those who would shudder at such an action knowingly. Is it possible that we, as a people who select our own rulers and enact our own laws, tolerate such ' bust • ness' as the above, in which hundreds of innocent persons may be poisoned in order to add a few dollars to some scoun- drel's pocket?" THE AGRICULTURAL HOLDINGS ACT, 1883.—A Westmor- land paper reports that the first claim under this Act in that county is now under consideration. Mr. W. Atkinson, late of Burnside Hall, now of Overthwaite, whose former farm has been repeatedly successful in farm competitions, and whose management of it was praised in Mr. Little's account of the prize farms at Carlisle, claims from his former land- lord £129 10s. Id., being part of an expenditure of £516 13s. 7d., on lime, cattle foods, straw, and manures. The claim has been heard before Mr. W. Little, agent to the Earl of Lonsdale, as umpire Mr. Holme being referee for the tenant, and Mr. Panchen; referee for the landlord. The farm consisted of about 600 acres of land, of which 135 acres were meadow land, 110 pasture land, and 96 arable. To show generally the way in which he worked the land, Mr. Atkinson in 1869 won the second prize for the best managed farm at the Kendal Agricultural Show, and in the following year, 1870, he also took the second prize for the best managed farm. In 1871 he carried off the first prize. In 1878 he again competed, and again took the first prize, and when the Royal Agricultural Society held its show at Carlisle Mr. Atkinson took third prize for the best-managed farm, competing with many wellknown men in the district. Mr. Atkinson in 1883 again took first prize at Kendal, and the report which was drawn up by Mr. Little on the occa- sion of the Royal Agricultural Show, showed that this farm had been managed in a way that was most advantageous to the tenant and also to the landlord. The answer to Mr. Atkinson's claim appears to depend on a contested interpre- tation of the Act, and net upon any question of Mr. Atkin- son's good management. One witness, by agreement, was called on each side, and the umpire will give his award in a few days. NOTES ON 'THE SHIRE Houses.—At the last meeting of , this society, in the Shrewsbury showyarda Mr. Walter Gil- bey, in the absence of Mr. P. A. Muntz, M.P., proposed the following resolution, viz.:—" That qualification No. 3 for mares foaled in 1880 or previously, shall be the same in Vol. 6 as in Vol. s,—viz ,—' That she or her progeny have gained a prize as a' Shire' or English cart horse, at one of the chief agricultural shows in the kingdom,' and not only at the London show or any meeting held by the Royal Agricultural Society of England, as the amended qualifica- tion stands at present." This was seconded by Mr. John E. Bennett, and discussed at some length, whereupon the Hon. E. Coke propoeed as an amendment the insertion of the words "the progeny not being less than a year old" after the word " progeny " in the resolution. This was seconded by Lord Egerton (of Tatton), and accepted as a compromise, and Mr. Mantz's resolution withdrawn in its favour. This being pat to the meeting was carried by 6to 5, whereupon the chairman submitted the original motion as amended, when the voting was 5 to 6, thus leaving the conditions of the entry for Vol. 6 the same as recommended by the Editing Committee on April Ist, and which have been communicated to members on the forms of entry.— Messrs. W. Thompson and Son, of Mayville, Missouri, shipped on the 17th inst., per the Beaver Line steamer Lake Huron, 11 Shire stallions selected in Lancashire and Derbyshire, and one Norman horse. The Shires comprise two three year-olds, Happy Jack, by Royalist and Prince, by Prince of the Isles 2nd; five two-year-olds, by Cardinal, What's Wanted, Cromwell, England's Glory, and Pride; and four yearlings, by Stanley, Cardinal, Prince of the Isles 2nd, and Noah. All are registered in the Stud book. They have been carefully selected, and some very promising youngsters are included. SOFT CHEESE AND PRESERVED BUTTER.—A Manchester Guardian correspondent writes :—The following Otte is a good example of what can be done by a small dairy-farmer. Having repeatedly, both in these columns and in lectures upon the subject, advocated a system of soft cheese-making as a profitable means of utilising skim and new milk, I was glad to be informed by a member of my audience at a recent agricultural meeting that he had for a whole year adopted the system alluded to, which he first became interested in at the last London Dairy Show. Be commenced by con- verting surplus cream, when butter was low in price, into curd and thence into cheeses; but although it paid him very well be thought that he might turn out an almost equally good cheese by mixing new milk and cream instead of giving whole cream. He therefore mixed two parts of new milk to one part of sour cream in a sheet which was stretched over a large vat. When poured into the sheet the mixture was thoroughly well amalgamated, and the sides of the sheet continually scraped to permit of proper drainage. After a time the solid matters were transferred to a clean sheet and tied with a string, the mass being then enveloped in addi- tional dry cloths, and a weight placed upon the whole to farther express the whey. When sufficiently solid, the curd was put into a hole in the ground just as it was, and left until required for use. In this way the whole thing can be controlled, for the curd will keep a consider- able time, and he finds that when the demand for his cheeses is large he can se qd them straight off; but when it is the reverse he can eithermake a smeller quantity or pre- serve them in the ground. The trouble is very slight, no rennet is required, and the curd is simply placed in moulds, and comes out as rich, or nearly so, as a whole cream cheese, which is saying a great deal. This individual sometimes makes two hundred a day. They are not sent to Shops, but retailed about the country, selling at a shilling each; three- pence of which goes to the retailer. In this way he finds that he can obtain 50 per cent, more for his milk than bt the manufacture of butter. I was glad to hear, after hav- ing advised those present never to Fell their fresh butter when at a low price (for it appears it had been as low as Bd. a pound). but to pot it until winter, that the farmer alluded to had practised this system, and had obtained Is. sd. per pound daring the past ten days for butter which he had potted in May, when it was at 81. It is perfectly trae that British buttermakers are the worat marketers in the world, and that instead of holding their produce and preserving it with care they force it upon the market, whatever the price may be, and then grumble at the result.

div.p: SEA.SONABLE HINTS.

Breeders of poultry should now begin to think about the future. Many will have already planned the composition of next year's breeding pen., and it is therefore wise in look- ing over the young stock, to select a few of the most likely looking cockerels for stock birds, and send these away to different parts of the farm, or even to runs on other places where they can have freedom, and put on that size and stamina which are so important in breeding stock. It is as well to have twice the number of cockerels so reserved than will be actually required, for accidents often happen when least expected, and birds do not always turn out in accord- ance with the views of their owner , so that it is best to be on the safe side, or disappointment may be the result.

div.head: RAILWAY FATALITY AT THELWALL.
div.p: RAILWAY FATALITY AT THELWALL.

Mr. T. J. Ridgway, coroner, held an ir;;;;;;;—Viednes: day morning, at the house ef Mr. Wright, the Pickering Arms, Thelwall, near Warrington, touching the death of a married woman named Louisa Ditcbfield, 53 years of age, who was killed by being run over by a train at Thelwall Station, on Monday evening.—Thomas Ditchfield, farmer, Thelwall, identified the body as that of his wife, who, he sad, left home about 8 30 on Saturday evening.—Thomas Jenks,6, Percy.street, Warrington, engine driver in the em- ploy of the London and North-Western Railway Co., said that on Monday evening he was working the light engine, No. 1792, from Timperley to Warrington. He ran through to Warrington, arriving at Arpley about 10-55. He noticed nothing unusual on the jaurney, or when he examined his engine in the shed afterwards. It would be about 10.46 when he went through Thelwall Station. and he saw a pas- senger train for Manchester standing in the station. He whistled as be went through. On examining his engine cn the following morning he found a boot at the back of the tender draw bar spring.—Mary Ellen Bowers Warburton, wife of a Heatley farmer, said that she was walking towards Thelwall Station in company with the deceased on the evening in question when they saw a person named Henry Moston, who was not quite sober. The deceased said that she must see him to the train, and they all proceeded to the station, both deceased and witness being quite sober. When they reached the platform the Lymm train was just drawing up, and deceased, speaking to witness and Moston, said, "Do not come in front of the engine, he may get killed." She also said" Let us go down here," meaning the end of the platform, "and cross behind the train." De- ceased went on to the line, turned round, and called to witness to come along. Witness was going on to the line when Moston said "Come beck, here's the express." Wit- ness stopped, and she saw the deceased turn her head, but the train came up, and, she though, the buffer caught de- ceased and knocked her down, killing her instantaneously. —Henry Moston, fustian cutter, Lymm, gave corroborative evid nce.—A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.

A train stopped at a station on a Texas railroad where a gang of workmen were digging a trench. A lady passen- ger, stepping to the station platform, asked one of the labourers what he was digging for. "For a dollar and a q'arter a day, mum," said he. The "'Judas Tree" received that name from the tradition that it was upon a specimen of this tree (the Cercis Sili- quastrum), near Jerusalem, that the betrayer of our Saviour hanged himself. It is very beautiful in all its stages. Very early in spring, flowers of a bright pale red burst out before any leaf appears, not only from every part of the branches, but from the trunk, piercing the thick, strong bark nearly down to the root in a very remarkable manner. These flowers or buds are gathered and used with other raw vegetables by the Greeks and Turks in salads. William Prudence, for embezzling large sums of moneY received hv him as clerk to the Liverpool Court of Passage, was at Liverpool, on Tuesday, sentenced to five years' penal servitude.

I can read writ' jog, even yours; and I don't want to be insulted by mile' tions on my education."

Mn. STANLEY AND GENERAL GORDON.—In an intervievf Mr. Stanley has freely discussed General Gordon's position, which he does not seem to think at all perilous. Mr. Stan' ley goes so far as to say that Gordon needs no help froln England, but is able to hold his own against the Mandi or to retire from Khartoum, defeating any resistance by, tbe way. "The Mandi," says Mr. Stanley," has no torpedo wherewith to blow up Gordan's steamers, and. it seems be, has no artillery. And even supposing his followers ban rifles, bows, and arrows, and the like, he could easily do what I did in 1877, when after every fight I collected the shields of my slain enemies, and ranged them round the gunwales of my canoes so as to form parapets. My canoes were only a foot or so out of the water; but with the long shields ranged round them they looked big and formidable. Gordon is a man full of resources, full of energy, and awn fall of genius." THE CONFERENCE ON EGYPT.—At the sitting held on Saturday, as England and Franca differed beyond hope of agreement, the Conference was adjourned sine die.-4* Waddington began by proposing that the new loin should be made a part of the privileged debt, that the second charge should ha on the ordinary debt, the third charge, that of 5' ministration and any surplus to be then given to the Egli)" tian Government, all sinking funds to be suspended for three years, and all deficits to be brought to the knowledge of the Commission of the Debt which, in concert with the Egyptian Government, should take means to cover it, btl no reduction of interest to take place without unaniml among the commissioners. the Conference to meet anew ID, time for the Budget of 1838. This proposal was rejected by Lord Granville as short-sighted, and he declared that he could not agree to give the Commissioners of the Debt a preponderance over the Government and the aff iirs of Egypt, adding, " We are then obliged with great regret V, declare that we have not been able to find in this Confer- ence a satisfactory basis for the arrangement of the financial affairs of Egypt." M. Waddington proposed to adjourn t,° October 20h, when Parliament would probably meet in tine country and in France. But Lord Granville replied that be could not wait till that date to take the necessary measur.eg in Egypt. To fix a date would be to tie our hands, while to adjourn sine die would leave us free to do what re thought best for the good of Egypt. M. Waddington twine demanded that the President should put to the vote his pro- posal to meet again on Oc'olJer 22nd. This Lord GranVlll° flatly refused, but said that another conference might be called after an exchange of views between the various Go: vernments. M. Waddington proposed to lay before the P 913 ference a proposition for the regulation of the indemnities: Lord Granville refused. M. Waddington submitted his Fr°, I int formally to the Conference. Lord Granville said • "As we have agreed to adjourn the Conference, we are. 0°... longer in a posion to discuss this question." M. Waddlegd • ton declared that it was a question of humanity. L°Yl Granville retorted that it was also eminently a financia, question. Then M. Waddington said: " I must protesaL: The President refuses me the right to speak. I repeat this is a question in which we are all interested, and whlsu. we can separate from the flnanci 1 question." Lord vine said he could easily repy to the arguments of French plenipotentiary if debate were not already exclude!' M. Waddington declared that under theta circumstances ne. could only lay his project on the table of the Conferenh_c:. In answer to Count Munster, Lord Granville announced t the Conference stood adjourned sine die.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Seronnev. The House met at twelve o'clock. SUPPLY.—The House then went into Committee of Sup- ply on the Civil Service estimates, commencing with the discussion of the vote for the Irish Constabulary. The vote W& s debated at some length by Mr. O'Sullivan, Mr. Dawson, Mr. Marum, and a number of other Irish members; strongly condemning the manner in which extra police were em- Ployed in Ireland.—Mr. TREVELYAN replied on behalf of the Government, stating that the charge per head for police Sri Ireland was only 7d, as against Is 6.1 in England, and Is Id in Scotland. THE CONFERENCE —Mr. GLADSTONE made a statement With respect to the Conference. He regretted to state that the Conference had separated that day without having effected the object for which it was called together, namely, the adoption by European authority of a plan for dealing With the financial difficulties of Egypt. There were three Principal points laid before the Conference, namely, the Prospective charges for the Government of Egypt, the necessity of a lean to meet the immediate wants, and the Prospective revenue of Egypt if the loan was to cover the indemnities for the incendiarism at Alexandria. The amount required would be eight millions, excluding these indemnities four millions. Her Majesty's Government re- quired that this loan should be a first charge, and that due

Provision should be made for the just but firm government Of Egypt, but difficulties arose between Her Majesty's Government and the Government of France, which refused to agree to any reduction of the interest under the law of liquidation. Her Majesty's Government submitted a plan LO meet the prospective charges on the revenue of Egypt. 1- The preference debt of eight millions, four and a half Millions being advanced in cash. 2. The interest on the other debts to be reduced by a half percent. 3. An allow- ance of five and a half millions for the expenses of the Government. 4. The payment Of the reduced half per cent. This plan win to be tried for three years, but the French Government insisted upon the charges beihg fixed as fol- lows :-1. The loan and privileged debt. 2. The Unified Debt with full dividends. 3. The expenses of administra- tion. 4. Any surplus to be wholly at the disposal of the Government of Egypt. Moreover, every question was to be referred to the Commission of the Caisse, and their decision Must be unanimous or the matter referred to the Powers of Europe. Her Majesty's Government objected to this plan, especially if the object of the Conference was to place everything at the power of a hostile tribunal, and give it the complete mastery over the affairs of Egypt. Her Majesty's Government was supported by Italy and Turkey, but as France would not agree, Germany, Austria, and Prussia declined to vote. The Conference had, therefore, adjourned without a day being named for meeting again. I He would not now go into the heavy responsibilities cast on Her Majesty's Government, The Anglo-French agreement Was in abeyance, and pipers would be presented on Monday. "—Replying to Sir S. Northcote, Mr. CiLADSTONE said the Government would have no proposals to submit on the sub- iect of Egypt during the remainder of the present session. The matter then dropped, and the report of Supply being agreed to, The House adjourned at 8-10 o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY. •

The Lord -Chancellor took his seat on tha woolsack at a quarter past four o'clock. THE CONFERENCE —Earl GRANVILLE made a statement respecting the Conference wisich, with some addition of de- tail, was identical in purport with that made in the Rouse of Commons on Saturday by the Prime Minister. The MAR- IS of SALISBURY congratulated the Government of Egypt 11130 n the failure of the Conference. Several Bills were ad- l'anced a stage, and at twenty minutes past six their lord- -BhiPs adjourned.

THE GOVERNMENT POLICY IN EGYPT.—Sir S. NORTH.. Itaittelot a little later, the PREMIER announced that next Y he would propose a Vote of Credit to undertake the re- "et of General Gordon should an evpedition become neces- -47, and to make certain preliminary preparations.—Vari- °he efforts were made to draw from the Prime Minister a statement as to the details of "the important step" projected and the amount of the Vote of Credit. EARL Norcranaooa's Mtssrog.—Earl GRANVILLE an- nounced that Lord Northbrook had been appointed to pro- ceed to Egypt to report and advise her Majesty's Govern- Tent as to what counsel they should offer to the Egyptian Oovernment upon the present situation of affairs in Egypt and as to the measure which should be taken by the Govern- !ll.ent. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—ThESDAY. The Speaker took the chair shortly before four o'clock. LORD NORTHBRO ,K'S MISSION.—QtIeStiOLIS, which were v.Otnisually few in numher, were disposed of shortly after :alt-Past four.—The Pi ime Miniater had not yet arrived, zral On the suggestion of the Marquis of HARTINGTON the Peaker temporarily left the chair. Whilst Lord Harting- ;ern was speaking the cry was raised He is coming." But 'oe arrival turned oat to be that of Sir Thomas M'Clure, Whe was greeted with an enthusiasm which greatly be- him. The Speaker had not got further than the (Igor when he was ,net by the Premier, who took his seat °P. the Treasury bench, the Speaker, amid laughter and cheers, resuming the chair.—The PREMIER, rising in a B°lnewhat breathless state, chiefly read from manuscript a C.tatement identical with that inude in the other House by ;Earl Granville with re.pect to the despatch of Lord North- took to Egypt. In reply to questions put by Sir Stafford aorthcote, Sir Henry Wolff, Mr. Cowen, and Mr. Balfour, te added that there would be no change in the tenure of ertl Northbrook's office at the Admiralty, his absence in gyPt being of a temporary character. He would interfere IVoith the position of Sir Evelyn Baring no more then Lord offerin interfered with the Consul-General. Lord North- would not gO with any special instructions, being a raernber of the Cabinet, and therefore fully informed of the views of his colleagues. PROPOSED GORDON EXPEDITION.—The House then went into committee, and the Premier moved a vote of Credit for Z 300,000 for the charges of a possible expedition to relieve General Gordon. In the course of a brief speech the Pre- Mier referred to and quoted the pledges given by the Go- Vernment, notably by Lord Hartingten, with respect to the relief of General Gordon. He dwelt upon the difficulty of comthunication with thi General, which had existed over a Period of four months, and quoted varbas telegrams con- eying such information as was accessible, and which went "" chow that the cmtingencv set forth in Lord Hartington's etatement upon which the Government were immediately Pledged to act, had not vet arisen. He did not believe that tPeriod of personal danger to General Gordon had arrived, wur they had now reached a time when Parliament °a about to be prorogued, and if during the iZcese the contingency did arise, the Government wtOyglet it beet to propose a Vote of Credit t, lel), whilst its granting would indicate the sanction of :filament for their acts, would enable them to proceed tairhout delay. In this connection the Prime Minister, veaning to refer to the Vote of Credit, alluded to it as "the Ole of Censure," at which there was much laughter. He for the slip, explaining that whilst a Note of ; cedit was a phrase unfamiliar to his lips, Ee was exceed- elY familiar with a Vote of Censure.—Mr Loam:THERE jilo)P°sed the aNt-., questioning whether the country was t4ld to send an army to bring back Gordon, their being thing more easy for him than to come away without such abo 'Mr Borax); on the pert of the Opposition, cordially sup- wiled the vote, whilst expressing the opinion that the Go- (i.rement bad "committed an act of folly" in sending L„Tefal Gordon on his mission.—Sir W LAWSON joined Mr „foottebere in OppoSirion to the vote ; whilst Mr FORSTER, 4"liPoorting the vote, expressed the opinion that the proposal v`..'elild have been submitted some weeks ago.—On a division 1, vote was carried by 174 against 14. 7nPLyh..--The Civil Service Estimates were then proceeded Some discussion afterwards took place on the Irish 54w., 001 inspectars' and the vote -was agreed to, as were also for Irish National School leachers' superannuation :"Ce• Eleven other votes were agreed to, and progress was • %Ported.
