div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS..-WEDNESDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS..-WEDNESDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at half-past twelve. New writs were issued for Ross and Cromarty, in the room of Sir A. Matheson, resigned, and for South Devon, in the room of Mr. J. Carpenter-Gamier, resigned. EDUCATION IN IRELAND.—In Committee of Supply, Mr. PARNELL raised a debate on University Education in Ire- land, and moved the rejection of the whole of the vote for ,the Qaeen's Colleges. He urged that the amount hitherto voted should be aided to the endowment of the Royal Uni- I versity. Mr. COURTNEY, speaking for the Government. said it had been determined to wait for further development of opinion before deciding to sanction any change in the ex- isting system. Lord R. CHURCHILL advocated the subsi- dising of all religious bodies in Ireland. Upon a division, the vote was agreed to by 100 to 35. The House adjourned at five minutes to six. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THIIRSDAY.

The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at 25 minutes past four o'clock. LORD NORTHBROOK, &C.—The Foreign Secretary was questioned as to the powers to be conferred on Lord North- brook as High Commissioner.—Earl GRANVILLE'S reply was that papers were being drafted, and that as soon as they had been approved by the Queen and had received the sign manual they would be presented to Parliament before the prorogition. He added that the Government of the Sultan had already been communicated with on the subject. The noble Earl in- formed Lord Harrowby that a treaty had been signed for the purpose of renewing diplomatic relations with Mexico on conditions honourable to both countries, and for the purpose of negotiating a treaty of commerce.—The Royal I assent was given by Commission to 56 public and private I bills.
Their lordships rose at 20 soin,ites to six o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS:I—THURSDAY.. ,

----- The Speaker took the chair shortly 'before four o'clock. QUESTIONS, ..tc —Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE stated that after consultation with his friends, he found that the gene- ral convenience would be consulted if he raised the debate on Egyptian affairs on a stage of the Appropriation Bill on Monday. Mr. GLADSTONE said the Appropriation Bill should stand first in order for that purpose. LOBI CLAUD Hemm- TON asked the President of the Board of Trade if he could now name the gentlemen who are to compose the royal commission with regard to merchant ship- ping. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN said he would make a statement to the effect desired before ' the House prorogued, but he was not in a position to do so now. —ln Committee of Supply on the Civil Service ervimates, Mr FAWCETT, when the vote for the Post•office and Fele- graph Service was under consideration, stated that the Government had come to the conclusion to relax some of the conditions of the licenses imposed on the telephone companies, and he explained the character of the modifica- tions that would be made. _
The Lords' amendments to the Trusts (Scotland) Bill were agreed to. .. _ .
The House adjourned at two o'clock.

div.head: FOREIGN NEWS.
div.p: FOREIGN NEWS.
EGYPC AND THE SOUDAN. GORDON AND THE REBELS.-MAJOR KITCHENER

AT DONGOLA. AS.SOIJAN, SIINDAY.—A merchant who escaped from Ber- ber arrived here yesterday. He states that Berber was stor- med by Bishareen rebels on June fOr, after severe fighting on botb sides, in which many were killed. The rebels have constrected a wall to the south side of Berber as a protection against attacks from General Gordon, who had captured several of their boats laden with provisions by means of his war steamers.

I CAIRO. SUNDAY—Major Wortley has successfully accom- plished his recognaistoce to Seimeh. He reports that he found very little water or fodder on the way, and be is of opinion that it is quite impossible for a hostile force to ad- vance on Assouan from the south by this route. Major Kit- chener arrived at Dongola on the evening of August Ist, and was well received by the Mudir, who showed him a letter in Arabic signed and sealed by General Gordon. This letter is to be sent on by post. Major Kitchener reports that he was favourably imDressed by the Mvdir, who declares that with 7,000 men he would undertake to relieve Gordon and re-open the whole of the Soudan. He begged Major Kit- chener to make his entry into the town in Arab costume. He also said that it would be better for no one else to come to Doagola, unless he brought with him a strong force. Standard. _ .

CAIRO, MONDAY. Several telegrams signed Kitchener have arrived to-day from Dongola confirming yesterday's news, and stating that at the invitation of the Governor he accompanied him to Debbeh to view the field of battle there two weeks ago, and thus convincina himself of the truth of the Governor's statement. Major Kitchener urges that rein- forcements should be despatched at once to Dona°la, as the Governor declares that with 3,000 men he will deliver Khar- tourn.—Daily Telegraph. ADEN, SATURDAY. Otliniel Orders have been given to bold a British expeditionary force of 300 men in readiness to reinforce the Egyptian garrison at Zeliah.

div.head: GENERAL GORDON'S LETTER.
div.p: GENERAL GORDON'S LETTER.

CAIRO, WEDNESDAY.—Major Kitchener telegraphs from Dongola that General Gofdon's letter to the Mudir may be briefly summarised as follows :—After stating that Khar- toum and Senaar still hold out, General Gordon says-- "The bearer will give you my news on his arrival. Give him any news you have as to the place to which the expe- dition from Cairo is coaling, together with its numbers. We have 8,000 soldiers." The letter, which.is written in Arabic, is dated the 28th of Shahan. The Major says that General Gordon, Colonel Stewart, and Mr. Power are all well.

Judgment has been delivered by the Court-martial held on the Turkish soldiers who recently mutinied at Assiout. Eight of the prisoners were sentenced to death and two were shot at Abassiyeh this morning. The death sentences on the remaining six have been commuted to penal servi ude for life. Another mutineer was condemned to pens' ervitude for 14 years. 1 AssonAN, WEDNE4DLY Nomq.—One hundred and seventy men of the first battalion of the Royal Sussex Regiment are expected to arrive here tomorrow. The presence of British troops on the Nile is exercising a good effect upon the Sheikhs of the Bishareen tribe attending the meeting near Eisneh.

div.head: CHOLERA.
div.p: THE CHOLERA.

MARSEILLES, SATURDAY, 8 30 p.m.—The official bulletin , gives the number of deaths during the last twenty-four bolus at forty-six, of which sixteen were of cholera.—Sunday. —The deaths have been fifty, of which fifteen were from cholera---Mondav, 9 p.m.—The number of deaths to-day has been forty-nine, of which twenty-eight are due to cholera, the resulvf the excesses of Sunday. TOULON', SUNDAY. 10 a.m.—One death from cholera oc- curred last night in the suburbs. Every day the number of persons returning to Toulon increases, and the town has almost resumed its wonted aspect.---0 p.m.—Ten deaths from cholera to-day. Thirty cases in the Bon Rencontre Hospital. TOULON, MONDAY, 10-5 a.m.—There were four deaths from cholera here last niLffit.-8-28 p.m.—There have been no deaths from cholera here to-day. One death has occurred at La Seyne, end two at Montfort-sur-Argens. ARLES, SATURDAY.—Four deaths from cholera have oc- curred here since yesterday. ROME, SUNDAY.—A. case of cholera has occurred ht the village of Lombriasco, in the district of Pinerolo. Several cases are reported from Vignarolo. MARSEILLES, TUESDAY.—Three deaths recurred here from cholera last night. Large numbers of fugitives are return- ing. BERNE, MONDAY NIGHT.—Four deaths from cholera are: reported at Alessandria, Turin, and Genoa. An undoubted case is reported at Geneva. TOULON, TUESDAY NIGHT.—Two deaths from cholera oC- carred in the suburbs last night. THE FRENCH ,REVISION CONGRESS.—EXCITED SITTING.

VERSAILLES, MONDAY.--LlThe-de-ogress of the two Houses met here at one o'clock this afternoon. M. Is Royer, Presi- dent, proposed the adoption of the Standing Orders in force during the National Assembly of 1871. at Bourdeaux, with certain amendments. This proposal was received with vio- lent interruptions from both the Right and Left, but, after a scene of considerable tumult, was agreed to. M. Jules Ferry then ascended the tribune in order to introduce the bill for the revision of the Constitution. M. Audreiux and other members protested against this course, as being in opposition to the standing order, which prescribes that the election by ballot of the Bureaux shall first be proceeded with. M. , Andrieux then also entered the tribune, and several deputies rose from their seats and formed a semi-circle round it. A scene of great excitement ensued, in the midst of which the President put on his hat and suspended the sitting.-- Evening—On the sitting of the Congress being resumed, the President announced that the Bureaux would be drawn for by lot. After this had been done, M. Ferry introduced the Revision Bill. M. Testelin made a proposal that the bill should be referred to a committee of thirty members elected by serutin de liste, which was agreed to. M. Ferry demanded urgency, which was adopted. VERSAILLES, WEDNESDAY.—The Committee on the Revi- sion Bill, acting in accord with M. Ferry has accepted the amendment of M. Andrieux declaring the ineligibility of all Monarchial pretenders as candidates for the Presidency of the Republic. The Committee has either set aside or postponed the consideration of all other amendments. FRANCE AND CRINA.—RUPTURE OF NEGOTIATIONS.

_ The Standard is in a position to state tbat the negotia- tions between France and China which were proceeding at Shanghai between the Viceroy of Nankin and thh French Plenipotentiary were definitely broken off on Sunday. Pasts, SITURDAY.—A Yellow Book on Tonqnin affairs was distributed among the members of the C.hanaber of Deputies this morning. France at first demanded 250,000,0001 as indemnity for the Langson affair, but in consequence of the publication of a decree ordering the with- drawal of the troops from Tonquin. only asked China to ac- cede in principle to an indemnity based upon the compen- sation to be awarded to the French soldiers who had been wounded and the families of those killed, and upon the sup- plementary military expenses caused to France by the Chinese attack. _ _
PARIS, TrESDAY EVENING.—The Siecle this evening an- nounces that the squadron under Admiral Courbet has taken possession of the harbour and mines at Kelung, in For- mesa.

_ PARIS, WEDNESDAY EVENING—The Temps of this even- ing has reason to believe that the Cabinet has decided, not- withstanding the rupture of the negotiations, to postpone the adoption of any coercive measures towards China until

div.head: FITE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. AUGUST 9, 1884.
div.p: FITE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. AUGUST 9, 1884.

the termination of the debate on the Chinese question is the Chamber of Deputies, which will take place after the con- clusion of the Congress. The National states that Li Fong Pao conferred this morning with M. Jules Ferry, and adds that this would tend to show that the pour-parlers have not been absolutely broken off. The French Resident at Hue has received instructions to only recognise the new King of Annam should he agzee to accept all the clauses of the treaty concluded with M. Patenotre. _ _

WASHINGTON, THURSDAY. The Commander of the United States Asiitic squadron has been instructed to take measures for the protection of American citizens in China in the event of outbreak of hostilities between that country and France. _
RAINHILL.

FIRE AT THE VICTORIA BOTEL.—OR Monday morning a fire occurred at the Victoria Hotel through the carelessness of a visitor, who fired the parlour curtains with a partly extinguished match. Damage to the amount of several pounds was caused to the furniture, by fire and water, before the fire was extinguished. ODDFELLOWS' DINNER. —OR Saturday afternoon the members of the Loyal Prince Alfred Lodge of Oddfellows, Prescot District, Manchester Unity, held a demonstration at Rainhill, meeting at three o'clock and partaking of a sub- stantial dinner at the lodge-house, the Coach and Horses Inn. About 50 sat down. Subsequently the members marched in precession through the village, headed by a band, and visited the flower show then being held. In the evening a meeting was held at which it was stated that the lodge now numbered 100 members, being a gain of ten during the year. The increase for the year in funds Was about £35, after the payment of expenses. A very enjoy- able evening was spent, the usual toasts being honoured in a hearty manner.

div.head: GENERAL NEWS
div.p: GENERAL NEWS

The Great Western Railway dividend was on Tuesday an- nounced at the rate of five per cent. The London and North-Western Railway dividend for the past half-year will be at the rate of six per cent per annum. Miss Becker has sailed for Quebec in order to be present at the meeting of the British Association, which this year Mee'S at Montreal. Miss Tetlow, who was injured in the Penistone calamity, died on Wednesday night., This raises the number of deaths to twenty-four. SIX PERSONS DnowNßD.—Mr. Irving. solicitor, London, his three children, and two watermen, have been accident- ally drowned at Guernsey. The grand jury at Dublin have found time bills against Messrs Cornwall. French, and Surgeon-major Fernandez, for the felonious practices with which they are charged. THE CORRUPT BOROUGHS.—The bill authorising the continued suspension of the writs foe Boston, Canterbury, Chester, Gloucester, Macclesfield, Oxford, and Sandwich will, it is understood, be passed without opposition. LIBERAL GIFT.—The Ewing ,Gilmour Institute, the gift of Mr. Ewing Gilmour, of Croftangea, to the inhabitants of the Vale of Leven, was formally handed over for public use on Saturday. The institute will cost about £lO,OOO. THREE MURDERS AND TWO SUICIDES.—TWO women have been stabbed to death by their husbands in Landskron, Moravia. A neighbour whO tried to save the woman was killed by the murderers, who then committed suicide. A WOMAN CHARGED WITH MURDER —At Dover, OR Tuesday, Elizabeth Connor was committed for trial on a charge of stabbing a labourer, named William Ken- nett, upon whom she inflicted terrible wounds with a long knife.

On Tuesd4y night a man named Fletcher tried to murder a woman with whom he lived at Halifax, by cutting her throat. Afterwards he proceeded to a quiet corner of the public park and there cut his own throat. He died soon after being found, and the woman is in a dangerous condition.

CAPTAIN WEBB'S DEATH- The widow of Captain M Webb has had placed in Oakwood Cemetery, Niagra Falls, a handsome granite monument over the rem tins of her husband, who perished in the rapids of the 24th July. 1893. The monument, which stands Bft high, is of Gothic design. WIFE MURDER.-4 Derby mechanic named Payne is " wanted " for the murder of lakit,wife on Saturday night. He threw a lighted paraffin 4AO at the won' tn. whose clothes were set on fire, and she died on Wednesday from the injuries so caused. Payne has not since been seen in the neighbourhood. A PRISON MATRON MURDERED.—OR Tuesday, a female prisoner in Millbank Prison attacked the chief matron and murdered her by strangulation. The officials are very re- ticent, but it is said the deceased was endeavouring to pacify the prisoner, who was notoriously violent, when she was murdered. An investigation is being made. A voung woman named Perry was indicted at the Central Criminal Court, on Wednesday, for the murder of an in- fant, the child of her employer, at Uxbridge. The prisoner was annoyed because the child cried whilst it was in her charge, and she strangled it. The jury found her guilty of manslaughter, and sentence was deferred. A sailing ship, the Tarapaca, arrived in the Mersey on Wednesday from Marseilles, where she had shipped a fresh crew. On the passage home one man died, with decided cholera symptoms, and several other members of the crew had suffered from choleraic symptoms. The vessel has been disinfected and placed in quarantine in the river. MURDER OF Two CRILDREN.—A young married woman named Rippin was on Wednesday committed for trial by the Grantham magistrates for murdering her two children, aJed respectively three years and thirteen months. The - prisoner, after a dispute with her husband, appears to have deliberately drowned the children in a pond and then tried 0 drown herself, but failed. SUSPECTED MURDER —The body of a married woman named Harriet Dyson, who was living apart from her hus- band, was found dead under a haycock at Womwell, on Wednesday morning. It is supposed the deceased had come to her death by foul means. She had a severe cut on the forehead, and her hands and pockethandkerchief were covered with blood. The police are investigating the affair. MILITARY RIOT.—A serPous military riot occurred at Sevenoaks, on Wednesday evening, originating in an assault on a private of the Royal Marines, on Monday night, by some men of the Warwickshire Regiment. Last night the ill-feeling culminated in a serious encounter between the pickets and the Warwickshire men, 20 of whom are under arrest. A large force of pickets afterwards patrolled the town.

harsa MuRDER TRIAL.—A man tamed Patrick Finnigan, in whose case a Sligo jury "disagreed "a few days ago. was again put on trial, on Wednesday, for the murder of Peter Doherty, a small farmer who lived near Rissane House, in county Galway, on the estate of Mr Walter Bourke, who was also murdered. Doherty took a farm from which the previous tenant had been evicted, and the murder was clearly agrarian. Finnigan was found guilty and sentenced to death.

_ BOY WORRIED BY A. Hummon.—On Saturday a boy nulled Leadbeater, seven years of age, was walking down a Birmingham street, when a half-bred bull terrier bitch sud- denly caught him by the cheek, pulled him to the ground, and commenced to worry him. Mr James Hinks rushed to the lad's assistance, and dealt the-dog several blows on the head, the effect being that the animal was rendered insen- sible, still, however, retaining its grip on the lad's flesh. The dog was destroyed. The boy Vies in a very precarious condition.

_ ROBBI'MY awn DEA.TIT ON A Prgu.—While an elderly gentleman was promenading the West Pier at Brighton, on Monday, his watch was snatched away by a young man, who made off with it. The Piermaster secured the thief, and at the sane time the gentleman who had been robbed, and was in pursuit, fell exhausted. Medical aid was 'pro- cured, but death, attributed to heart disease, had taken place. A card on the dec.ased bore the name of "W. A. C. Tweedie, 22, Cavendish-road, Kentish-town." The man in custody gave the nam-t of John Wade, and said he resided at Hoxton.

SHOCKING TRAGEDY AT CHATHAM.—At the Engineers' Barracks, Chatham, shorty after six o'clock on Wednesday night, the sound of a discharge of fire-arms was heard by the sentry, who gave an alarm, and on search b-ing made in the rear of the officers' quarters, the dead body of a young woman named Statham, whose husband is groom to an officer, was found with the mark of a revolver bullet throu7gh her breast. A civilian servant. named Amos Chick, aged 47, who has been arrested, stated that he was cleaning the revolver, which ha thought to be unloaded, when it exploded, the bullet passing through the window at which the deceased was sitting at needlework. THE DUKE OF MARLBOROUGH'S PENSION—In the Chan- cery Division, on Saturday. before Vice-Chancellor Sir James Bacon, the question of the commutation of the Duke of Marl- borough's pension was heard. A short time ago the Vice-Chan- cellor was asked to sanction the arrangement which had been arrived at. His lordship suggested that he should have before him some evid lace that the whole of the members of the family approvcd of the arrangement. Mr. Stirling on behalf of the Treasury, now stated that the commutation had been approved of by all the members of the family, including Lord Randolph Churchill. Under theso circumstances, the Conrt e,,nli,ined the agreement which had been sanctioned by the Treasury. A SERVANT Linn TRACKING A THIEF.—At the Assizes at Chelmsford last week, on the trial of a man for stealing a watch and chain at a house at Southend, it appeared that he had put on "sand shoes," which are noiseless, and find- ing a street door left open, he quietly entered, went upstairs into the drawhag-room, and, seeing a gold watch and chain, he took it up and went off with it. He was, however, ob- served by the servant maid, who resolutely went out of Southend along the road, and meeting a young man, she told him her object and got him to go with her. The man walked on nearly three miles, and, probably finding that he was being followed, threw the watch and chain in'o a clump of bushes, where they were afterwards found. The prisoner was convicted, and Mr. Justice Denman then directed the girl to stand forward, telling them they should each receive £2, an announcement which gave great satisfaction. ANCIENT ORDER OF FORESTERS.—The jubilee meeting of the High Court of the Ancient Order of Foresters began on Monday in Manchester. The proceedings took place in the Free Trade Hall. where about 600 delegates assembled on Monday. The High Chief Ranger, Mr John Bowler, of Manchester, took the chair. Alderman J. Hopkinson (deputy Mayor of Manchester), the Mayor of Salford (Alderman Makinson), and the Mayor of Ashton (Alderman Walker) were present —The High Chief-Jtanger, in his addrese, wel- comed the delegates to the city, and spoke of the labours of the men mostly connected with Manchester, who in 1831 effected the reform of the Order and its re-establishment in its present form. That day they had some 609,000 Wm- berg, with courts scattered over the globe. Their initiations exceeded 1,000, per week.—The court adjourned early, and the delegates with members of the Order and kindred societies went in procession to the racecourse, where a gala was held.

THE ALLEGED DEFALCATIONS BY THE WIGAN BOROUGH ,TREASURER.--William Holt, late treasurer for the Corpora- tion of Wigan, who was apprehended on Friday evening, charged with the falsification of the borough accounts, was brought up in custody before this borough magistrates on Saturday. The warrant specified that he wilfully, and with intent to defraud, falsified the cashbooks by entering as haying paid several items, whereas he knew at the time that the said entries were false. The Bench remanded the pri- soner and agreed to accept satisfactory bail. Later, how- ever. Holt was again brought up and charged that, on the 9th February, 1883, he did receive for and on account of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses of Wigan £l5O from one Sarah Moss. which sum he did fraudulently and feloniously embezzle —Mr. T. Swarbrick,one of the burgess authorities of the Corporation, said he had seen the receipt from Holt for the mcney given to Mrs. Moss, and had ex- amined the treasurer's books, but could find no entry of the £l5O. Prisoner was tberenoon remanded on the second charge.—The Magistrates' Clerk said the magistrates had no option in the previous case but to grant bail; in this it was discretionary.—Holt: I will stand my ground; I will not go away.—Mr. Peace said he was instructed to obinct to the prisoner's admission to bail.—Holt : Oh, don't, Mr. Peace, you need not be afraid.—Dr. Roocroft (the presiding magis- trate) ; Holt, I must tell you that I am very reluctant to detain you, but in the face of the opinion of the Town Clerk I have no alternative but to refuse bail.—Holt was then taken beck to the cells.—On Wednesday Holt WAS further remanded on charges of embezzlement and falsification of accounts. It is stated that the prisoner's deficiencies, so far as ascertained, amount to over £5,000.

div.head: MR. H. STANLEY.
div.p: MR. H. STANLEY.

OSTEND, SIINDAY.—Mr Stanley, the African explorer, was received here yesterday afternoon by the King, in an audi- ence which lasted an hour and a half. At seven o'clock Mr Stanley, the Due d'Aumala, and several other persons, had the honour of dining with his Majesty. Mr Stanley is ex- pected to remain here for three d FIGHTING IN SOUTH AFRICA. . . .

CAPETOWN, Jrtv lOrrt —Samuel Barolong, who claims the chieftaincy of the Barolong territory. has attacked J baba Nchir, his brother Xepinare's place, and, having taken the inhabitants by surprise, succeeded, after several hours' fight. log, in turning them out. Xepinare cut his throat after the battle. The President of Orange Free State. who acted as arbitrator between Samuel and his brother, and decided against the claims of the former, marched to Thaba Nchir, and summoned Sarmel to submit. On his refusal the Presi- dent annexed Barolong territory, and has called upon Samuel to surrender.

CAPETOWN, WEDNESDAY EVENING.—A severe engage- ment has been fought between the followers of Montsioa and the Boers, in which many were killed, including several Englishmen. The Boers were defeated. SOUTH AFRICA.

CAPETOWN, SATURDAY.—Mr Rhodes has been appointed Commissioner for Bechuanaland, and has left for tha, coun- try. Mr Mackenza will shortly come to Capetown in ordi.r to confer with the Governor. It is officially announced that a very large majority of the inhabitants of Stellaland have accepted the British Protectorate. ANTI-CLERICAL DEMONSTRATION AT BRUSSELS.

BRUSSELS, WEDNESDAY.— A tumultuous scene occurred this evening on the termination ot ths sitting of the Cham- ber when members were leaving the House. A large crowd collected and hooted the Clerical deputies on their appear- ance. The police made several arrests, and had to afford protection to the various Ministers and deputies while leav- ing. Ihe police repeatedly dispersed the crowd. A number of people hooted the Liberal deputies. AN IMPERIAL MEETING AT ISCHL.

ISCHL, WEDNESDAY.—The Emperors of Austria and Ger- many arrived here at noon to-day from Ebansee, where the Emperor Francis Joseph had gone to meet his imperial guest. The meeting between the two monarchs at Ehansee was of a most cordial character. The Empress of Austria awaited the arrival of their Majesties at Ischl railway station, out- side which an immense concourse of people had assembled. The Emperor and Empress of Austria accompanied the Em- peror William from the railway station to his apartments at the Elizabeth Hotel.

_ SEVERE EARTHQUAKE IN ITALY. ROME, THERSDAY.—Four shocks of earthquake were felt between two and four o'clock this morning at Fraxati and Albano. In the immediate vicinity of this city, at a quarter past three o'clock a rather violent shock occurred, which caused great alarm among the inhabitants and summer visi- tors at Castelli Romany. There was no loss of life.

div.head: WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB
div.p: WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB
SPORTS.

On Saturday afternoon the second athletic festival held in connection with the Warrington Football Club this year was brought off in a field near St. James's Church. On the previous occasion the success of the sports was to a consider- able extent marred by the very inclement weather, but on Saturday this WAS everything that could be desired. As a result there was a very large attendance of spectators, and altogether the sports were of a most satisfastory character. The following are the officials and committee :—Judges : Messrs J E Warren, J Critchley, H Ashton ; referee and handicapper: Mr T R Sutton ("Athletic News"); clerk of the course : Mr T Pemberton ; starter: Mr P Lawless ; hon. sec., Mr J R Calvert; committee : Messrs Grey (chair-. man), GTaylor, J Myles, F Turner. div.head: ASHTON.
div.p: ASHTON.

ASHTON LOCAL BOARD —The monthly meeting of this Board was held on Wednesday. Our report is held over. BOWLING MATcit.-1 matca at bowls between Havdock and Ashton was played at Haydock, on Saturday, and re- sulted in a win for the home tearn by 29 points. PARR LANE DAY AND SUNDAY SCITOOLS.—The annual treat to the scholars was given .on Siturday, when, headed by the band of the Lincashire Hussars, they marched through the village, and afterwards sat down to an excellent tea in the schoolroom. The evening was spent in a field kindly lent for the occasion by Mr. Clarke.

div.head: GOL BORNE.
div.p: GOL BORNE.

CONSERVkTIVE Pic-sic.—The fourth annual pic-nic in ' connection with the Golborne Workingmen's Conservative Club was held on Tuesday. About thirty members and friends left the club in three waggonettes at nine o'clock en route for Hale, the seat of Colonel Blackburne, whose permission had been obtainell to visit his extensive grounds, greenhouses, &c. The company sat down to an excellent tea at the Child of Hale Hotel. The delightfully fine weather crowned the day's j mrney a success. THE TRADESMEN'S HALF-HOLIDAY.—The Tuesday half- holiday, established a few months ago by the principal Shopkeepers and tradesmen in Golberne, appears to be fal- ling away—at least, so far as the grocers are concerned. Hitherto, all the grocers except one (Mr. Luke Radcliffe, High-street) closed their establishments on Tuesday after- noon at two o'clock. Lately the agreement has been broken by several shopkeepers.

The Earl of NorthbrOok will, it is stated, probably leave London for Egypt by the Indian mail, via Brindisi, on the 31st instant. It is stated that his mission to Egypt will not occupy him more than two or three months. . The man named E. Edwards, chargedwith the murder of two of his children at Plymouth, was on Wednesday com- mitted for trial. His wife was arrested at the same time, but there is no evidence against her. The commander of the United States Asiatic squadron has been instructed to take measures for the protection of American citizens in China in the outbreak of hostilities between that country and France. _

THE OLDHAM lift/10;1;1:M Oldham, on Thursday, Harry Swindells was charged with the murder of James Wild, on the 16th July, last year. The prisoner, who was separated from his wife, came to her on the day named. Wild was sent for to eject him, and in a scuffle the priso- ner shot him dead. Swindells escipe4 but returned to Oldham last Monday morning, saying he wanted to give himself up. On the application of the Public Prosecutor, the case was remanded.

- - LANCASHIRE AND YORKSHIRE Thinveay.—Tbe report for I the past half-year states that the gross revenue for that period has been £18.358 more than in the corresponding six months, and the working expenses £ll,lOl less ; Cu the other hand, the charge for interest on Additional capital has been £28,437. The balance of revenue applicable to divi- dend on the ordinary stock is .2306,515, and the directors recommend a dividend at the rate of 4 per cent, per annum, less income tax, payable on August 12th, and to carry for- ward a balance of £22,656. The amount of capital ex- pended during the half-year for general purposes has been £398,854, against £521.200 authorised by the shareholders at the hall•yearly meeting. At the ensuing meeting the directors will ask for authority to expend £507,500 on capital account for general purposes daring the current half- year.

div.head: FLOWER SHOW.
div.p: FLOWER SHOW.

On Saturday, the seventh annual exhibition of the Rain- hill Floral and Horticultural Society was held in a spacious field near the village in very favourable weather. The show proved very successful, and was visited by a large number of people. The exhibits were fairly numerous, and were acknowledged to be of a good qcality. They were staged in a tent 100 feet long by 50 wide, erected by Mr J Howard, of Liverpool, the staging being the work of Mr H Flower, florist, of R ainhill, assisted by the committee, amongst whom Messrs A Cross and G W Rawlins took an active part in the general arrangement. Foliage plan's of a fine description were placed in the centre of the tent, and the staging round the test was appropriated for plants, vege- tables, and flowers. In the open classes, on account of the Sefton show being held on the same day, the erfries were , not quite so numerous as was the case last year, but in the cottagers' classes they may be said to have never been equalled, competition being unusually keen, and the ex- hibits being altogether superior both as regards quantity and , quality than has been the case at any previous exhibition held under the ausp'ces of the society. Mr P P Ker, of 1 Aigburth Nurseries, has usually exhibited a good number of ! plants, but did not do so this year in consequence of the Sefton Park show A programme of athletic sports was gone through in the afternoon, and towards evening the visitors generally indulged themselves in dancing to the music of Roughdale's band, conducted by Mr Beesley. Amongst the visitors were the Mayor of St. Helens (Mr Baxter). who took a number of prizes, the Mayoress, Mr H Bromilow, Dr Tyrer, Stu. Refreshments were supplied by Mr Williams, of Prescot. Messrs W Tunninghen, of Allerton, and G Miller, of Wavertree, acted as judges, and their awards gave every satisfaction. Mr J Rudge made a very , able secretary. In all there were 63 entries. Special prizes were given by Messrs E Johnson, H Bromilow, Joseph Bramham (Liverpool), T Davies (St. Helens), and G W I Rawlings. About £35 was offered in prizes. div.head: HUYTON.
div.p: HUYTON.

Bowts.-0a Saturday afternoon the grounds of the H.C.B. and L.T.C. (Huyton Crieket, Bowling, and Lawn Tennis Clubs) presented a lively appearance, the elite of the neighbourhood having assembled to witness a main of bowls. The prize was a massive silver cup, presented this year by Mr J Farrington, of Roby Mount, Roby, to the club, this making the fourth piece of plate which has been the subject of annual competition between the members. There were twenty-six entries, and the play throughout was exceedingly good, the cup being wen by the hon secretary, J F Edison, in the final round with the veteran C S Adlrich, who had run up with his usual careful play. SUDDEN DEATH —Mr S Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest at the Rose and Crown Inn, Huyton, on the body of Mr Thomas Higeinson, aged 72 years, a rice miller, carrying on business at. 41, Upper Frederick-street, Liver- pool. Mr Samuel S Higginson, West Hill, Huyton Park, stated that the deceased, who was his father, reside i with him, and the last time he saw him alive was on Friday night. Next moraing they found deceased dead in bed. Dr Packer, who had previously attended the deceased, con- sidered the cause of death to be disease of the heart, and the jury gave a verdict to that effect. The funeral took place on Tuesday afternoon, and was of a private char- acter.

- DAMAGING A WIRE FENCE AT HUTTON QUARRY.-At tho Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Edward Begg and Alfred Heys, I sds, were summoned by John Powell, farmer, Whiston, for damaging a wire fence at Huyton Quarry, on the 29th ultimo.—Mr Mckenzie, of Prescot, appeared for the complainant. It appeared that the complainant owns a field behind the Blue Works, and from time to time consi- derable damage had been done by lads breaking the wire fence and taking the wire away. On the date named he saw the defendants swinging on a piece of wire suspended from a tree ; and at erwards saw the lads pulling away more wire from the fence.—The Bench said the lads were deserving of a good flogging. They were fined 2s 6.1 and costs each.

TEMPERANCE DEMONSTRATION AT HUYTON. The first annual united demonstration in connection with the Huyton and Huyton Quarry branches of the Church of England Temperance Society was held on Monday after- noon, and was of a very successful and encouraging char- acter. Both branches have been in existence for about five years, and there is little doubt they have done some good and exercised an influence for the better in bath places. Some months ago it was arranged with the Liverpool branch of the Church of England Temperance Society that that branch, with the Huyton and Huyton Quarry branches, should hold a joint demonstration in Knowsley Park, but the proposal had, with a feeling of disappointment, to be abandoned on account of the railway company being unable to afford the facility and accommodation for the members of the Liverpool branch, which it had been hoped they would do. It was, however, thought advisable by the com- mittees of the local organisations that a gathering of some kind should be held to lessen the disappointment felt by their members. At a subsequent meeting the first Monday in August (Bank Holiday) was chosen as the day upon which to bold the demonstration; and for this purpose they secured a field connected with Brook Farm, Blue Bell-lane, Huyton, which was very kindly lent bf Miss Rigby. The weather was beautifully fine, and throughout the afternoon Huyton and Huyton Quarry presented a very busy appear- ance. About one o'clock the Whiston brass band, under the direction of Mr Corns, pmceeded to Huyton Quarry Schools, and here the members and friends of that society were formed in processional order. The children were very tastefully dressed and had a very neat appearance. They marched to Huyton Church School, and here the Huyton members joined the procession which then assumed great proportions. A large crowd of people witnessed the proceedings, which excited considerable attention. The precession afterwards paraded the village and went to the field kindly lent by Miss Rigby. At the entrance to the field an artistic arch of flags and banners had been erected, and the scholars passed beneath, the eight being an attrac- tive and pleasing one. The arrangements in the field for the enjoyment and amusement of these present were of the I most complete character, and reflected the highest credit upon the gentlemen entrusted with that task. They were I successfully carried out by the Rev. Canon Penhryn, Rev. D. Tyrer, and the Rev. D. H. Hubbard, who were willingly assisted by the committee of both societies. An excellent programme of sports, consisting of foot races, sack races, wheel-barrow races, obstacle races, tugs of war dre, was gone through. Several balloons were sent on an aerial voyage during the afternoon and evening and highly pleased the Youngsters ; while the elder portion indulged themsnlves in 'dancing to the strains of the Whiston Brass Band. The en- joyment was heartily kept up until dusk, when the parties separated. Unfortunately, during the afternoon's proceed- ings an accident of a painful and severe character occurred. While the wheel-barrow race (in which the competitors

were blindfolded) was being run a little girl sat with her legs under the rope for keeping back the spectators. One of the competitars accidentally ran over her legs and broke the left thigh of the poor girl, who had to be conveyed home, where she bas since been attended by Dr Parker. Br.yonci this nothing occurred to mar or interfere with the proceed- ings in any way. Refreshments were supplied on the field and were under the superintendence of Mr. Webster, assis- ted by several ladies.
HUYTON LOCAL BOARD.
The monthly meeting of. the Iluyton-with-Roby Local

Board was held at the Local Board offices, Huyton, on Toes. day evening, when there were present Messrs Siddeley (chairman), Sumer, Parker, Brown, Cooper, Burnyear, Har- rison, Swift (clerk), Worrall (surveyor), and Dr Hall (medi- cal officer.) The minutes of the last meeting were read and confirmed.

THE RAILWAY STATION.—Mr Cooper asked if any steps had yet been taken by the railway company to carry out the suggested improvements at the railway station.—The Sur- veyor replied in the negative —Mr Cooper: There was some- thing about erecting a cab stand, has anything yet been done? —The Clerk: No. The ship canal has taken up much of their time lately and now when that is over they will corn- mence soon no doebt.

MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.— Dr Hall, medical Officer of Health, reported that during the month of July the nom- of deaths in the township was as follows :—Huyton 4, Huy- ton Quarry 1, Roby none, total 5. Mr Parker said it was rumoured that a child had died at Roby from smallpox about a fortnight ago, but the doctor reported there had been no deaths.—Dr Hall said a child had died at Huyton from measles, but there had been no death at Roby from small- pox.

ITHE SUPPLY OF WATER AT HORN'S SMITHY.—Mr Ban- ner remarked that in consequence of a circular which had been received from the Local Government Board it WA6 their duty to see that the water in their district was as pure as it possibly could be. He thought the water at Horn's Smithy was not pure, and he suggested that the medical officer be asked to test the water and see if it was pure.— The Chair. , man remarked that be was in that district on the previous I Thursday and he found that the whole of the cottages were Without water as the pump was dry and out of order. Some of the people got their water from the puhlichouse, and one of the tenants told him that they paid 7s per year to the I Liverpool Corporation for allowing them to fetch water from i the pulffichouse and they had also to pay 2d per week to I the publican for drawing the water from the tap. Others I got their water from a well, he believed on Lyon's farm. It, Ihowever, smelled badly and tasted badly, but it was the only water, except rain water, that they could get. He thought that whoever owned the cottages ought to be compelled to put in a proper supply.—Mr Banner: I think so too, but I also think that Lord Derby, to whom they belong, does not know of their present condition or he would not allow them to remain in that condition.— The Chairman remarked that he had intended to raise the matter himself.— Dr Hall said when the some question was discussed last year he advocated that they should get a supply of water to the houses, but it was then decided that Mr. Lyon's farm, from which the bulk of them got their water, was within a reasonable distance; ani there might be some difficulty about getting the pipes there. —The Surveyor explained that in 1882 Lord Derby's repre- sentatives arranged to have water put in the houses, and in fact the order was issued for it, but when they came to the expenditure the order was c incelled. Toe total cost would amount to nearly £3OO. The Water Engineer asked to tap the mains at the Horn's Smity, but it was objected to and the whole thing fell through. ANOTHER SMOKE NUISANCE.—At a meeting of the High- I way, Sanitary, and Lighting Committee, held on the 29th I ult., the Surveyor reported that he had watched the smoke issuing from the chimney of Messrs Maybury, Marson and Sharpe iron works; and the committee recommended that that firm should be summoned to abate the nuisance.—The minutes were passed. FINANCE.—At a meeting of the Finance Committee, held on the sth inst., the Treasurer submitted his account which showed a balance in favour of the Board of .£944 3a31. Accounts amounting to £.212 10i 11:1 were recommended for payment.—The minutes were pissed. This was the only business nf interest.

div.head: PRltk(Er• •
div.p: PRltk(Er• •

Excunstox.—The annual excursion in connection with the Prescot Working-men's Society took place on Tuesday, when about 800 persons took advantage of the brilliant weather, and thoroughly enjoyed the scenery, Sze., of Mat- lock and Buxton.

PLUCKING CLOVER AT WHISTON. Henry Lester and John Lyon, lute, were summoned at the Prescot Petty Ses• siona on Tuesday, for stealing a quantity of clover, value 24, front a field near Whilton colliery, the property of John Powell. Mr Mackenzie, of Prescot, appeared for the prose- cutor. On the date in question the prosecutor saw the lads in his field plucking clover. They got a good armful each and were walking away with it when the prosecutor caught them The defendants said they had pluckPd the clover to feed their rabbits. They were each fined 2s 6d and cnsts.

A WHISTON CASE AT ST. HELENS COUHT.—On Wed- neslay, at the St. Helens County Court, before Mr T P E Tnompson, iade, llobert Preston, grocer, Whiston, sought to recover £4 ISs 31 from Wm. 'Rose, of Whiston, on ac- count of groceries supplied to the defendant's wife.—M: Swift appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr Riley defended.— The plaintiff's case was that the goods were supplied with the defendant's full knowledge and consent, but this was denied by the defendant. The parties came to an arrange- ment wherel-y the plaintiff accepted payment of a stated sum in settlement of his claim.

TRESPASSING IN SEARCH OF MUSHROONS.—At the Pres- cot Petty Sessions on Tuesday, three middle-aged men, named Thomas Hunt, Richard Birch, and Edward Byrom, pleaded guilty to trespassing in a field of growing potatoes near Shaw-lane, the property of William Cook, farmer, Pres- cot Hall. It was stated that the defendants were searching for mushrooms, and in doing so damaged the potatoe field to the extent of 23. The Bench stated that no one had a right to trespass in search of mushrooms or anything else, and imposed a fine of 53 and costs, in addition to making an order for the payment of the damage, PRESCOT SCHOOL Bonn—A. special meeting of the Pres- cot School Board WAS held at Mr Cross's office on Friday evening, for the purpose of appointing a successor to Miss Duke, late headmistress of the iris' school. The members pre- sent were Messrs W L Evans, H Fogg, J B Sanders,W Golds- I worth, and H Cross (clerk). It was resolved that Miss Har- ris of Astwood Bank. near Redditch, be appointed head-mis- trees of the girls' school in the room of Miss Duke. Miss Harris will enter on her duties on the 18th inst, when the schools re-assemble after the holidays: and her salary will be £BO per year, with a portion of the Government grant. THE MAINTENANCE OF A P&THER.—James Salt, a copper refiner, at Garston, was summoned at the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday last, to show cause why he should not contribute to the maintenance of his father, at present chargeable to the Prescot Union.—Mr S H Hartley (clerk to the Board of Guardians) saki the defendant's father was an old and impotent person, 70 years of age, and he was totally unfit for work. Some time ago he made application to the Guardians for relief, and they granted him 33 per week. The defendant's two brothers consented to pay is each per week towards the cost of their father's maintenance, but the de- fendant would not do that. He was in receipt of a per week.—The defendant said he was perfectly willing to con- tribute to the support of his father; and the Bench ad- journed the case for a morth for an arrangement to be come to.

A NEGLIGENT HUSBAND.—At the Prescot Petty Sessions, in Tuesday, before Messrs F Earle and W L Evans, William Livesev, a bricklayer residing at Eccleston, was charged under a warrant with neglecting to maintain his wife and child, whereby they became chargeable to the Prescot Union.—The prisoner pleaded gailty.-11r S H Hartley (clerk to the Guardians) stated that the Guardians were not desirous of sending the prisoner to gaol if he would take care to maintain his wife and child in the future. They had had considerable trouble with the prisoner, who, it was supposed purposely absented himself from work in order that he could not be called upon to maintain his family. A previous employer of the prisoner had stated his willingness to find him work if he would only attend to it.—The prisoner alleged that he was subject to fits, and could not attend to his work in cousequence.—The Bench said they would adjourn the case for a rnanth in order to give the prisoner an opaertnnity of coining to some arrangement. CHARGE OF MAKING A FALSE STATEMENT TO A POLlCE- SERoEsyr.—Anthnny McKechuie, a military-looking man. was charged at the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday last, with making a false statement to P.S. Bull.—P.S. Bull stated that on Tuesday night, the 29th July, the prisoner visited the Prescot police station and said he wished to give himself up as a deserter from the 10th Brigade of Royal Artillery at Kinsale on the 13th December. 1880. He (wit- ness) asked him if he was a deserter and he said he wee; although witness told him that if he was making a' false statement he was liable to be sent to prison. On the follow- ing day be was committed to gaol to await an escort. But it was found he was not a deserter, and witness had since charged him with making a false statement and he replied I was in drink at the time."—Superintendent Barker said the prisoner had been seven times in custody as a deserter, and he had served two three months' imprisonments for falsely representing himself as a dserter.—The prisoner stated that when he was in drink his mind wandered and he felt himself to be a deserter.—The Bench committed him to prison for three months with bard labour. COWARDLY AND BRUTAL ASSAULT.—Before Messrs. F. W. Earle and W. L. Evans, at the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Thomas Marmon, a powerful-looking young fellow, residing in Hill-street, Present, was charged with assaulting Joseph Stabley, corn miller, Eccleston, on the 22nd July.— The prisoner said he was in drink, and did not know any- thing about it.—The prosecutor stated that be was driving through Prescot with his pony and trap and stomped at the B ack Horse Inn. Shortly after he had entered the house the prisoner and two or three other men followed and pri- soner said "Do you belong to the -- horse and cart out- side," and he (witness) replied that he did belong to a horse and trap outside. The prisoner thereupon said "You had a mate o. mine locked up for 14 days and I'll pay you for it." With that the men set upon him. They struck him on the face, giving him a black eye and cutting his forehead; knocked him down and violently kicked him on the shoulder. He had never seen the prisoner before, and, the assault was entirely unprovoked.—The Chairman: You are a nice specimen of the Prweot rough; you get in drink and as- sault the first man you see, and who did not know you or bad done anything against you at all. Bat we are determined to put down thiB sort of thing, and we will let all your friends know it. You will go to gaol for two months with hard labour.

BIDING A BICYCLE WITITOPT A LAMP —At the Present Petty Sessions on Tuesday, John Wild, a respectablv-dres- sd voting man, was summoned for riding laMycle without a lamp en the night of the 27,h June, in Derby-street, Pies-. cot. —The defendant pleaded guilty, and the Bench imposed a fine of 5s and costs.

PRESCOT HIGHWAY BOARD.—Tuesday last was the day appointed for the bolding of the monthly meeting of the Prescot Highway Board at the offices of Mr H Cross (clerk). As the requisite number of members to form a quorum were not present the meeting had to be Postponed. There were present Messrs W L Evans and Tyrer, W Goldsworth (survevor), and H Cross (clerk). PRESCOT BOARD OF GIIARDIANS —A fortnightly meeting of the Present Board of Guardians was held at the Union Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday, when there were present Mr J T Hall (chairman), Rev T Finegan, Messrs Newsome, Dobell, Birchall, Matthews, Gerrard, Seder, Tvrer, Fisher, Buckley, P Longton. E Johnson; S Marsh, Meadows, and S H Hartley (clerk).—The C'erk stated that the Workhouse master reported there were 435 inmates this week, 432 last week. and 420 in the corresponding week of last year. There 153 boys and girls in Kirkdale School and Pantasapb Orphanage. The vagrants relieved this week numbered 47, and in the corresponding week last year 55_ A letter was read from the Local Government Bo;.rd inquir— ing if an amount of £52 4s Id, surcharged by the district auditor to Mr. W. Tyrer. ex-chairman of the Board, had been paid. This sum, it appeared, was in connection with the salary of an assistant overseer.—The Clerk said he bad replied to the Local Government Board, stating that the sum had not been paid, and that he (the clerk) did not sur pore Mr. Tyrer had any official knowledge of the surcharge hav- ing been made—Another letter was read from the Local Government Board, who had examined two sets of plwns for proposed alterations at the workhnuse. They were of opinion that the plan which provided for the erection of a new infirmary on land to the east of the workhouse, and for appropriating the existing inhrmary to the aged and infirm inmates was far more satisf ,ctory and better calculated to meet the future requirements of the union than the othe plan. They, therefore, recommended the Guardians to adopt the plan suggested, and he would he glad to receive plans and estimates for carrying the scheme into execution. In reply te a question, the Clerk said the estimates were £l5OOO and £17.009, and the Local Government Board approved of the ohm which would in- volve an expenditure of £17,000. The mstter WAS referred to the Building Committee.—The Clerk said he had received a precept from the Clerk of Ilie Peace for the Guardians to pay £6,179 3. 7d for county rate purposes. Jr. was an in- crease of £l2 814 d, which was very satisfactory, consider- ing that it was based upon the new valuation of the Uniou. which was much lareer than before. The valuation was in- creased something like £40,000; brit on an appeal it was reduced by £23,000, leaving it £17,000 increase. The Gnardians expressed their eathfection that the appeal hal bren prosecuted successfully.

PRESCOT LOCAL BOARD. The monthly meeting of the Prescot Local }hard was beld at the office of Mr Cross (clerk), on Wedoesd4v evening, when there were present Messrs C Spencely, J S Preston, W Hatton, H Cross (clerk), W Goldsworth, junior (represen- ting his father, surveyor), and Dickenson (nuislnce inspec- tor.) The minutes of the last meeting were read and con- firmed.

BIRTHS AND DEents.—The monthly report of the Reg- istrar (Mr P Chorley) showed that during the month of July the deaths were as follows Prescot 18, corresponding month last year 9; Ecclestm 0, last vs ,r 2; total 16, last year 11. The births were: Prescot 28, corresponding month last year 19; Eccleston 3, last year 1 ; total 31, last year 20.

MISCELLANEOUS.—Mr Goldsworth stated that Mr Leslie had been communicited with with refetence to the Board's objection to the plans submitted by him on the ground that be had not complied with the byelaws in not giving sufß- cient yard space to his new property in Derhy.street. Mr Leslie wrote in reply stating that he was willing to comply with the Beard's requirements. The Boyd pissed the plans as altered.—Some conversation ensued as to the alleged oh- struction to the footplth ciused by Mr Morton in front of his shop premises, and who wrote expressing regret that he had created an obstruction. He would do all he could to avoid it in future.

THE SANITARY STATE OF THE TOWNSHIP.—An exten- sive and carefully prepared report on the sinitary state of the township was read by the Chairman. ['he report dealt first with the removal of slop refeee ; and pointed out that for that purpose it was the duty of the Sanitary Authority to see that a public sewer was provided ; and that the owners of the houses constracted good house drains ' • and it might fairly be said to be the duty of the householders to see that the slops were properly taken away by the drains. Many backyard spices ware found lessened in size by wooden erections of various kinds—pigeon cotes, hoe cotes, rabbit hutches, and in some cases p'g styee. Such erections should be discountenanced by the Board, owners, and occu- piers alike: and they could be readily dealt with by the authority if they were shown to be a nuisance injurious- to health. The lime-washing of all yard walls and the inside walls of privies was recom- mended, And a list of existing nuisances were submitted for the consideration of the Board ; the report concluding with the hope being expressed that there would be a continuation of the progress they had hitherto made for the benefit and improvement of the districe—The chairman ' remarked that all middens connected with shinpons and stables should be regularly and prope:ly cleaned out. An accumulation of impure matters should not be allowed—Mr. Prestou agreed with this suggestion and said that in warm weather the stench thet arose was fearful, and it vitiated the air. He moved that all persone have notice given to them to clear away all nuisetces or legal proceedings would be taken. Mr. Hatton seconded the motion which was agreed to. This was all the business.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY AFFILIATION CASE.
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY AFFILIATION CASE.

At the Prescot Petty ;sessions, on Tuesday, before Messrs. F. W. Earle and W. L. Evans, an affiliation case which ex- cited a cunsiderable degree of public interest was beard. Mark Kellet, a married man, aed landlord of the Eagle and Child public-house, Prescot, was summoned to show cause why he should not contribute to the support of the illegiti- mate child of a single woman named Ann Hesketh, of which be was alleged to be the father.—The defendant, who was represented by Mr. Swift, barrister, Liverpool, denied the paternity.—The complainant stated that she resided in Askers-street, and was a single woman. She ha% a child born on the 9th June, and Mark Kellet was the father of it. It was her first child. She was employed by the defendant as a domestic servant on the 2nd August, last year, and on the 10. h September last she and Mrs. Kellet staved up until late waiting for Mr. Kellet to come home. Mrs. Kellet asked hers(witness) to stop up, and she did so. He came home about one o'clock, and she shortly afterwards went to bed. She had not been in bed long before a quarrel arose between Mr.and Mrs. Kellet, and the defendant turned his Iwife out of the house and locked and bolted the doors. He then retired to his own bedroom, and shortly afterwards entered her (witness's) room She tried all she could to pre- vent him, but be forced his way in, and notwithstanding her struggles carrieu out his designs. He was the father of !her child —Mr. Swift : Have you any witnesses 7—Wit- ness : No, sir.—Mr. Swift thereupon sat down, and remarked that the case could go no futther.—af,er a consultation between the magistates and the clerk, Mr. SwiTt added that the defendant was a thoroughly respectable young man, who was married and had two children. He was the keeper of a licensed public-house in Prescot, and he was prepared to give a categorical denial to the woman's allegations, and she was si informed a long time ago. lie supposed, however, as the complainant had no witnesses that there was nothing for it but to dismiss the case.—The Chairman: Have you not got any witnesses of any kind ?—Complainant: No sir, I have not.—The Chairman : We must dismiss it then as you have not brought any witnesses.—The Complainant: Cannot I give an explanation why he went out and let his wife in again? —The Chairman : No. If you can get any witnesses you can bring him up here again; bat this time we cannot hear it as you have not brought any witnesses.—The complain- ant again essayed to speak, whereupon ti.e clerk said: There are no witnesses, and the case cannot go any further.—The Chairman : The law will not allow us to make an order if you have no witnesses.—The complainant: Cannot yen allow me to give an explanation how he went ?,-The Clerk: No, we cannot.—The complainant : I think the law is very wrong then. It is very hard this, for one who has borne a good character and always bad a good situation before going to him. Now lam disgraced for ever, hnd a character is all that a servant has to depend all:op.—The Chairman : It is bard for you, but we can do nothing more.—The parties then retired, and as the defendant was leaving the coed the complainant's mother attempted to strike him, but the police officers prevented her. She was ultimately put outside the court, when she violently declared that she would "do " for him yet, if she had to serve seven years for it. .1111.
The Swansea coal trimmers have struck work for better remuneration.

Contracts for over 50,000 tons of shipping have been booked by the Clyde shipbuilders during the past week. There are inquiries for 50,000 tons more. At the last meeting et the medical officers of health for London a general opinion was expressed that England would not he visited by Asiatic cholera this year. Much regret is felt at the breakdown of Mr. Trevelyan, and his consequent preclusion from Parliamentary duties. The bodies of two Irish harvestmen were found partiaNy burnt in a barn at Spalding., on Thursday morning. How the fire occurred is unknown. The body of a male child was found in a bag on the North London Railway, at Poplar, on Thursday morning. Death had resulted from violence. The police are making inquiries. An extensive outbreak of English cholera has occurred at Rishton, near Blackburn, and hag extended to Clavton-le- Moors, a large number of persons being under treatment at both places. eaornf GeeotoidnßTeemf ptt eh:a n members Goonthc, lodge-room, Pt. theko Hope fdgEre4E:Sßlte7l-rsee7°:',:n—o Lodge Monday evening. Truth saps, Lord Petre will take his seat in the House of Lords daring the autumn session. He will be the first Catholic Priest who has ever sat there since the Reformation.

A deputation oft British workmen are about to proceed to Germany, Austria Holland, and France to inquire into the condition of the Austria, sugar industry and the effects of the bounty system. A verdict of wilful murder was on Thursday returned by a coroner's jury against tne gamekeeper Whitley for causing the death of a min named Elford, at Tollard Royal, by striking him on the head with a hurdle stake.

A fire broke out en Thursday afternoon in the warehouses of Messrs. Bitkett Brothers, Grundy-street, Liverpool, which were stored with cotton, sugar, and other produce balong4m2 to v minus merchants. div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, AUGUST 9, 1884.

M. BRIGHT at the great Reform Demon- stration at Birmingham, on Monday, pro- pounded his plan fpr the Reform of the House of Lords. It has the merit of extreme simplicity, but the objection to it that will be generally taken just now, when the nation is ! up in arms against the Upper House, is that which was taken at the meeting—it will be regarded as "too lenient." Mr. BRIGHT'S proposal, and, as it is not the first time that ' he has made it, it may be accepted as the outcome of matured thought, is that the veto 1 of the Lords to reject bills sent up to them by the Commons should be limited ; they should have power to reject a bill once; but if what was practically the same bill was sent up to them next session, after being again passed by the House of Commons, it should not be in the power of the House of Lords to throw it out. To take the case at present before the country ; the Franchise Bill will fall through as a measure rejected by the Peers; but if the bill were to be re-presented to them after the autumn session the Lords would be bound to accept it; they would , have exhausted their power of veto. It must ' be confessed that, on the face of it, this does not go very far in the way of reform. It still leaves us what Mr. Bright has termed an "hereditary and irresponsible House of Legislature," and that, as we have his au- thority for saying, "cannot be a permanent institution in a free country." The lion will, still be in the path, but some, if not all, of his teeth will have been drawn. Everything, as it seems to us, would depend on how I the brute thought fit to behave after the operation; if he took to gnawing at every- thing that was presented to him he might be as troublesome as before, if not quite as powerful for evil. To drop the metaphor, if, the Lords, after being limited as to theirj veto, should, as the Tory Caucus, use to the fullest extent the remnant of their power in order to thwart Liberal legislation, they might still be a thorn in the side of the nation. When the closure was proposed in the House of Commons with a view to crippling the obstructionists, it was con- tended that the Opposition were about to be gagged. but we have seen that, notwithstanding the so-called gag, there has been more waste of time than ever by useless talk; obstruction has been less direct, but it has been none the less obstructive. And so it may prove with the House of Lords; the veto, limited though it be, may be exercised so often in obedience to the dictates of the Tory party as to still I preserve to the r'eers the unenviable charac- ter they possess of being a nuisance to the nation. It is due to Mr. BRIGHT to say that he does not apprchend such difficulties as the outcome of his proposal as we have shown( to be possible. It is more likely, he thinks, that the Peers will follow the example of the Crown, and consult their dignity by declin- ing; to exercise a veto which, while bringing

them in conflict with the people's representa- tives, may finally be over-ridden by them. It is certainly not much encouragement to a man to show fight when it is obvious from the beginning that it is within the power of his antagonist to beat him in the encounter. Assuming Mr. BRIGHT'S view to be the cor- rect one, it would follow that the House of Lords would become a sort of unattached Committee of Legislation, which might prove useful in revising work when it was not within its power to destroy it. It is notorious that it is with great difficulty, under present condi- tions, that either party in the House of Lords can secure a large following, even when the occasion is regarded as momentous, and the in ference as to the Peers who are "not even known to the door-keepers" is that they would not take the trouble to attend the House at all when such common people as Commoners, but one remove from the streets," could snap their fingers in the next session at anything they might do Mr., BRIGHT, looking at the situation at all sides, urges that "we should make no more dis- turbance than is absolutely necessary to effect the object we have in view." and he reminds more ardent spirits that we "must have by some means or other the consent of the House of Lords to the change which it is proposed to make.". He probably :hinks that the Peers could be brought, under the pressure of public opinion, to con- sent to the clipping of their wings, , whilst they would not under any cir- • I cumstances consent to take themselves. altogether off the scene. He is so moderate, and so truly conservative in proceeding on lines of the Constitution, that he is the more likely to succeed. But the great merit of Mr. BRIGHT'S scheme is one which he has not I himself named—not, we are quite sure, be- cause it is not perceived by him, but rather because he deems it prudent not to dwell upon it. And it is this: if the Peers were once deprived of the power of rejecting a bill a second time, it would be a comparatively easy matter, if they proved intractable, to institute a further reform of the Upper House, , or for that matter to go the length of abolish- ing it. All that would then be required would be that a bill, dealing with them as the nation thought best, should be presented to them. If they rejected it, what matter ? It would. be presented a second time, and become law in spite of them. It will thus be seen that Mr. BRIGHT'S proposal is of a more search- ing and far-reaching character than is ap- parent at the first glance. It would put a lever in the hands of the people which would enable them, if they liked, to overturn the House of Lords in a strictly constitutional way. It would place the sword of Damocles —the sword suspended by a single hair—over the heads of the Peers, and that, we take it, would bring about a much desired result ; it would either mend or end them,

Tiig Provisional Committee of the Man- chester Ship Canal scheme have lost no time in facing the somewhat appalling issue placed , before them by the rejection of the Bill on the part of the Select Committee of the House of Commons. They met on Tuesday, and unanimously resolved that "the move- ment to connect Manchester with the sea by a Ship Canal should be continued and prose- cuted to a successful issue." It is now pro- posed to disarm the opposition of Liverpool by adopting an alternative scheme which will • avoid the estuary, Sir WILLIAM Foßwooo, on behalf of the Liverpool Town Council, and Mr ASPINALL, QC. on behalf of the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, having; during the recent inquiry, committed thefll- - selves to neutrality, if the plans were altered • so as not to interfere with "the estuary either along the northern or southern shores." It is needless to say that the Ship Canal Com- mittee still think that it would be best to make
use of the natural water-way from Run- corn to the sea; but as it does not

appear possible to overcome the fears of those in authority as to possible injury to the port of Liverpool, it is now being determined to do the next best thing—and that is, construct a canal from Manchester to the sea without relying on the estuary. As we stated last week, the feeling of disappointment in Man- chester is exceedingly strong. Speaking at a meeting of the City Council one alderman said the result was 'perfectly monstrous; such a waste of public energy, public money,• 1 and patriotism seemed to him to deter men from suggesting almost anything which would , be for the weal not only of the city, but also the welfare of the nation at, large "; and, he added, "it was disgraceful such a matter should be left to chance legislation." At the Salford Town Council a resolution was come to in which the re- jection of the bill was spoken of as "a great calamity ;" but the feeling seems to be pretty general that it is no use crying over spilt milk—big as is the spill in this case— and what is now to be done is to make the 0 best of what for the moment is looked upon . as a bad job. The matter was referred to at a meeting of the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday evening, and as there is a pros- pect, under the new scheme, of the canal keeping more on the Lancashire side of the 1 Mersey than was originally intended—thus bringing it nearer the town—we are quite sure that there will be no abatement of the enthusiasm of the inhabitants in favour of the Manchester Ship Canal.. or

BANK Holiday on Monday last was, we are glad to note, devoted to a large extent to de- monstrations in favour of Temperance. The Band of Hope Procession and Gala at War- rington was an experiment, but it proved, thanks to the energy and skill of the pro- moters, so wonderfully successful that we, venture to predict that it will become an annual institution. Earlestown and Newton paved the way on Saturday with a United Tem- perance Demonstration, In the St. Helens dis- trict the Huyton and Huyton Quarry branches of the Church of England Temperance Society also made a good display, whilst Runcorn was gallantly to the fore with the z 3th an- nual demonstration of the Lifeboat Crew Division of the order of the "Sons of Tem- perance." The weather, upon which so much depends in these out-door demonstrations, was fortunately all that could be desired, and the result was that young and old who took part in the proceedings greatly enjoyed them- selves. There was a time when teetotallers were looked upon as dull, stupid sort of people who foolishly deprived themselves of all rational means of enjoyment; but the most hilarious bacchanal would not bring such a charge against them now, after wit- nessing the festivities of Monday last. The boot is rather on the oLher leg. for it is be- ginning to be perceived that the temperate man is the one who best knows how to enjoy himself. He is really ‘• refreshed" by what he eats and drinks, and, gaining strength by healthy exercise, he "can keep it up" hour after hour. go home and sleep soundly, and get up in the morning happily free from

They are conscious—many of them—that it would be no worse if they themselves were teetotal- lers, but habit has become a second nature to them, and they are conquered by it. Not so with the little ones ; with them, just as the twig is bent so the tree will be inclined, and Temperance Reformers, seeing the truth of tills, are acting wisely in seeking to train up the child in the way it should go. By all means let the children by made happy, and all the better when they can enjoy themselves out of doors, as was the case On Bank Holi- day.
