MEASLES AT WIDNES.—At the present time measles are -very prevalent in Widnes, ani as a consequence the attend- ance of children at school is being much reduced. Comaarsslowess' &karmic —This election has been fixed to take place at the Market Hall, on the 4th September, and the list of voters is undergoing revision. • WintraC.E.T.S.—On Thursday, at the weekly meeting of this society, the Rev C Ramfitt presiding, the Rev A P H Wilson delivered a lecture on "The social and moral as- pect of temperance." •• THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL —On Friday, the 15th just, a meeting will be held in the Free Trade Hall, Man- chester, in furtherance of the Ship Canal. The meeting, it Is expected, will be addressed by several members of Parlia- ment, and other well-known gentlemen. UNIVERSITY Daciexas.—On Friday, the let August. the annual graduation ceremony took place at Edinburgh Uni- versity. We observe the name of Mr Andrew MacLennan, of Widnes, in the list presented to the Lord Chancellor for the degrees of Bachelor of Medicine and Master in Surgery. RUNCORN FOOTBALL Com—Having now gained a re- putation of no mean character in the football world daring the past two seasons, Runcorn Fontbalft*Club h a been en- abled to make engagements with some of the leading clubs for the forthcoming season, and many excellent matches may be anticipated. THEFT OF VEGETABLES.—At Runcorn Police Court yes- terday, before Mr James Handley and Captain C W burst, William Barker, of 22, Union-street, ,who is employed at Johnson's soapery, was charged with stealing two turnips from a field at Higher Runcorn, belonging to Mr 8 B Chadwick, J.P. The Bench imposed a fine of 10s and costs S's 6d. It appears thefts have previously been very. frequent. A VIOLENT STEPSON AT RUNCORN Yesterday Peter Alexander Atherton Hankinson, a married man, 31 years of age, described as a worthless fellow who would not work, was brought before the magistrates at Runcorn Police Court, on a warrant executed by PC Wallace. He was charged with assaulting his stepfather, Robert Winterbet- tom, on the 26th July. The prisoner was fined in the total sum of £1 3s 4d. • ODDFELLOWS' CELEBRATION AT DITTON.—The anniver- sary of the Loyal Heart of Oak Lodge of the Independent Order of Oddfellows M.U., at Dittoo, was celebrated on Thureday. About fifty members assembled at the Ball Inn, in the forenoon, and walked through the lanes of the dis- trict, headed by the Ditton Brass Band. On returning to the lodge dinner was partaken of, and the usual loyal and patriotic toasts were honoured. Tam NEW PUBLIC OFFICES FOR Wirnags —Yeeterday, the General purposes Committee of, the Widnes Loca Board had an interview with Mr. Holme, the architect, for the new public offices; and had also under consideration the letter from Mr. R. H. Holden with reference to making provision in the new building for a free public library. At present, as the public are well aware the Board only intend to erect the public offices, but we understand that the plans for the Town Hall include a rqom which will be well adap- ted for the purpose of a library'. " BRUNNER, MOND, & CO., *INNINGTON:••At an extraor- dinary meeting of the firm of Messrs. Brunner., Mond, and Co., alkali manufacturers, Winnington, heal in Liverpool yesterday week, a renolutton was unanimously passed to increase the nominal capital of the company from £600,000 to £1,500,000, by the creation of 90,000 new shares of £lO each. The next issue of the shares of the company will be of 45,000 ordinary shares of £lO each, and 22,500 7 per Cent. Preference shares of £lO each. We understand that Messrs. Brunner, Mond, and Co. have agreed with Major Orred or the purchase of four acres of land at Weston Point, for the purpose of erecting a chemical works there. It will be remembered that this firm has certain rights to the brine of the Mersey Salt and Brine Company, which they will probably use in the manner which has been so successful at their Northwich works. MARRIAGE OF A. RUNCORN GENTLEMAN.—Tho quiet Yorkshire village of Debcrosse-imSiddleworth was on Wednesday roused from the usual lethargic appear- ance it presents by an event in which a general, we mighb say universal, interest has been taken—that is the marriage of Miss Hirst, eldest daughter of Mr John Hiret. P, of Ladcasile, Dobcrose, to Mr Robert Newton i Davies, of Liver- pool, and son of Mr Davis, a well-known resiJent of Run- corn. Eleven o'clock was the hour appointed for the care- mony, and soon after the hour had strnck the wedding party made its appearance, and, to the etrains of the" Wedding March "proceeded up the aisle. It Sentieted Of the bride and bridegroom, and the following bridesmaids :—Miss Lily Hirtti Pieter of the ride;h Miss Davies, sister of the bridegroom; Miss Hirst, Miss Jessie Hirat, Miss Alice Barber, Miss Gertrude Wrigley, cousins of the bride ; and Miss Katie Robinson. Groomsmen :—Mr John Watt+, beet man ; Mr H L Hirst, brother of the bride; Mr A Davies brother of the bridegroom; MriA Sheard, and Mr J Eccles. The party also included Mr and Mrs J Hirst, father and mother of the bride ; Mrs DaVies, mother of the bride- groom; Mr and Mrs Gabriel Davies, MIT A Davies, Mr and Mrs John "James Hirst, Captain T B ,fliret, Mrs T A Hirst, Mrs Doig, Mr Simpson (partner of the bridegroom who is a merchant), Mr F Richard- son, Mr Hensliall, Miss Dawson,- . and Miss Barber. The ceremony, was a choral one, and the Rev. Hugh noir, rector Of the church, officiated. At Ladcastle a sumptuous breakfast was partaken of, and subsequently the happy pair' left for Edinburgh. The Runcorn employ es of Messrs. Simpson and Davies had a holiday in honour of the event. NEW BOOKS, kc.—Part 4 of Cassell's "Book of Health" deals with diets and liquids, and gives information I e "Fah". matters which will be found valuable to those who are sick and to those who are well. " Popular Gardening" loses nothing of the variety or freshness which marked the first number. Among the subjects specially dealt with this month are—" The life history of plants," "Common hardy' flowers,"" Rose culture," "Suburban gardenina," "The Vine and its fruit," and "The kitchen garden." Part 7 of "The Encyclopselia Dictionary" sustains the high char- acter of this extraordinqry work, which vihen completed will be a library in itself. "The Family Magazine" by the same firm is particularly strong for August. The continued Stories maintain their interest, and the short sketches are bright and instructive. Mr. C. F. Gordon Cumming deals with "The newspapers of the world," Mr. Gordon Stables has "A story of strange meetings," and there is a paper oy. Mr. Karl Blind on "The white lady of the Berlin Castle." "The Quiver" for August is specially well illustrated. It is in no wise lacking in other respects; while as much may be said of Cassell's "Little Folks" and "Familiar Wild • Flowers!' Messrs. Goubaud and Son, Bedford-street, Covent Garden, keep pace with the times with their three excellent fashion journals. The current nnmber of "Le Monitear de la Mode" contains over 100 illustrations, be- sides four beautifully coloured and highly finished fashion plates, dealing with everything in the way of female dress, from " travelling chapeaux" to "bathing and shrimping costumes." " Myra's Journal of Dress and Fashion" ((1.) is close at its heels. The August number to hand is pro- fusely illustrated, and contains the usual coloured plate and pattern sheet with ample explanation " Myra's Threepenny Journal" on the same lines is well worth the money. "The' English Illustrated Magazine" (Messrs. Macmillan and Co.) scarcely reaches its high level in the way of picturesque illustration, but what there is is still wonderful for sixpence. The articles specially illustrated are "Cutlery and.Qutlers at Sheffield" by Mr. H. J. Palmer; "James Ward " a sketch in which the artist is critically and symnalhetic- ally treated by Mr. F. T. Piggott; and "A Master Builder" by the authors of "Historic Winchester." Mr. Swinburne contributes some characteristic verse under the title of "A Ballad of Bark ,;" and, among other things, there le a racy article—" Houghton Scrip "—by Mr: Archibald Forbes. An "extra" from the office of the Pall Mail Gazette, entitled "The Peers and the People," is issued at the price of one penny, and should be in the hands of everyliody:at the pre- sent critical time.

The fortnightly meeting of this Authority watt held on Tuesday afternoon at the Workhouse, Dutton. Tuere were present Messrs J Ashton (in the chair), Rev J Warburton, J Mclntyre, J Smith, F A Wallington, J Weir, J E Hamilton, E Aaron, H Linaker (clerk), and W Ii Linaker (deputy clerk). FRODSRAM WATER SUPPLY —A letter was read from the Local Government Board with reference to the proposed scheme of water supply for the township of Frodsham„ and to state that they were prepared to sanction the borrowing by the Rural Sanitary Authority of a small own (say £200) for preliminary expenses to enable the Authority to search for water on the distinct understanding that no pipes or permanent works excepting the well and edits are con- structed until the Board %ere informod as to the quality and the quantity of the water obtained. It was added that the Board had no objection te offer to the proposal of the Authority to obtain tenders for the preliminary works with- out advertising. TRE NUISANCE AT STRETTON —A letter was read from Mr James Marson, Hill Cbffe, Warrington, stating that he had received the Authority's letter of the 20,11 July, with copy of the report of the committee appointed by the Authority to inspect the polluted cattle • drinking pond at Lower Hall Farm, Stretton, and he was obliged to the committee for their kind attention to the matter. He quite approved of the plan suggested by the committee for abat- ing the nuisance, and he wasglad to hear that the Authority were willing to carry out the work, which would, no doubt, make a great improvement in the condition of the pond. He did not think he should have troubled them at all had it not been for the sudden discharge of the large accumulation of liquid manure sent from O'd Stretton Hall by a new sewer which they found a fresh service for the supply of a large additional quantity of sewage to the pond, and which he brlieved had been made without the sanction of the Authority. ALLEGED POLLUTION OP CANAL.—A letter was read from Mr Henry Collier, Bridgewatbr Naviz,ratian Comp tny, Limited, Manchester, drawing the attention of the Authority to the drainage of houses and works into a brook which is a feeder of the Runcorn and Latchford Canal The brook in question runs from Halton past the tanneries of Mr Pier- point and Messrs Ockleston, under the Krithrevater Canal near the house of Mr Wright, and to the Old °my Canal at a point opposite the alkali works of Messrs Wigg dz Co. The pollution of the canal by the 9(eWige turned into the brook is very objectionable, and he shout I be glad to know that the Sanitary Authority would take into early oensidera- tion some means of preventing the sewage finding its way into the brook.—Mr Wear said there was a great nuis- ance caused by the canal. This last fortnight it bad almost been past bearing. He thought the see, ege which caused the nuisance came down the river from Manchester and other places and got into the canal.—The Clerk said it appeared that it was contributed to in the autholity's JiVict. At the monthly meeting of ,the Runcorn Board of C nu- missioners, on Wednesday, after the reporters bad retired from the room. the members had under their consideration Mr. W. H. Linaker's (the law clerk's) bill of costs in the action Beasley v. Commissioners. The items in the bill anabunted to the total sum of £560, and we understand that a motion for the payment of the charge met with opposition from a certain quarter as being excessive, but that the general disposition of the members was to quietly settle the matter. Mr. Linaker agreed to reduce the amount to £5OO, and as be bad previously had £230 on account, a cheque for £270 wee signed. The bill will not be taxed. It is stated that about £3OO of that amount charged represents pay- ments made out of pocket by Mr. Linaker te counsel, wit- nesses, dtc.,
A DISEASE SPREADINGF STREAM AT_RUNCORN.

At the monthly meeting of the Board ef Commissioners, on Wednesday, the Highway and Sanitary Committee sub- mitted the following report by Mr. M. Barker, the surveyor —"I beg to report that I have made an inspection of the Old Quay Canal -at Runcorn, Manchester, Latchford, Old Trafford, and some intermediate places. I find its appear- ance and odour pretty much the same the whole length. It is in a polluted and feoted condition from one end to the other, and it seep b to be evident that the source of such pollution is at Manchester, from dye works, sewage, and other matters, but from whom and from how many con. tributors it would be impossible for me to ascertain. I find that in the district of Runcorn there is a copious flow of tannery sewage and some house drainage from property in the township of Halton, which makes its way down natural water courses into the said canal some little distance beyond the Old Quay Pottery, adding its quoto to the above pollu- tion. I have taken three samples of the water and had them analysed, such analysis will be laid before you. No. ,1 sample was taken beyond the Runcorn district just below the point turn bridge. No. 2 sample was taken in Runcorn, opposiqt the Old Quay Pottery; and No. 3 sample was taken just below ,Old Trafford Bridge, Stretford-road, about two miles below' Manchester. I may add that the appearance is the 'worst at the Runcorn end, the cause being that it remains somewhat stagnant, producing a scnm on the surface, while the upper portions are more or less always in motion."— Consideration of the report was deferred.

How DEBTS ARE PAID UNDER TER NEW BANKRUPTCY ACT.—Williarn Lightfoot, who had followed the occupation of wheelwright, and lived in Spring-street, was summoned to show cause why he should not be sent to gaol for dis- obeying an order of thecourt. Ma Henry White, builder, was the acting creditor, and Mr T A Like appeared on his be- half.—lt appeared that the defendant on the 9th Mara ap- plied under the new Bankruptcy Act for the liquidation of hie debts, which were approaching £5O, by an administra- tion order. At that time it was shown that he was capable Of paying his creditors at the rate of 38s per month, and an order for this amount was accordingly made by his Honour. The defendant had, however, only paid one instalment of 103 during the period which bad elapsed since that, time, although in answer to his Honour and Mr Lake he admitted that with the exception of one month he had been in re- ceipt of wages varying from 30s to 31s per week.—The de- fendant alleged that he was unable to pay 36e per month.— 'Mr Lake observed that the creditors had allowed the de- fendant plenty of time to pay, and had not pressed him in the least, but be had apparently no disposition to par. Re suggested that his amour should suspend the operation of the order for a short time in order to enable the defendant t) pay the arrears -The defendant said when he'obtaiaed the administration order Mr Moores said he would -forgive him a debt of £8 which he owed him for rent, but he now claimed that debt, and had seized big (the defendant's) tools and materials. Reproduced a letter from Mr Moores in sup- port of his conteetion, but it proved to be simply a notice to quit.-114 Honour observed that the fact of this debt being hr existence cast susnicion on the manner in which the order was obtained, The defendant did not seem to Make any attempt to pay anything. The better plan would be to annul the order, and leave the defendant to the mercy of his creditors.—After some further discussion, Mr. Lake suggested that the order should be reduced to £1 per month, and his Honour reduced the order accordingly.—His Hon- our pointed out to the defendant that he was liable to be catninitted to gaol at once for 42 days for disobedience of the order, and informed him that the order was not made to be trifled with, and he must be prepared te deny himself and his family some things ia order to pay his creditors. His Honour then formally made an order of £1 per month, the first payment to be made on the 26th inst. AN ACT OF RETAMATION.—John Worrall, Church-street, Frodsham, sued Martha Gone, of Overton, for £1 16a wages for work done. Mr. Hitehen appeared for the plaintiff and Mr. Lake for the defendant.—From the statement of Me. Hitchen it appeared that the plaintiff was a labourer and in the year 1878 occupied a house belonging to the defendant. During that time the plaintiff worked 12 days for the de- fendant, emptying ashpits and attending to the garden, at the rkte cf Ss per day. This amount was always considered to have been set off against the claim for rapt, but some weeks ago he received a rummies for £2 5s 61 for rent, and, being an ignorant man did not know that he should have made a' counter-claim. ' Judgment was given against bum. The plaintiff and his wife gave evidence' and Mr. Lake Con- tended for the defence that the plaintiff was only doing his duty when he emptied the ashpits, as the tenants had to do the work in turn. He did one day's work in the garden for the defendant; and for this 3s was deducted from the arrears of rent.—He called the defendant and her son in behalf of his contention, and his Honour said that he looked upon the case as an act of retaliation on the part of the plaintiff„ be- cause he was sued for his rent. It wascontrary to all prac- tice for the landlord to empty the tenants' ashpits unless there was a distinct agreement to do so. lie could not help thinking there had been some false swearing on the part of the plaintiff. Judgment for the defendant. A RUNCORN JEWELLER AND ELLIRDRESSER AT VARIANCR. —.limes Sutton, jeweller, Church-street, Runcorn, sued George nebbington, hair dresser and tobacconist, in the Same street, for the sum of L6.—Mr. Lake appeared for the plain- tiff and stated that prior to June last Mr. Sutton occupied a shop number 3, Church-street, where he had certain shop and window fittings and counter, dm, used in connection with his business. Mr. Sutton was leaving that shop and the defendant became the tenant and agreed to take the fit- tings at the sum of V. Repeated applications had b-en made for payment, but the defendant declined to pay.—The plaintiff, John Caygill, joiner,' and William Sutton were called to prove the agreement —Defendant contended that after the bargain was ,made certain fittings were removed, and he therefore declined to pay the money.--Hie Honour said upon each evidence as that given by the plaintiff and his witnesses the,defendant's defence was hopeless.—Judg- meat was entered for the plaintiff.

div.p: RUNCORN CO OPERATIVE SOCIETY: STORMY SCENES.-- , _

The annual meeting of the members of the Runcorn Co- operative Industrial and Provident Seciety, was I held on 'ruesrley evening. Great interest was taken in the appoint, went of secretary, and the large room of the society's premises in Churcb-street was filled to its utmost capacity, nearly one-half the audience being women. Mr Dyer occu- pied the chair, and there were present on the platform the members of the committee, the auditere, the secretary pro. tem., and Messrs Wood and Appleby, of Manchester. In their 44th half-yearly report the committee of management state that the total sales amount to £32,332 153 2d, being a decrease of £2,322 Ns 2iel compared with the correspond- ing period of last year. The 'profits realised, after paying interest and trade expense', amount to £4,358 193 9J, which, lees checks purchased and drapery club bonus and correction ' of errore Of members' claims last half-year, left the net amount disposable of £4,211 123 10J. The committee sug- gested that a dividend of 2361 in the £ be paid, witch would absorb £4,011 103, leaving a balance of £l7O 23 101 to.be carried over to the reserve fund.—After the chairmen had opened the meeting, Mr Fitzpatrick complained that the balance sheet bad only ten placed in the hands of mem- bers that night, and asked if there wee any objection to the adjournment of its ceneideration until Thursday evening, as there were two or three matters which did not meet with his approbation. (Einar, hear.) He further pointed out that in the half-year ending December last the balance sheet showed that a sum of £4 per week had been expended on printing, and he wished to know if it had been signed as correct —The Chairman replied that the delay in issuing the balance sheet had occurred through the auditors not having squared the books up in time.—Mr Wood (of Man- chester) remarked that last year in caneequence of certain unfortunate circumstances he was called in to assist in pre- paring the balance sheet, and he then told them that while he would not be responsible for the correctness of the balance sheet in its details, they might accept the result as correct. The particular item mentioned by Mr Fitzpetrick might have been wrongly classified. He painted out that this half year Mr Appleby and himself had spent many days in proving the membership share account, end they had found under profit and lossaccount errors to ,the extent of £79 03 51, which they had co*rected. They had now put the matter on such a btsis that the accounts would not go wrong again.—Mr Fitzpatrick was not satisfied with the ex- planation. (Hear, hoer.)—Mr Wood pointed out that if the meeting was adjourned the payment of the dividend would be delayed.—Mr Appleby (of Manchester) remarked that the balance sheet had not been audited by pmfessionel ac- countants. It had been prepared by Mr Wood and himself, but the details had been audited by the society's own audi- tors, and he and Mr Woid did hot take upon themselves to say the items were cerrect. They had spoilt seven days in trying to make correct data with regard to future transla- tions on members claim,. They had found no less then 150 errors, and they had bestowed much labour' to make them right.—Mr Fitzpatrick moved that the consideration 'of the balance sheet be deferred, and that the other business be proceeded with.—Mr Povey seconded the motion.—Mr D Worthington asked why didn't the committee 'force the secretary and the auditors to have the balance sheet before the members three days before the meeting as provided by resolution. (Applause.) tie had examined the items in the balance sheet, and itm thought it was the b.st and most honourable balance sheet that had been presented to the members. (Applause.).—Mr Mood Bed the balance sheet , was prepared and fiaished last Friday, but when he and Mr Appleby came to look at it they were satisfied something was wrong. If that balance sheet bad been issued as it was then needs out there could only have been a dividend of 23 31 in the paid, but Mr Appleby and him- self found out errors to the extent of over £5OO. (Seheation.) That would enable them to pay a dividend of 2s 61. (Applause.)—The meeting by an Almost unanimcus vote decided that the consideration of the balance sheet should be proceded with, and Mr A Povey read the statement of accounts—Mr Worthington pointed out that there was a loss ot nearly £3OO in the boot and shoe depart- Ment, but this was satisfactorily exp!fined as a m ere error, that instead of taking 25 per ctent, off the sellipg price there bad only been 5 per cent, taken off. After some further discussion upon the report it was unanimously adapted.— The election of °fibers was the next business, and Mr Jonah Evans was re-appointed treasurer 'without a dissentient voice. Mr W Upton, the secretary pro tent, was then nominated for the office of secretary amid a perfect storm of cheering, and the waving of voting cards. Mr John Littler, whose name was received with hisses, and Mr John Withington were also nominated, and a ballot was demand The Chairman pointed out that as at least five persons were in favour ot such a course, the voting would have to be done in that manner. This statement Was received with load cries of disapprobation, and the ladies excitedly stamped their feet and shouted that there was no need for the ballot. Preparations, however, for the ballot were made, and it vms announced that each person who had a voting card would be given a cheque to place In the ballot box. Immediately the audience crowded •nund the platform, where the com- mittee were in excited conversation together, and men wed women stood upon the forms. The hubbub was worthy of a hustings in the days of open voting at parliamentary elections, and to judge from the countenances of many of the audience, had there been any eggs that hl lost their sweetnese, cabbages, or dead cite, near at heti; they would have quickly travelled towards several objects of their wrath upon the platform. The billet box WAI placed in pesition, and Mr W Rhodes commenced to distribute the checks. Mr Watson contrived above the din that prevailed to make it known that be objected to Mr Rhodes giving checks out. lie added, amid great cheering, that that gentleman was one of the greatest enemies that Mr Upton had upon the com- mittee. Mr Rhodes then mounted the steps leading on to the platform, and, gesticulating in an excited manner, he delivered a speech to Mr Watson, but not a word could he heard, so great was the disturbance and noise ant mgst the audience. Mr Watson then charged Mr Rhodes with giving two or three checks to one perhon. A perfect roar greeted this statement, and there was an almost unieereel shout of "Vote with these "—these being the voting cards which soma of the women held out and shor4 in a manner worthy of a witch when delivering a curse. The disturbance hav- ing. continued some minutes, showed no sings of abating, Mr Appleby ascended a form. Be, was able, after much knocking on the reporter's table with a stick and a free deal of shouting, to restore something like quietness. He remarked that be had attended many meetings of coopera- tive societies, and one in particular he rerrembered where a loss of upwards of 620.000 was declared; but never in the whole of his experience had he attended aineetlog which was conducted so disgracefully and so unreasonably as that one. (Loud cheers.) lie aeked them to attend to the business in a rational, reasonable, and dispassionate manner, and went on to argue the there was no need of the hall( t that evening. (Cheers.) From what he had seen they all appeared to have the courage of their convictionte—(cheers) —and he suggested that he and Mr Wood, who were not at all interested in the election, should be appointed tellers in the ordinary way of voting. ((,heers ) Mr Wood also mede a speech which bad the effect of further pacifying the persons present who bad been in favour andience, and the of a ballot withdrew their demand. Mr Appleby and Mr Wood were then appointed tellers, and the election was pro- ceeded with. the voting resulted es follows :—Uptnn 104, Littler 17, Withington 13. Ha found, how- ever, that tbere were now five alternative schemes for bring- ing a Ship Cant! from Liverpool to Manchester. At pre- seat there were tev ) schemes receiving most Attention. The first was to take the calm! through Warrington and Fern- worth to Garston, and the second Was to come along the Cheshire side to Wig,* Brothers and Steele'e works, then take Along the river tall to Haleheed, aid through the lead to Gerston. He suggested that the Legal and Parliamentary Cmamittee, which had previously had charge of the in etter, should keep a watchful eye upon the operations of the Ship Canal promoters, and endeavour to induce them to adopt such a scheme as would be of benefit to the town of R tocorn. Tine RIGHTS OF THE Faueliordowas —Mr. Pritchard said some years ago there was a committee 'formed on the free- holders' question; but since he had been a member of the Board he had never heard of any meeting being held by that committee. Ile should like to know if it wae still in exis- tence. The freeholders bad certain rights at Higher Run- corn, and if those rights were invested in a public body like the Commissionete respecting the ratepayers the laud might be utilized for the public good, recreation grounds or per- haps more Drodtable uses than that. If this committe was not in working order he thought it should be at once put in a condition to perform its functions and take action—Mr. Speakman tic] some three or four years ago he was ap- pointed by the freeholders of Rancorn as their chairman, • and Mr. W. Handley was appointed secretary. Now, he wanted to know how long that appointment lasted, or whether it was continuous until death released him. He might tell them that no work bad been actually done, al- though there had been some encroachments since his ap- pointment. He did not know by what authority the Brine Company had laid their pipes on the common land, or erected their tank. Certainly as chairman he had had no voice in sanctioning such works, and if he bad any locus standi at all he should be glad to move if he could get a secretary who was alen willing to move. He did not know the position he toned in with regard to the freeholders of Rencorn.—The Chairman said from what he understood the freeholders at this meeting passed a resolution authorising the Commissioners to secure common land under the Control of the Board, and Mr. Linaker was asked to assist the com- mittee and to define the steps they were to take. An enjoyable holiday was spent, and daring the afternoon the newly-ap- pointed organist, Mr J Lytbgoe, gave an orgaa recital in the Parish Church of Townley. Stumps OP A CRIPPLR.— Peter Miller, an aged man and a cripple, who cut his throat last week under circam- Eances previously reported, died from his injuries at his residence in Winwick-road late on Wednesday night. The deceased, who had been somewhat deprewd in spirits, Wag found struggling in a ditc'd near llowley•lane by a woman whose attention bad been a.tracted to the spot by the screaming of some children. When filen it was discovered that his throat was severely out, and a knife was after- wards found in the iminediate neighbourhood. He was at once conveyed home and • be injuries attended to by Dr Adams, bac from the first little hope of his recovery was en- tertained.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON, THURSDAY.

It would be difficult to find in political history a parallel to the sudden, swift, and Complete discomfiture of the Op- position at the present moment. For weeks they have been looking forward to an opportunity of again playing their tramp card in criticism of the policy of the Government in Egypt. It will not be forgotten that some weeks ago they actually brought fdrward a third vote of censure, which was ' swallowed up by a dramatic movement on the part of" the servile majority " who, kicking over the traces and flouting their leaders, refused to set aside public. business in order that the Conservatives might orate. Fince then the progress of affairs has been watched with feverish anxiety. Sir Staf- ford Northcote urged on from behind being ever ready to raise :debate on 'Moons .promising subject. The Con- ference met from time to time and it Was evidently impossible whilst the plenipotentiaries were still in session that the question should be raised and debated in the House of Commons. There was no ground even for complaint of dilatoriness on the part of the Government. They had pledged themselves to push the matter on as fast as possible, and they were undoubtedly doing so. Still the days were speeding by and the end of the session was at hand. Mem- bers were anxious to get off for their holidays, and at length a common understanding was come to. Members might go, but they were not to go far, to report themselves and their various movements to Mr. Zowland Winn, as ticket-of-leave men at stated intervals reported themselves to the police, and to be always ready to come to town for the critical division expected.

Then came the end of the Conference, the announcement of which by Mr. Gladstone in the Home last Saturday drew,forth a loud burst of exultant cheering from the Con- servatives. For the moment things looked well. The Con- ference had failed, and surely some of the consequences of failure must attach to its promoters. But a day's reflection showed that this was a misconception. It was seen and acknowledged on all hands that the failure of the Conference was the best Possible thing that could have happened to the Government. Indeed, so clear was this position that Con- servativsrs began to suspect the whole thing was a movement of deep strategy on the part of the simple and guileless looking gentleman at the head of her Majesty's Govern- ment. He had, so they say, being bound to say something, called together the Conference with the certainty of its failure and with a full knowledge of the immense strengthening of his position that the mere attempt coupled with failure would accomplish. In pursuance of his frequently announced policy of deference to the concert of Europe he had summoned the Powers and submitted his plan. The narrow view taken by France had prevented common concurrence and the whole thing bad come to naught. But Mr, Gladstone hed placed himself and this Country beyond reach of reproach. The state of affairs in Egypt no one questioned, was sa critical that immediate action must be taken. If it could be taken with the caasent of the Powers so much the better. But it must be taken, and since Europe could not agree England must act, all which worked for the good of the Government.

These considerations checked the ardour of the Conserva- tives through Sunday and Monday. Their hesitation WAS shown in the terms of Sir S. Northcote's question. He asked for a day, not en which he might move a resolution, whether vote of censure or otherwise, but on which affairs in Egypt might be "discussed," a way of putting it which left them free to shape their actions according to circum- stances. Mr. Gladstone, in his reply, incidentally men- tioned, as if they were matters of course, the two steps de- termined upon. One the vote of credit for the relief of Gor- don, the other the mission of Lord Northbrook to Egypt. This announcement cltaway the last chanee end final hope of the Censerratives. They instantly satisfied the public mind, and presented no aspect for party att wk. At a meet- ing held in Sir Stafford Nortbcote's room, on Tuesday, it was decided to throw up the sponge. The long-threatened vote of censure mniniously wriggles out of eight, and the pent up indignation of the Opposition with a Government they cannnt datnage finds issue in the common-places of speech-making on the Appropriation Bill. If Sir Stafford Northoote was unhappy and embarrassed with Lord Randolph Churchill in open revolt, his position becomes unendurable now that Lord Randolph is once more "my noble friend," and has been formally admitted to the councils of the leaders. On Monday, whilst the reconcilia- tion was still hut a few days old, Lord Randolph effusively testified to his personal submission. Mr. Gladstone sug- gested tleat it would be more Convenient to take the discus- sion with respect to General Gordon on the Vote of Credit than to raise it, as it might, have been raised, on the Diplo- matic Vote which occupied Monday night. Lord Randolph of course dissented, and threatened to discuss the matter when the vote on account of General Gordon's expenses was reached, thus forestalling debate on the Vote of Credit. Sir S. Northcote timidly expressed the opinion that it wthild be better to postpone the discussion till the Vote of Credit was reached, whereemen Lord Randolph at once yielded and matters were so arranged. Yesterday, however, the novelty of the situation having worn off he broke out again. Sir S. Northcote had at the Meaning of the sittiog agreed to take the discussion on Egypt on Friday, thus giving an op- portunity for supply to be closed to-night and the machin- ery of the Appropriation Bill set working. In the courts of the afternoon Lord Rendolph Churchill arrived, and finding that the most inconvenient course would be to take the de- bate to-day, insisted that it should be so arranged. He plan- ted himself on the front. Opposition Bench by the side of Sir S. Northcote, and worried that amiable gentle nan into acquiesance with his views. At a quarter to six in the even- ing Sir Stafford recanted his opinion, expressed at a quarter to one in the afternoon, and amid expressions from the other aide of " sairprise and regret declared he would raise the discussion at to-night's sitting. Having thus tasted blood Lord Randolph went on the rampage, and in imitation of one of Mr. Biggar'is familiar Wednesday afternoon performances, blocked the progress of all the remaining business. In November Lord Cairns will have additional trouble on his bands beyond that of the effort that must inevitably be made to tame Lord Salisbury and -do what can be done to avert the fate of the House of Lords. The Garmoyle- Fortescue case will be on at that time, there being no truth whatever in the statement recently put forward that the &fide had been arranged out of court. The damages are .laid at A 20,000, and I believe the nearest approach to that sum which Lord Cairns has been willing to pay in order to avoid the scandal of trial in open court has been £7,000. Miss Forteseue's case is, however, far too strong to permit her accepting a compromise on such a basis. It is well known that the letter in which Lord Garmoyle conveyed to the lady his decision (or rather that of his respected parents) to break off the match was couched in terms that may 01 described only as brutally coarse. This letter is a exized possession of the lady's counsel, and it is expec, enu that wheq it il read in court it will have a notable effAct upon the amount of damages. There was no reason apparent to the cuter worm why the Garmoyle-Fortescae case should not have come on before the Courts rose. Explanation is fots*rl in some quarters in the fact that, also among the c ins da for special jurors, was that in which another eminent judicial personage has a family interest. But just wleen the special jury causes were within reeasureeble distance the judges calmly announced that they would net hear them till af:er the long vacation, and thus the evil day was imistponed. It involved many persons in enorm ius expense and trouole, and protraction of anxiety. But their lordships personal cenvenieoce had to be considered, and so the causes were postnoned. Miss Fortescue herself hid an engagement in the United Stites f-r the winter, which she is, of course, obliged to forego, though I Isalieve the j iurney ie only postponed, and she will appear in America, same time next year carrying her sheaves with her. She is now playing a quiet part in "Our Boys," where her preseuce does not excite that measure of interest at one time looked forward to by an enterprising manager. Mr. Gladstone is perhaps the most variowsly painted, and certainly the most widely photographed public man of the age. Everyone knows or has heard of the eplendid picture by Millais, which, by the way, was en view at Edinburgh at the time of the last Midlothi en campaign. Now, on the verge of another Midlothian campaign, the Premier is once mom sitting to the same artist. The picture Mr. Millais row has in hand is Intended for the Deans Hall of Christ Church College. .Oxford. Mr. Gladstone gave his first sitting early in July, but the artist has already made con- siderable prevail* with the work, which promises to be an improvement even on the last. Oae advantage from a pictorial point of view is that on this occesion the Premier is in nis robes, which hang well on a figure we are apt to forget is tall and stately. I remember at the splendid page. ant of the opening of the Law Courts, Mr. Gladstone then stood by the Queen in his robes as Chancellor of the Ex- chequer, the very Last time I believe he wore them. His manner is always dignified, except:when he is squabbling

div.p: with Mr. Warton or Lord Randolph. But no one who has Sean him only in the dress which Mr. Carlyle used to describe as appropriate for a forked radish can coneeive the t measure of dignity lent to his carriage by the black siik robe with its massive gold braid. There stood on or near the dais lords, marquises, dukes, and a' that; but, apart from Other considerations, the most dignified figure present was that of the great Commoner. A scheme iion foot to bring about a great American ex- . hibition in London. The promoters have got so far as to. fix a day of opening, which is to be the Ist of May, 188& Other arrangements more troublesome to make are not quite so far advanced. The p:rforinance, if ad, quately carried out, will be on a scale commensurate with the vastness of the American continent.

1 One of the most ridiculous and indefensible of the 9maller foibles of society just now is to have headings onnotepaper printed in large plain type. As the notepaper, particularly that used by ladies, is often very small, this gigantic letter- ing has a ludicrous effect. If the proper kind of person were to have his or her address printed backward, or in tha middle of the sheet, the communication being written round it, it would speedily become fashionable.

- _ THE INQUEST. Mr. Husband, deputy-co oner, held an inquest on Satur- day at the honee of Mr. Lake, Buttermarket-street, War- rington, touching the death of Mr. Thames Saxon, land- lord of the Fox Inn, Warrington, which occurred on the previous day under circurnstaaces already reported. On the jury ceming forward to be sworn, a Mr. William Robinson ote'ected to take the oath.—The Coroner : On what ground? —Mr. Robinson : Ido not believe in a Christian God ; I object to take the oath on that account.—You don't ! And you object to take the oath on that ground? Yee.—Do you believe in anything else? I believe in performing a pro- tniee —Have you any other reason for objecting to take the oath? don't just think of any at present.—That is the only reason ? Yes.—it is not because you want to get away ie a hurry or anything of that sort? No.—Simply because you do not believe in a Christian God ? Yes.—l do not, of course, presume to swear you under the circumstances, but at the same time it would be very unfair as the law stands at present that you should leave until the inquest is over, as you have been summoned on the jury, because I have been told—whether there is any truth or not in it I do not know—that it is getting to be a sort of a habit by some persons for the purpose of getting off coroners' juries. I do not presume that that is your reason, and under these circumstances I will ask you to wait until the inquest is over in case anything further is to be done in the matter, but it happens that there is another juryman present to take your place. I presume there is no other juryman present who does not believe in a Christian God ?—Margaret Saxon, widow of the deceased, then gave evidence. She appeared deeply agitated. Witness mid that she rose at 6-30 the pre- vious morning, leaving her husband in bed. At 7.15 she received by post a letter addressed to her in the handwriting of her husband. When she had read the first two lines she ran upstairs to the bedroom and saw the deceased with his throat cut. Seeing blood all over the bed, she ran down- stairs screaming and called Mr. Allen, of the Pelican Inn. The blood was all over the counterpane, sheets, and carpet. Information was then given to the police and Dr. Joseph sent for. Deceased lived until about one o'clock the same thy. She thought he was about fifty years of age. Busi- ness matters had been troubling him of late. In reply to Mr. Robert Davies, solicitor, witness said that she and her husband were at his (Mr. Davies's) office on Monday, when Mr. Davies advised her husband to make out a list of his debts. Deceased was very low and despondent and shed tears in the room. Mr. Clarke, from the brewery, spoke very kindly to him and told him not to put himself out of the w ty. Her husband'e brother died in a lunatic asylum, its which be 'was confined 15 years.—The letter received by the widow was then read, but the reporters were requested riot to make its ntents public.—P.C. eingleton deposed to finding a razor and two pools of blood on the bed. He had doticed the deceased on the day before his death to be in a very dejscted condition —llle jury returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased committed suicide whilst temporarily insane.—The Coroner slid that he had every respect for a man's religious opinions, but he had thought it only fair to the oth..r jurymen that the objecting person should remain in the room until the close of the inquest.

Tam ST. HELENS V INERS' AGENCY.—Mr. John Cross, who took d conspicuous part in the late agitation of the West Lancashire colliers against a reduction of 10 per cent., has rosigned the pos,tion of miners' agent for the St. Hderle district. A fe-ling in favour of working the district by lodge representAtives, instead of by an agent, is said to he gaming ground, but as yet no steps have been taken to fill the Vacancy.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF THE REFORM AGITATION.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF THE REFORM AGITATION.

GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse, Warrington, on Wednesday morning. There were present Messrs. Greening (chairman), Derbyshire, Ap- pleton, Jolley, Cooper, Brown, Harrison, Hunt, Wn. Houghton, Humphreys, Greenall, the Rev. G. F. Roberts; J. C. Sutton (clerk). and S. Sutton (assistant clerk.) THE MEDICAL CHARGES AT NEWTON. I On the minutes of the Finance Committee coming up tor confirmation, Mr. DARBYSHIRE said he noticed that the ac- counts for expensive medicines for Newton township were 2s more this quarter than last quarter, and last quarter they were thought to be excessive. When compared with the other portions of the union—Warrington and Latchford— the charges for expensive medicines for Newton were very high indeed. He did not say that it had not been necessary to give them, nor did he say the medicines had not been all used or anything of that kind, but the charges did appear to be very high in comparison with other parts of the dis- trict. He thought it would only be proper if the medicines for Newton were got from proper qualified druggists, in the same way as at Warrington. The Guardians, be thought, could not allow that state of things to pass over without mention and without investigating these accounts. It was a very proper way for the Board to procure medicines through Dr. Watkins, but he as a member of the Board should prefer that they were got from some respectable chemist. He would not make any motion, but he thought that was the proper course to take —Mr. APPLETON: Give notice to move.—Mr. HioNT could not see what the Board could do in the matter. All the medicine that had been administered was recorded in the book; the book had been brought before the committee, who examined it and found every house and person to whom it had been given marked down.—The CLERK suggested that the subject should be considered by the committee at New- ton, and what he would recommend would be that instead of taking the accounts in the whole when presmted to them they should, when the doctor's book came before them, con- sider each individual case. That would give them an oppor- tusity of knowing how to deal with that question.—Mr. Huter said the committee had nearly looked through the whole of the book last time, and he did not see what earthly good they could do. Every person's name was there.—The CLERK: Then you cannot expect anythinemore. If they said that the doctor had virtually done what he ought to have done under the circumstances then there was an end or it.-4r. APPLETON thought that when they were paying Ss more per thousand ill Newton than'in Warrington it was a fair thing to raise an argument upon, and it was a proper thing for the Board to take into consideration, because there was such a disparity between the chaeges for Newton and for Warrington.—The CLERK said they could not suppose that the committee at Newton, who knew the people, were not in a position to advise that Board whether the charges were correct or not. Until the committee did that it seemed to be entirely impracticable for the Board to deal with the matter there. There was a special committee ap- pointed under the authority of law the district relief committee of Newton and it seemed to him that those gentlemen who administered re- lief in Warrington or other parts of the district were not in a position to say whether the Newton relief had been given rightly or wrongly.—Mr. JOLLEY had no doubt that Dr. Watkins would not administer medicines unnecessarily, but what the Guardians wanted was that those medicines that were recommended by the doctor should be supplied by a respectable chemist, and they as a Board of Guardians ought to know how the prices tallied with the prices in Warrington. They did not dispute that the doctor supplied the best medicines he could ; but there was thus principle in- volved that the doctor who supplied these medicines might perhaps supply them more promiscuously when having a profit upon them. He did not say that was so, but it might be so. Seein,e that the charges they paid were double what they were in Warrington, he thought the proper way out of the difficulty was to have the medicines supplied by a chemist. He proposed that they be obtained from a respect- able chemist of the neighbourhood.—The CLERK thought they had not evidence sufficient before them as to their be- ing excessive charges. If the Newton Committee would like to know what the charges were in Warrington he could send them a list of charges; but he thought it would be inconvenient for them to adopt such a resolution unless they had previously got some basis on which to base it.— Mr. APPLETON: The basis is good enough when we are paying 61 to Warrington Is. The basis is good enough to work upon.—The CLERK said he found that it was part of Dr Watkins' contract to supply these medicines. He should suggest to them as the proper course that the matter be left to the Newton Committee.—Mr JOLLEY : Will you send them a list of the other charges?— The CLERK: Yes.—The Rev. G. F. ROBERTS said that he did not see why if in one case they adopted one mode of supplying the medicines they could not adopt the same mode in the other. If in this part of the Union medicines were supplied by chemists why not in another.—The CLERIC said there was a distinction drawn in the consolidated orders, as it would be exceedingly difficult in some rural districts to administer medicines in that way.—Mr JOLLEY did not think that would apply to Newton.—Mr APPLETON: You cannot call our district a rural district —The CHAIRMAN did not think there was any evidence that Dr Watkins had been imposing on the people ; there was no such evidence whatever.—Mr DARBYSHIRE : There is no such feeling.— The CHAIRMAN, continuing, said he agreed with Mr Roberts that it would be better to have a uniform system where it could be applied. Dr Watkins might be a different dis- penker of medicines to the doctors here, and might think it the cheapest plan to give them the medicines in the way he gave them so as to bring the patients round more quickly. At any rate there were many things to be taken into account before coming to a determination ; and he thought the proper plan was for the Newton Relief Committee to have the list from Warrington, which Mr Sutton would very gladly supply, and for them to consider the two lists toge- ther.—This was agreed to, and on the motion of Mr DARBY- SHIRE, seconded by Mr APPLETON, the accounts were passed.

DEMONSTRATION AT BIRMINGHAM. A great meeting was held on Monday night in Bingley Hall, a vast building capable of holding 20,000 people. Long before the time announced for the opening of the proceed- ings every portion of the hall, except the far end of the area, was crowded with people. No seats were provided ex- cept on the platform and in the balconies, and for more than an-hour a surging crowd, tightly packed, stood in the body of the hall waiting the arrival of the speakers. The wait was enlivened by singing a series of well-known Liberal songs, such as "The People's Anthem," "The Liberal ` March," and the less familiar "People and Peers," and in cheering the names of members of the Government and local Liberal leadees. Mr Gladstone's name was received with great enthusiasm, and repeated cheers were given for Mr Bright and Mr Chamberlain. Mr Jesse Collings, M.P., was recognised as he came upon the platform, and was heartily welcomed. Mr Broadhurst's appearance was greeted with three ringing cheers. Mr G Dixon, Mr Powell Williams, Mr Arch, and Mr Schnadhorst also had a special welcome. Other gentlemen on the platform were Mr A Brogden, M.P., Mr Alderman White (ex-Mayor), Mr R Tangye Mr F Wright, and Mr AC Osier. Mr Bright entered the building at half- pest seven o'clock, accompanied by Mr Chamberlain, and for several minutes the hall rang with vigorous cheers, which burst forth afresh, followed by a verse of "Auld Lang Syne" as Mr Bright, haying taken the chair, rose to open the businese of the meeting. Perfect silence was not secured indeed before the chairman had spoken two or three sentences, and the right hon. gen- tleman, who now indicated that he might speak, rather strongly impressed upon the vast assembly the necessity of keeping quiet, and then called upon Mr George Dixon, a tried and trusted Birmingham Liberal, who has represented the constituency in Parliament and is intended to so again, to move the resolution. The duty was performed in a speech not the less effective because it was brief. Mr R Tangye, following, had at first to contend against considerable noise, caused rather by the pressure than the disorder of the now packed area. Somewhat unexpectedly, Mr Chamberlain being next on the printed programme, the Chairman now took the opportunity of delivering his speech. For ten minutes he was not a little hindered by his own admirers in the body of the hall, men who were so anxioue to signify their agreement with his sentiments chat they shouted aloud at various points. These ripples of ill-advised support ran , through that portion of the spe ch in which the ' peers in their various capacities were described, at least to the description of their entrance to the temple of honour through the sepulchre of a dead ancestor. Here there was a temporary lull. On his proposing to inquire what the peers bed done in the past, after the quotation from the 73rd Psalm, there was a resumption of restlessn .ss and a demand to turn some- body out. This proposal was, however, rebuked by Mr. Bright, who proceeded to explain tha the peers constitute a breed that has not changed, and to discuss the remedy for the difficulty now presented to the nation was necessary. He said that a creation of peers would only dispose of the pre- sent difficulty. He claimed to have for 40 years exerceeed a Conservative influence, inquiring if the reforms of 1832, 1847, and 1867 had not been granted what would there be of the Conservatism of the Conservatives to conserve at this hour. He demanded whether the people were to submit or to curb the nobles, and a reedy response was forthcoming. The proposition to limit the veto of the Lords, leaving them their social privileges but depriving them of absolute power, was worked out by the right hon. gentleman amidst all the difficulties of increasing hoarseness, but enforced clearly to the end. Mr. Bright persevered, but as his voice weakened the inconsiderate friends strengthened their too zealous in- terpolations. The voice was strongly raised in the remark that" Your fathers curbed the Crown ; we their sons can curb the nobles;" and the speaker shortly afterwards sat down amidst prolonged cheers, renewed as the audience, with a unanimous shout of "Aye," leaned to their feet to pass the resolution. A remarkable demonstration broke out at the uprising of Mr. Chamberlain. There had been no more significant cheering at any previous portion of the day, no more spon- taneous exercise than the singing "for he's a jolly good fellow," or the anti-climax of cheers at the end of it. Al- though the crowded people in the area were more quiet than they had been during the previous half-hour. Mr. Cham- berlain, however, gripped their attenti in at last by his vigorous attacks upon the Peers, and more especially by his banter of Lord selisbury, as the chief conspirator who shrank from the confession of his crime. The story of the man who declined to get into his shower bath without an um- brella took splendidly, but the cheering at the application of the history to the action of the Commons with regard to two million of voters was quite as significant as the accompany. ing laughter. The meeting listened with approving interest when the speaker declared that it was time to take stand against the arrogant pretensions of the Lords, as it had previously done when he warned the Lords themselves to take heed, and it was sympathetically excited during the ani- mated delivery of the concluding indictments which cul- minated in that droll quotation— Alas, un-onseions of their doom The little victims play. Henceforth there was no need to hush the over-zealous. Every sentence was vociferously appleu4ed, and immense enthusiasm crowned the fervently delivered peroration. The audience began to melt away after this speech, and they went home gleefully congratulating each other that Birmingham at least had at Bingley Hall, through its two members, spoken with no uncertain sound about the House of Peers. The remaining speeches by Mr. Broadhurst, M.P.. who was warmly received, and by Mr. Joseph Arch—an old acquaintance in these parts—and others, were short and earnest, and the final reeolutiora of thanks to Mr. Bright was a fitting close to the demonstration.

A great out-door demonstration io favour of the Fran- chise Bill was held at Darlington, on Saturday. A proces six), headed by bands, marched to Pierremont, where ad- dresses were delivered by Sir Joseph Pease, Mr. Thedore Fry, and Mr. Joseph Pease, M P.'s, and Sir Henry Havelock Allan, in support of a resolution protesting against the action of the House of Lords.
At Devizes, Sir Thom is Bateman spoke, supporting the action of the Lords, and disp-ovin.; of the p)licy of the Go- vernment.

A Conservative demonstreion was also held at Nuttall Hall Ramsbottom, Lancashire, at which resolutions were adopted recording approval of Lord Salisbury's leadership in the Howe of Lords on the franchise question. Mr Carbutt and Mr Woodall, members of Parliament. addressed a large open air meeting on Saturday evening near Newport, Mon. Resolutions were passed condemning the House of Cords for rejecting the Franchise Bill, and ap- proving the policy of the Government in proroguing Par- liament to an autumn session in order to pass the Bill. An out-door demonstration and procession in support of the Franchise Bill was held at Stockport, several thousand people taking part in the proceedings. Mr Rylancls, Mr Pennington, and Mr Hopwood, members of Parliament, were the principal speakers. At Southampton a similar procession paraded the streets to one of the public parks, where Mr Henry Lee and Mr Illingworth delivered addresses. At both demonstrations resolutions were passed in support of the Franchise Bill and condemning the House of Lords. A county demonstration in favour of the Franchise Bill was held in Bedford. Lord Tavistock, Mr Whitbread, Mr Howard, and Mr Maguire spoke. Resolutions for the Bill were carried with acclamation.

Mr FIV Grafton, M.P., laid the foundation stone of a new Liberal club at Accrington, and in the evening public meetings were held. Mr Briggs, M.P., and Sir Ughtred Kiy Shuttleworth delivered speeches in support of the Franchise Bill and denouncing the House of Lords. At Petersborough a large Liberal meeting ended a motion for the total abolition of the House of Peers.

A demonstration to protest against ths rejection of the Franchise Bill was held on Monday afternoon on Peckham Rye, and was attended by repreaentatives of various political clubs throughout the Metropolis, about seven thousand per- sons being present. Mr. Sydney Burton, MP.. speaking to a resolution approving the policy of the Government and protesting against the unchecked power of the House of Lords, expressed the opinion that the Upper House was a very necessory institution, and said he would rather see it reorganised than abolished. A Liberal demonstration at genfield, near Brighton, on Monday, passed a resolution supporting the Govern- ment.

Mr. D. Maclver, M.P., speaking at the Birkenhead Con. servative Picnic on Monday, said he regarded the collapse of the Egyptian Conference without regret, as no benefit could be expected from it. He characterized the franchise agitation as dishonest, and originated by the Birmingham caucus to keep the Government in office. -

• A meeting of the Liberal representatives of the polling districts in the South-West Riding of Yorkshire, held at Wakefield on Monday, appointed a committee to select can- didates to contest the division in place of the Hon. W. H. Fitzwilliam and Mr. W. FL Leatham, the sitting members, who have announced their intention of not seeking re- election. On the motion of Mr. Leatham, a resolution was passed expressing a hope that the Franchise Bill would take precedence of every other question. A Conservative demonstration, presided over by Lord Tredegar, was held in Tredegar Park, Newport, Monmouth- shire, on Monday, and addressed by Lords Carnarvon and Cranbourne. Lord Carnarvon said the attack on the House of Lords meant an alack on the Crown and other institu- tions which had secured prosperity to the people. The failure of the Conference should be cause for congratula- tion, as the conditions proposed would have brought mis- chief and dishonour on the country.

Sir S. Northcote, speaking at Hughenden Manor, where the Landon and Westminster Working-men's Constitutional Association held their annual picnic, expressed his deep regret at the change which had taken place in our foreign relations since Lord Beaconsfield guided the policy of Eeg. land. Therwanted to know what the Government would do in the recess. As to reform, the House of Lords were quite willing to deal with it on true and scientiric grounds. —Mr. W. H. Smith, who also spoke, protested against legis- lation under pressure. At a conference held in London on Wednesday a league was formed having for its object to "prevent the House of Lords from continuing to obstruct, mutilate, and defeat leg. islation." the means to be adopted to tide end being to re- strict the legislative veto of the House of Peers and to stop the creation of kereditary peerages. Sir W. Lawson was present at the conference, and he said that per.onallv he was In favour of a bold, straightforward measure for doing away with the House of Lords altogether. If the House of Corn- ii ens refused supplies the thing would be done. He &K- -w sted the formation of branches of the League through- out the country, as in the case of the Anti-Corn Law League

div.p: THE COST OF VACCINATION CASES.

The CLERK Siid he had, as instructs 4 at last meeting, ap- plied to Mr. Buckton, clerk to the Newton bench, for the par- ticulars of the bill of charges sent in to the Board of Guar- dians in respect of the vaccination prosecutions at Newton. The former bill amounted to £l2 78, while the bill of par- ticulars which bad been sent amounted to £l3 44—Mr. AP- PLETON : We had better stick to the old bill I think. (Laughter.)—The CLERK said that Board did pay towards the cost of the police at Newton. He did not know what a constable's wages were per week, but it would take one two hours at the outside to deliver 15 summonses, and a charge of £4 was made for the constable. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. HAR- RISON : These are deemed to be magistrates' clerk's fees.— The CLERK: They are for the services. Mr HARRISON: But still they are magistrates' clerk's fees—The CLERK : It is really a magistrates' clerk's bill.—Mr. APPLETON: Do you think the policeman gets that? Mr. HARRISON : No, no. ' —Mr. JOLLEY : Why say constable service 34 when the con- stable gets nothing.—Mr. HARRISON: It is called the con- stable's fee.—Mr. JOLLEY : Yes, it is using his name to make up a bill.—Mr. HARRISON: The money will no doubt go to the magistrates' clerk.—Mr. BROWN: It is a great shame.—The CLERK said it was certainly an animaly that when a policeman got L 1 per week £4 should be charged for two hours work.
THE CALLS.—In answer to a question the CLERK mid a list of the calls owing by the various townships, and he was instructed to write to those townships which still owed two calls

_ A COMPULSORY SCHOOL BOARD —The CLERIC mentioned that in consequence of the omission to provide sufficient school accommodation at Great Sankey, the Edecation De. partment had decided upon enforcing the appointment of a compulsory School Board.—This concluded the business of public interest.

EARLESTOWN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY% —0 a Mon day evening the quarterly meeting of the shareholders was held in the Co-operative Hall. Earle-street ; Mr W Davies (pre- sident) occupying the chair. There was a good attendance. . The balance sheet showed that the receipts for the quarter were £4,137 3.44 d, on which there was a net profit nt £540 198.5 p. From this a dividend of 2s 61 in the £to the members was declared, and a bonus of £l3 103 3d to labour. Messrs J Jones and J Moss were elected to serve on ths Committee of Management ; Mr J Teece was re-elected auditor ; and it was decided to take up shares to the extent of £lOO in the Rochdale Corn Mill. Cartunw OF AN ALLEGED HORSE STEALER.—Con- siderable excitement was occasioned in the neighbourhood of Market-street, Earlestown, on Monday evening, by the apprehension under somewhat singular circumstances of one of a tribe of gipsies on a charge of stealing a horse, the pro- petty of Messrs Richard Evans and Co, of Haydock. Some time ago the firm missed one of their horses from a field and nothing further was heard of it until Monday when a labourer employed by Messrs Evans observed the animal among a number of others in charge of a tribe of gipsies encamped on the plot of land bordering the road to the Common, opposite the Baptist Chapel, Earlestown. Infor- mation was given to the police and an officer from St. Helens inquired into the matter. As a result one of the gipsies was taken info custody, much to his "surprise." He denied the charge, but he was conveyed to St. Helens and locked up until Tuesday, when he was brought up at the Town Hall and remanded. The accused was again brought up at the St. Helens Town Hall on Thursday, when he was discharged owing to no evidence of identification of the horse as the property of Messrs. Evans being forthcoming. CIIIIRCII AFFAIRS AT EARLESTOWN.—The petition to the Bishop of Liverpool praying for the removal of the Vicar of Earlestown (the R9V T R Matthews) was forwarded to its proper destination on Tuesday, after having been signed by over 700 parishioners and members of the con- gregation. A communication has since been received from the Bishop's secretary acknowledging its receipt, and stating that any proposal for exchange of livings would have to come from Mr Matthews In the first instance. This reply is tooled upon by the parishioners as most unsatisfactory, for as it will be noted the answer to the petition does not say anything about whether the Bishop has power to remove I the vicar, or whether he will do so, an expression of opigion to which effect the petitioners were anxious to obtain. There was only a very meagre attendance at each of the 88EViCeS on Sunday last, there being about 20 present on each occa- sion. It Is stated that since Sunday the vicar has succeeded in obtaining a new carat!, who, we believe, has already Visited a good many parishioners. It is rumoured that the vicar is about to leave the town for some weeks, and one pariahioner has expressed the opinion that that is to give the n.w curate an opportunity of gathering in the "cen- tered " in the absence of the vicar. Whether he will succeed n doing this remains to be seen. •
