'IRE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, AUGUST 9, 1884. WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. A monthly meeting of this Council was held in the Council Chamber, Town Hall, on Tuesday evening, the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) presiding. There were also present Aldermen Burgess, Kean, Webster, Holmes, Thewlis ; Councillors Greening, Caldwell, Francomb, Wal- lington, Dixon, Mackie, Barker, Broadbent, Monks, William Pierpoint, Whittle, Wright, Brown, and Marsh. THE MANCHESTER 6HIP CANAL. The MAYOR said the only cornmunicatiox he should have to trouble them with was one dated July 18,h from Mr. Whitworth, the secretary of the Manchester Ssip Canal. It stated that at a meeting of the Provisional Committee he was instructed to say that it afforded them much pleasure to offer for the Council's acceptance, on behalf of the Warrington Musentn and Library, a copy of the minutes of the proceedings before Parliament in connection with the Manchester Ship Canal Bill. Tho proceedings would occupy two or three volumes, which would be sent at the close of the case. He (the Mayor) presumed they would be vory glad to have that present. (Hear, hear.) I Dr. Mrecxim asked, when referring to the Ship Canal, if I they would allow him just one moment to make a communi- cation regarding the notification that had just been read. He was sure it would be a pleasure to all of them to know that, within the last three hours, the Canal Committee had had a special meeting, the most crowded he had ever been present at, and they had come to the unanimous decision to proceed with the making of the canal from Manchester to Liverpool by Warrington. They would be pleased when he told them that that resolution was proposed by one of the most respected and best known men in Manchester, Mr. John Rylands ; that it was seconded and supporteVy the Mayors of S;ockport and Salford ; and that it had in every respect the most unanimous approval. They would perhaps be more pleased when he told them that taking the benefit of experience the committee had decided to get rid of the estuary theory that had been so long a bugbear, and they were going to cleave closer to the Lancashire side of the river. In fact they were going to come much nearer to War- rington than they ever proposed before. Out of the five alternative schemes they had had in view, and which he had had the pleasure of seeingthat day that had, pro, ten. t., agreed to teat which would mean that the canal should cross from opposite Hite Head and make its way to the deep water at Garston. It had been not so much his intention to tell them that as to tell them that the engineer asked him as a per- sonal favour to state to the Council of the borough at the first opportunity that under the altered circumstances he would be extremely obliged if the Council, or the committee in charge, would allow tneir borough surveyor or any other gentleman in authority to meet him at an early day to see whether any better tarps than what had been agreed upon in the la-I bill could be come to with Warrington. The committee realised the kindness shown by Wallington in many respects. Mr Leader Williams, who, they knew, was the very essence of good nature to begin with, was very anxious that at this early stags something should be done, if it could be done, in connection with the position and the extent of the docks, to make Warrington more satisfied than it had hitherto been. ([dear, hear.) Mr BROADBENT Said he had been very much interested by the information Dr Mackie had given them ; but be rose more particularly to say that they should express their thanks for that really very valuable present of those volumes. It was a valuable presentation, as the volumes I contained a great mass of very valuable information which would be interesting to Warrington for all time, whether the canal was made or not. (Hear hear.) Dr MACKIE said he had omitted to mention that the com- mittee had been moved chiefly to the alteration of the course he bad named to get rid of the estuary, by the ex- tremely kind nature of the remarks and the evidence given by Sir W B Forwood, and also by the remarks of the coun- sel employed by the Liverpool C.rporation and the Liver- pool Dock Board. That had been specially mentioned, and it was only common fairness that he should re- peat it. Alderman WEBSTER seconded the vote of thanks for the presentation of the volumes. The MAYOR said the volumes had reference to perhaps one of the most important events that had taken place for a , very long time past, that was the making of a ship canal, which, it appeared, was not even yet done with. The vote of thanks for the presentation was then carried I unanimously.

to keep their parents, and more particularly cases of chil- dren who were of the street arab class, and were perhaps, un- fitted and unsuitable to join the children at the ordinary schools, and who seemed to require for their successful treat- ment something of the nature of an industrial school. He was not prepared on the spur of the moment to say more, but he thought that it woald do no harm to bring that as- pect of the subject before the Council. There was a great difficulty to be met, and he thought there was a great need for such a school as he had referred to. Alderman BURGESS remarked that the observations of Councillor Broadbent led up to ono final issue—a School , board.

Mr. CALDWELL did not think there was any necessity for a School Board, as there were schools enough in Warrington to accommodate 1.200 or 1,300 children. As regarded rag- ged children he Was of opinion that there many schools that would receive them willingly. If they had a School Board there would still be ragged children. Alderman WEBSTER said that the subject was one which constantly engaged the attention of the committee. As a rule persons were not summoned until they had been twice before the committee and they found that there was a de- ficiency on the part of parents more than children in some cases. No doubt there was a need for such a school as had been mentioned—there was a greater need formerly—but he did not think that there was any necessity at the present moment for children to roam the streets if their parents had any desire to send them to school. As Mr. Caldwell said, there were schools that would be glad to take them.

MUSEUM, LIBRARY, A.NI> ARTS COMMITTEE. Alderman WEBSTER moved, and Councillor CaLnwEra, seconded, the addpcion of the minutes of this committee. In making the proposition, Alderman Webster observed that there were now in the Art Gallery three fine pictures by Turner, which was a great acquisition. They were not mentioned in the report because the matter had not yet come officially before the committee. Mr. MONKS thought that it would be desirable that the committee should tak3 steps to inform the public when any such acquisitions were received.

Alderman WEBSTER said that that was generally done. Mr. WHITTLE said that he should like to know what was paid for the pictures. He had been told that they were not worth looking at, and that £4O was paid on them for insu- rance.

The MAYOR agreed with Coancillor Monks that it was desirable that when pictures from such an eminent artist as Turner were sent to Warrington some means should be taken to give the fullest publicity to the fact. It was desirable that the public should know what a treat was in their grasp.
Alderman Webster : It has not yet come officially before the committee; I simply mentioned the fact to give publi- city to it. I have no doubt next month it will appear on the minutes.
Aldermen BURGESS and THEWLIS also spoke on the sub- j.ct, after which the minutes were duly passed. TOWN HALL, PARK, AND BATHS COIEWITTEE.—MUSIC IN
THE PARE. After the reading of the minutes of this committee. Mr. Dlxos referred to the possibility of getting the wall re- moved in front Of the Town Hall, but no action was taken lathe matter.

Mr. MONKS drew attention to the question of music ic the park. He understood that several years ago there were several bands in the town willing to perform for public amusement in the park, but since then, he thought, very little action had been taken to encourage such a movement, They would all admit that the performance of music in the park was an amusement which it was most desirable to en- courage—(hear, hear)—and he should be glad to ascertain before the summer was over what steps had been taken, and if it was the intention of the committee to take steps in the matter.

Mr. BROADBENT was glad that Mr. Monks had introduced the subject. He did not know whether the committee had been lax, but it so happened that in one of the finest sum- mers they had had that century there had been less music in the park than before. He quite agreed as to the elevating effects of good music, and if the introduction of the subject stimulated the committee it would be a good thing. Dr. MACKIE : I called the attention of the committee ai our last meeting to this subject, and there was some satisfac- tory. answer given,but I do not remember what it was.

, The MAYOR said that some two months ago he was waited upon by a member of one of tne bands which had been in the habit of playing there, who reminded him that last year no notice had been taken of them, and consequently they did not play. He (the Mayor) said that they must resume their playing, and if the Town Council refused to pay, he would himself pay it. Since then the band bad regularly played, and were now playing quite as frequently as they did a year or two ago. When he brought the matter before the committee the action that he had taken was fully endors(d, and, therefore, as the committee said it would pay all expenses, it was really an order of the com- mittee.

Several members continued the discussian, Alderman WEBSYER remarking that ifathey could have the band of the Workhouse boys in the park it would be a treat, as he him- self heard it the day before and was delighted—The MAYOR said that the band played exceedingly well, and he thought that their services might be obtained.—The subject then dropped. _
'.ll;e minutes of the committee were adopted on the motion of the MAYou, seconded by Mr. WHITTLE. - - _ _
THE PIZICE OF GAS.

In moving the minutes of the Gas Committee Aid. Holmes expressed his pleasure in asking them to make a reduction in the price of gas of 3d per 1,000 feet. The committee ware unanimous that the time had now arrived when a re- duction should be made, but they were not precisely unani- mous as to the amount. He thought it would be needful for him to trouble them n with a few figures to show how they arrived at that amount. For the year ended the 25th March last the total amount of profits made was £13,657 4s 21, out of which had ta be paid to the Borough Treasurer annuities and interest and in repayment of debt, £lO 693 168, leaving a surplus after all payments of £2,963 83. 22. It was on the baeis of that surplus that they proposed te make the reduction. A reduction of 3d per 1,000 feet would absorb £1,925, taking the sales of gas at about the same figures as Dion of last year. That would reduce the surplus to about £l,OOO. They thought it was only a fair thing to adopt that course, and not to divide the whole of their profits,—to do as public bodies, divide a part of their profits and carry forward the balance. Since the Corpora- tion purchased the gasworks they had paid off £132.54 in reduction of the debt, by instalments, ranging over the last four years. The price of their residual products was variable, which he looked upon as another reason why they should not absorb the whole of their products, as a reduction in the price of the products would mean a corresponding one in their income. This would be the second reduction made in the price of gas since the Corporation took the works, which he thought was a satisfactory thing. Dr. MACKIE said that the committee were unanimous as regarded a reduction of 3d. per 1 000 feet, bat after that their unanimity ceased. He wished to mention that at Stockport gas had been reduced to ge 6d, at Ashton to 2s 72, and in the city of London to 3s. 21. ; in Warrington it stood at 38. 3d. He asked why should Warrington lag behind and not be able to sell gases cheaply as other places, especially when it was considered that they had coal fields so near. The g is cost 2s. 62. when it was ready to go to the meters of the consumers, and why could it not be sold at less than 3s. 31. The poor niin who consumed less than 100 feet was charged 34. 31.; the shopkeeper who might be supposed to burn up to 200 000 feet 33.11., and the large dealer who might use up to 4,000,000 feet would, under the proposed reduction, be paying no profit, while the others would still pay a profit though a decreased one. The large dealer would pay no profit and the small consumer would be paYing 61, 81, or 92, as the Case might be. He was wishful that the large consumers should get the benefit of the 31 reductiou, but he thought they should allow the small consumer more at any rate in the charges they were about to mike. He thought 28 82 would be a fair amount to charge upon a total of 150,000,000 feet. Such reduction to 2s 8.1 to small consumers, and t 2s 6.1 to the large ones would allow a reduction of 72, 61, 54, and 3d respectively. He then moved "that the minutes of the Gas Committee be passed except those referring to the reduction of the price of gas, and that the same be sent back with a view to a further reduction." Mr. Dixox ascended the resolution.

Mr. FRANCOMB spoke in favour of the original minutes, for he firmly believed that every one would be perfectly satisfied with a reduction of 31 per 1000. He had never yet heard a single person grumble about the price of gas, and he thought it Nas the wisest course to reduce it gradually. It was preferable to jumping by leaps and bounds. Mr. MONKS remarked that though it might seem well to say that the large consumers were getting gas at cost price, it was a fallacy, for if they had not large consumers their loss would be greatly increased, as the more the make the less the cost. The proposed reduction was no more than equitable, and the small consumer would get his gas. having regard to the quantity that was made, at a cheaper rata than the large one After a further discussion, Dr. MACKIE said that he had previously been given to unders,and that the profits amounted to £4,000. After hearing that that was a mistake, and that they really only amounted to £2,900, he would ask his seconder to allow him to withdraw his amend- ment.

Councillor DIXON refused to withdraw, and the amend- ment was than put, with the result that 15 members voted against and one for. The minutes of the committee were then passed in their original form. This was all the business of public interest.
A woodturner named Checklev, in custody at Walsall Heath (Birmingham) Polica Station for stealing slippers, committed suicide on Thursday by hanging himself in his cell.

DISPUTE BETWEEN CAB PROPAIETOBS.-At the St Helens County Court, on Wednesday, before Mr T P E Thompson, judge, W G Dixon, cab and coach proprietor, Bickerstiffe-street, St Helens, sued Joseph Harris, cab pro- prietor, Crescent Hotel, Liverpool-street, for the recovery of £9, alleged to be due for the loan of a horse, injury to the animal, and constaluent expense by hiring another horse.— Mr J P Meares represented the plaintiff, and Mr J 0 Swat appeared for the defendant, who had a counter-claim of £l2s against the plaintiff for the hire of a horse.—On the 28th June the plaintiff visited the defendant's yard, and hired a horse, stating that it was for a funeral. It was, however, used in a waggonette, and it was returned on the Sunday morning bruised and cut in several places.—The parties to the action ultimately came to an arrangement, whereby the plaintiff accepted £Bln settlement of his claim, including his costs, and to settle the counter-claim of the detenclat

div.head: PREPARING FOR ACCIDENTS.
div.p: PREPARING FOR ACCIDENTS.

On the adoption of the minutes of the Watch Committee being moved by the MAYOR, and seconded by Mr. FRAN- COMB, Alderman HOLMES asked if the police farce was pro- vided with means of carrying injured persons in case of an accident happening, such for instance as the frightful ac- cident at Peuistone. He thought it was the duty of all towns to be provided with such things. Alderman BURGESS said they bad a carriage for infectious cases, but they could not carry injured people in a carriage that would give them small-pox. (Hear, hear.) There should, he thought, be provision made for accidents. He ' had just beard before coming into that roo:n of a man being killed at Latchford, and that was evidence enough that there was a necessity for something of the sort. _ _

The MAvori did not think they had anything of the kind even in connection with the Infirmary. Alderman HOLMES thought they had some means of car- riage in connection with the Infirmary. lhe MAYOR: If there is anythice• at the Infirmary there would be no difficulty in getting a loan of it in the event of an extreme case.
--- The matter was then left to the Watch Committee to deal with. STREET IMPROVEMENT ANT) LIGHTING COMMITTEE.

In the minutes of this c immittee it w;;Tec—o-m-r—n—e.ndeci. that an account for half.year's lighting of the borough be I allowed, amounting to £l,lBB 1.61. Id., and that the follow- ing plans be approved :—Pan of 12 houses in Selby-street, off Lavely•lane, for Mr. John Lloyd ; plan of alterations to the Independent Methodist Sunday School, in Brick- street ; plan of two houses and shops In Winwick-street, for Messrs. J. and T. Edwards, of Liverpool. Mr. BROADBENT moved, and Mr. BARKER seconded, the adoption of these minutes. Mr. DIXON moved as an amendment that the minutes be passed without the clause recommending the payment of £l,lBB 16s. 7d. for the half-year's This amendment was not seconded.

Mr. BROADBENT .tid he supposed Mr. Councillor Dixon thought that if they reduced that large amount it would en- rich the town. But, as they knew, it would only be passing money out of one pocket into nother. If it would be any gain to the municipal purse he was sure they ought to try to knock something off the committee, but as it would mit it was not a matter of very supreme importance. At the came time, when they made a comparison with what they were paying for street tempi with what other Wroughs paid. he believed that they found that they were below the scale of other boroughs. It would not make the slightest differ- ence. and if they were to get the amount reduced to £5OO it would be no gain.

• Alderman BURGESS: And if you made it £2,000 you would be no losers. The MAYOR: Quits so. The minutes were then adopted. TILE WOOD PAVEMENT. Alderman KEAN, ill moving the adopion of the minutes of of the Paving and Sewerage Committee, said there was no- thing of importanee to refer to in connection with the minutes excepting the experiment which was being made with wood pavement in inkey-street. They would see that a number of persons had memorialised the committee in order to have a portion of the street paved with wood which the committee bad never intended to touch until they knew the result of the experiment. Therefore they had replied to the memorial accordingly. Until they knew the result of the experiment it was useless to attempt to go fur- ther with the wood pavement. Mr. WRIGHT seconded the adoption of the minutes.

Alderman BURGESS said he only wished that the chair- man of the Paving and Sewerage Committee would take the earliest opportunity, now that the wood pavement was laid down, of letting the Council have the fullest information as to the cost of th.t piece of pavement as compared with the same length of the street in sett pavement. He was glad to find that the Paving Committee did not intend to go fur- ther with the wood pavement until they had had the fullest opportunity of testing the merits of the two systems. He thought it would afford great guidance to the Council and the town generally if they could see what the cost was as compared with the cost of sett pavements. Dr. MACKIE hoped the attempt to test tho wood pavement would be treated in a very generous spirit considering the part of the town to which it is applied. It was that part. • where perhaps of all others wood or noiseless pavements were most desirable. He had an office there more than 20 years ago, and he applied tn the Town Council of those days to have a noiseless pavernent laid down, but the answer was that the turn at Market Gate was so remarkably sharp that ' unless horses tnadd'a hoise they would be sure to run over ' somebody. (Laughter.) There was something in that ; but he was very glad that at the end of 25 years they had a ITown Council which was at any rate inclined to try what he suggested. The MAYOR said that it almost seemed an anachronism to question what would be likely to be the result of au exneri- meot of wood paving, because it had been tried before in so many places, Liverpool, Manchester, and London in particu- lar, where the traffic was enormous, and had proved to be a great success, and, certainly, as regarded these who lived in the immediate neighbourhood, it was a question that they should consider in a generous manner, even though the ex- pense was more than the old paving.

Alderman BURGESS thought that it would be time to take the question into consideration when the subject came for- ward for discussion. He sitnrolv asked for a return of the cost for future discussion. Alderman KEAN thought that the suggestion of Alderman Burgess was a very proper one and said that he should take care that every information was given to the Council on a subject of such importance. It did not merely affect the Paving and Sewerage Committee, but the whole town, and he might say that every member of the Committee was anxious to do the best they could both for the comfort and convenience of traffic, and of the shopkeepers in general. The subject should have their serious consideration, and the Committee would lay before the Council at its next meet- ing full information as to the cost in every particular. (Hear, hear).

div.head: SCHOOL ATTEND&NCE COMMITTEE.
div.p: SCHOOL ATTEND&NCE COMMITTEE.

The adoption of the minutes which were not of public in. terest, was proposed by Alderman Webster and seconded by Councillor Wallington. Mr. BROADBENT said that he was reminded that they hod bad several cases in court that day of boys and girls who were brought up for non-attendance at school. Some of the cases were very difficult to deal with—not so much as regar- ded school fees—but cases where children were required

• BAND OF HOPE GALA. The Warringtom Band of Hope Union held a demonstra- tion and gala on Bank Holiday, the success of which ex- ceeded the anticipations of even its most sanguine promoters. The most complete arrangements had been made for the demonstration, but it was thought by many that the town would be almost emptied by the various Bank Holiday ex- cursions which ran from Warrington in all directions. For- tunately this fear, though perhaps it was a justifiable one was ill-founded, as during the procession that took place the streets were crowded, and there was a constant stream of people entering the field in which the subsequent gala was held. The weather, too, was favourable, and everything therefore was conducive to success. Promptly at two o'clock in the afternoon the various Bands of Hope affiliated to the union assembled in front of the Town Hall, where the scene presented was most pic- turesque. The variety of costume and colour, the gay banners and bannerettes, and the glinting of the sun's rays upon the brass instruments of the bands and uniforms of the players, made a pretty picture, and the beauty of the weather conducted to the general enjoyment. Indeed, it was one of the Queen's days" as to weather, bright and genial ' as English summer day could be. Good order was uni- formly observed, and tke staff of constables on duty in the park and its environs IXd no more arduous task than the pleasant one of watching an interesting scene, and paying a little due attention to the proper regulation of traffic. Though not so large as the gathering that assembled on Walking Day, the one under notice was in its own way fully as successful, and, in consequence of the numbers not being so large, traffic in the streets was far more comfort- able. When everything was in readiness, and the various component parts of the procession had been placed in proper position for the start, three lusty cheers were given to greet the Mayor and Mayoress of Warrington, who were watch- ing the proceeding with manifest interest. Responding to this spontaneous expression of feeling, The MAYOR gave a short address, which he prefaced by a reference to the ladies present. Although children, he said, were very interesting, yet it would at times be a somewhat monotonous spectacle without a sprinkling of ladies, whom he regarded as something in the light of a flower bed amidst the greensward. The spectacle they were assembled to witness was a most interesting one, and he only remembered one in Warrington that cou d be called a rival to it, and that was Walking Day last, when the Salvation Army, greatly to their credit, picked up the children—the waifs and strays and the destitute—from the streets and wherever they could find them, brought them into that enclosure to be regaled with tea and buns, and ,nado the poor little souls happy for one day, at all events. That was a great act of kindness on the part of the Salvation Army, without whose kindly in- terfereace those poor children would have had no holiday. The Army was evidently a great movement, was destined to do a great amount of good, and had in fact already achieved great things. Perhaps all would not understand the forms and ceremonies of the army, but it was evident to all that they were such as were calculated to reach those whom the ordinary religious organisations failed to touch. All should wish the army "God speed" and not quarrel with it on account of the means to which it resorted to gain its ends. That present assemblage, forming as it did the union of the Bands of Hope, was a most interesting one, because it was full of hope for the future. He remembered how, many years ago, when a Band of Hope was first formed in War- rington, many people ridiculed it, and said that it was de- sired to make children take the pledge who would probably . never taste drink. The only temperance people then were ' the ltechabites, and that Band of Hope that was then formed had more in it than to most people appeared on the surface. It was instilling an aversion to iutoxicants into the young minds of the children, and the boys and girls of that day were men and women of to- day. He was not sure but that the wave of remperance that they had beard of as spreading over the land, was not the result of the formation 20 years ago of these little Bands of Hope. The Mayor concluded his re- marks by congratulating the Union on the fine weather with which they were favoured. (Applause.) On the conclusion of the Mayor's address the roll of the drum and the sound of music announced that the procession was on the move, and as the gay banners flaunted in the air from every appropriate position, the long procession as it emerged from the Park was watched by a large number of specmtors, who lined the route that had beforehand been [ decided upon. The procession was headed by the marshals, Messrs T Prince, James, NV Roberts, and Smith, and with it ; walked the Revs W Mules, J Yonge, J McTurk, E Moore, T Rippon, and the well-known temperance advocate, the [ Rev J P Anderson, of Liverpool. The Workhouse band ' led the way, playing forward the Buckley-street school, ' which was followed by the Howley-lane Band of Hope and the Runcorn Seamen's Mission fife and drum band, the ; members of which, in their picturesque nautical costumes. • introduced a novelty into the effect which was very pleas- ing. The Wesleyans of Buttermarket-street and Silver- i street, and the Emmanuel Church Sunday School, accom- panied by the Legh-street band, took the next position, • followed by the St. Paul's contingent with their band. At the rear were the Wycliffe Band of Hope and band, and the ; members of the Older of Good Tempters. The route taken to [ the ultimate destination of the procession at Latchford was through Sankey-street, Legh-street, Edgeworth-street, [ Bewsey-street, Tanners-lane, Witiwiek-st., Horsecnarket-st., Bridge-st , and Wilderspool-causeway. No hitch occurred during the march and the children all appeared bright and I hopeful, the music of the bands having a most inspiriting effect alike on old and young. It is estimated that about [ 3,000 persons walked in the procession. When the ground at Latchford was reached the proccosion was disbanded and the abstainers proceeded to enjoy themselves in various ways. The general public were admitted at a very reason- able charge, and it is estimated by those competent to judge of such matters that there were present in the field nearly 10,000 people So successful was the gala that we are able to state that it has left in the hands of the committee a handsome surplus, after paying all exoensee, that will be handed over to swell the funds of the Union. Such a re- sult, when so little was expected in some quarters, cannot but be deemed satisfactory. The committee bad made every preparation for the enjoyment of all, and their efforts met with a just success. A refreshment tent, where none but temperance " drinks " were dis- pensed, supplied the wants of the thirsty. Dancing naturally formed a principal feature of the enjoy- ment and the several bands were busily engaged at intervals, those people who were disinclined to the pastime of " trip- ping it" derived some pleasure from the music and the ani- mation of the scene. In addition a programme of athletic sports was gone through, and speaking, iecitation, and sing- ing contests formed a unique and attractive portion of the dav's entertainment. limo Rev. J. B. Anderson acted as lodge of the speaking and recitation contests, Mr. Joseph Podinore of the singing contests, and Messrs. T. Prince and W. Roberts of the sports, Mr. J. A. Youge acting as starter.

The fist event on the programme was a recitation contest open to boys and girls between the ages of 12 and 16 and there were no lees than 25 entries. The first prize fell to the lot of G. H. Shaw, Wycliffe, the second to W. Alford, St. Paul's and the third to Jesse Harrison, Buckley-street. In event 2, a singing contest open to boys only, J. Fairhurst, Howley, and J. S. Place, Wycliffe, took first and second prizes re- spectively, out of five entries. In the third event, an open speaking contest, the prizes were gained by the elder cone- p,titors, and were generously given up to the children who took part in 'other competitions. In the singing contest for girls, Lucy Ashley, Bank-quay, took first prize, Miss Bate, St Paul's, second. and Isabella Berton, Emmanuel, third. In the recitation contest, open to boys and girls under the age of twelve, Lucy Booth, Buttermarket-street, took first posi- tion, J Leach, Buckley-street, second, and Alice Murrell, Buckley-street, third. An open 100 yards handicap flat race was contested in five heats, the first in each heat to run in the final. There were 26 entriea. The first prize Was awarded to J Williams, Buckley-street, 2 yards, the second to T Booth, Buckley-street, 8 yards, and the third to H Ed- wards' Bank Quay, 4 yards. The tug of war contests, of which there were two, created no little amusement. In the first, for bays under 16, the Bank Quay Mission team were victorious over the Wycliffe team, and in the second, for youths over 16, the Bank Quay Mission team was success- ful, the defeated opponents being the Buckley-street team. An open 100 yards egg and spoon race, open to girls, re- ceived 19 entries. It was productive of considerable amuse- ment and laughter. E Tanner, Silver-street, was first, and E Helsby, Emmanuel, second. The last event, a sack race, was also entertaining. T Brookes, Emmanuel, gained the first award, and C Critchley, Wycliffe, the second. The recitation, singing, and speaking contests took place on the grand stand, and were attentively listened to, those who made themselves favourites with the audience receiving ap- propriate applause. These contests, considering the circum- stances under which they were held, were very good. After the oistribution of the prizes a temperance meeting was held, the speakers delivering their addresses from the grand stand. They were listened to ZIT a fairly numerous audience, and frequent applause was elicited. The CHAIRMAN, Mr. IL A Naylor, president of the union, after an allusion to the gentlemen who were about to speak, said that it was a matter for great congratulation that they had seen at that temperance demonstration such a large concourse of people; they should also be thankful that the warm weather had been so favourable to it. He supposed that it was the first mating of the kind held under the auspices of the union, azd he hoped that it would conduce to the future prosperity of the united temperance movement. (Applause.) Mr. J. B. ANDERSON, Liverpool, thought that the fathers and mothers of Warrington should be proud of their chil- dren, for they had seen a good speeimen of them that day— standing on that platform and declaring for temperance and the Gospel in such a way as they had done. It was far better to have plenty of the two "C's" than the two "D's." The former meant "Cheap and Clean"—cold water, and the latter "Dear and Dirty "—intaxicants. (Laughter.) Clean- liness was next to Godliness, and the more of cold water that they had inside and outside the better would it be for them and for everybody concerned. He knew that it was not wise to introduce politics, but he would say that if he had a vote in Warrington he would sooner that his right hand should wither than that he should give a vote for the liquor seller. (Hear, hear.) In their Town Council and Houses of Parliament they should have those to represent them who would shut up the public house, close the brewery, end put the fire out of the distillery. He urged parents to Aet their children a good example. Why should they hear if Hmalid Liverpool, outcast London, wretched Warrington, end drunken St. Helens? Let them endeavour to change such names and bring up their children to be true temper- nee men and women.
The Rev. J. YoNem fully believed that temperance would !wake people physically strong as well as mentally clear. Ile reloiced at the success of the deraoustratiou, as ha bad

thought that Bank Holiday would have been against it in consequence of so many 'raving the town. They would, however, have. cause to look back upon that Bank Heliday as a grand day for the temperance cause in War- rington,

Ihe Rev. F. MOORE expressed his gratification at seeing so large a gathering in favour of temperance. He thought with great regret of the approaching departure from War— rington of the Rev. T. Rippon. He was personally son," that Mr. Ription was going away, for in him he should lose a thorough, steadfast, and genuine freed. (Hear, bear.) Warrington had, he said, an unenviable notoriety for drunken females, and he bad on a recent Nunday evening seen girls of the age of about 13 or 15 years rolling drunk on the pavement. It was a shame that girls of all persons should be found drunk on the streets. He urged all to adhere- to temperance. . _

lhe Rev. TnatwAs RIPPotq, in the course of a short address, said that he regretted to leave his temperance friends in Warrington, for he had never found truer or better. He had, however, the knowledge that he had c?n- tributed to raise the temperance standard, and was leaving .it a prominent and permanent factor to work out the refor- mation and regeneration of Warrington. Referrring to the speech of the Mayor, he said that he believed Alderman Harrison was one of the best Mayors Warrington ever had, who had always lent his influence to anything that was for the good of the town. He then referred to the excellent work done by Mr. William Roberts and the committee, and,con- eluded by moving a vote of thanks to Mr. Naylor for pre- siding, remarking that that gentleman had done a great deal in the town and district in aid of the temperance cause. Mr. WILLIAM ROBERTS seconded the motion, remarking tha that was the largest temperance gathering that had ever been held in Warrington. They bad only just formed the Union, he said, but it was their desire that the demonstra- tion should become an annual aff air, and that all sectionS of the Christian Church should join with them in the pro- motion of temperance. The resolution was carried with applause, as was also a vote of thanks to the committee, and the preceedinga then practically terminated, aa, it being nearly dusk, the field was rapidly emptied, and a move was made homewards. All passed off pleasantly to the close, and excellent order was preserved. The committee deserve credit for the com- pleteness of the arrangements. The following gentlemen comprised the committee :—Mr William Roberts (chair- man); hon. secs., Messrs W Ford and J A Yonge ; Rev W Mules, Messrs Thomas Prince, J W Hayward, A H Dann. W James, W Smith, J Ashley, Thomas Dale, E Plinston, F Willtams,J Hodzins and E Howard. Donations were received from Mr McMinnies, M P., Mr William Crosfleld, Alderman Harrison (Mayor of Warrington), Mr William Beamont, Mr R A Naylor, Mr John Naylor. Mr Job n Platt, Mr Zahn' Armitage, Mr John Rvlands, Mr William Long, Mr Robert Garnett, Mr Charles Broadbent, the lira/John Yonge, Alder- man Chandley„ Mr William Gill, Mr J Fl Gornall, Mr E J Guest, Mr Thomas Carter, and Mr J Walker.

EARLESTOWN. UNITED TEMPERANCE DEMONSTRATION. The annual demonstration in connection with the United Bands of Hope and Temperance Societies of Earlestown and Newton was held on Saturday afternoon. Fortunately for the gethering, the weather was beautifully fine; and a better day cocht not have been desired. The societies taking part in the proceedings were the Wesleyan Methodist Band Of Hope, the Congregational Band of Hope, the Baptist Band of Elope, the Primitive Methodist Band of Hope, the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Tempters, the Sons of Tem- perance Friendly Society, and the Gospel Mission Blue Ribbon Army. The members of these organisations gathered at their respective head quarters about half-past one and shortly afterwards marched to the Earlestown Mar- ket-place, where they were drawn up in positions previously decided upon. 'Tbe members of the Crow-lane Congrega- tional Band of Hope were conveyed to the market ground in a lorry kindly lent by Mr. Atty, of the Liverpool Re- formatory- School, Newton, while the members of the Sons of Temperance Friendly Society had not a statud place the arrangements as they were associated with the Band of Hope connected with the denomination to which they be- longed. A goodly number of the members of the Hope 01 Earlestown Lodge of Good Template was also similarly accounted for. Shortly after two o'clock the various de- tachments of the great temperance army had gathered in the Market and been placed in their proper positions. Though there was a great majority of juveniles in the ranks, the assemblage was a striking and imposing one. The large banners floating in the breeze, with the fluttering flags and bannerettes to be counted by the score, and the rendering of lively airs by the Mean and Lawton Temperance Brass Bands made the scene a stirring and lively one, and created an enthusiasm and a heartfelt interest in the work among the friends of the temperance movement. A large crowd of interested spectators gathered from all parts of the town to witness the proceedings ; and among the gentlemen present were the Rev J M Fairburn (Wesleyan), Rev F N Shimmin (Pri- mitive Methodist), Rev W C Tayler (Baptist), Rev A Cobb (Wesleyan minister from Canada), and the officers of the various organisations. The Rev 1V C Tayler gave out the well known hymn "Sonnet the battle cry! see l the feels nigh," which was heartily sung by the assembled company; Mr Barcroft conducting. A tnonstre procession was after, wards formed under the directions of the following gentlemen who officiated as marshal's : Messrs George Clarke ((loot Templare), William Mitchell (Sons of Tem- perance), F Eachus (Blue Ribbon Army), and 0 Pickett (Wesleyan), along with the energetic and obliging secretary (Mr Richerd Higgins). The order of the different societies in the procession had been previously decided by billet, and consequently little difficulty was experienced in the task of arranging the "ranks." First came the members of the Irlaus Temperance Brass Band, conducted by Mr Burchall, and they were followed by the members of the Wesleyan Metho- dist Band of Hope. They were beided by a large banner beating the words "Earlestown Wesleyan Methodist Band of Elope " in red and blue letters on a white ground;. and in front of the members walked the Rev. J. M. Fairbourn (resident minister), and the Rev. A. Cobb (of Canada), and other gentlemen. In all about 100 male and 90 female members were present. The next in order of procession were the Good Template, the members of the Juvenile Temple, headed by their worthy superintendent, Mr. F. Newman, coining first. The juveniles numbered 16 girls and 12 boys; and the adults 12 females and 21 males, total 61. Many of this number wore their replies and other emblems. of office. The Blue Ribbon Movement was next represented in the proceselon. First cime a large binner bearing the words "Gospel Mission Blue Ribbon Army, Earlestown," on one side, and on the other were the words "God bless the Temperance cause." About 110 females and 90 males were included in the ranks. Next Came the Lowton Temperance brass band under the conductorship of Mr. Ashton ; and they were succeeded by the Primitive Methodist Bendf Hope. The large banner carried in front bore the words "Primitive Methodist Band of Hope, Earlestown," in blue letters on a white ground with a blue border. Immediately following were the Rev. F. N. Shimrnin (resident minister), Ml. James Woods (school superiniendent), Mr. Arrowsmitise Mr. Dickens, iSzc., and about 86 female acci 60 male members of the society. Heading the males was, another burner bearing the words " Earlestown. Primitive Methodist Sandier School." The Baptists, who followed, numbered about 70 females and 28 males, and were headed by a banner containing the words Baptist Band of Hope," immediately behind which were the Rev. W. C. Taylor (resident minister) and Mr. G. F. Aveline. • The Congregationalists brought up the rear of the proces- sion, and they were led by their bamner, upon which was inscribed " Coneregational Sunday School, Earlestown." The members present numbered about €O, the sexes being about equally divided. It will thus be seen that about 340 males and 410 females—a total of 750 persons—took part in the procession. A large number of small banners and symbols depicting the evil effects of the drink traffic were carried in the "ranks," The bands discoursed popular airs as the procession marched through the streets of the town, and in every street a large crowd assem- bled to witness the demonstration. On. arriving at the large field connected with the Viaduct institute (which had been kindly lent for the occasion) the members of the various societies were again drawn up in stated posi- tions, aed each society distributed refreshments is the shape of tea, coffee, buns, kc., to it members. The DMAIC were admitted at a small charge. and various games and amuse- ments were afterwards indulged in.. Balloons were sent up at intervals, and in other ways the juveniles were amused and interested, wkile the bands played for dancing. The rejoicings were kept up until dunk, when the company began to separate. All present seemed to have thoroughly enjoyed themselves. One of the principal contest°. in the course of the after- noon's enjoyment was a "tug of war" between teams re- presenting the IVesleyan Methodist Band of Hope, the Bap- tist Band of Hope, the Primitive Methodist Band of Hope, and the Good Tempters. The "battle "excited great in- terest. In the first round the Baptists dofeated the Wee,- leyans, and the Good Tempters dispesed of the Primitive Methodists. The final tie between the Good TemplarS and the Ikeptists resulted in a victory for the Good Tern-' plars.

A report was presented to the Wesleyan Conference on Thursday with regard to the Thanksgiving Fund, Bow closed. The report stated that out of a total of £503,000 proraised, nearly £298,000 had actually been Paid, and the loss from unfulfilleel promises, occasioned by deaths and commercial depression, was about £B,OOO.

DISTURBANCE A LODGE DINNnE AT RAINTOM—At the St. Helens County Police Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. Thomas Pilkington, Thomas Jones, a young man, hailing from the Nortla-end of Liverpool, was charged with unlaw- fully wounding Thomas Hart, a drawer, who lives at School-brow Rainford.—Prosecutor stated that be was at the annual Sinner of the Shepherds' Lodge, which was held at the Star Inn, Rainford, on the previous night. About half-past six o'clock prisoner and several other men, who did not belong to the lodge, came up the stairs, but were prevented from entering the room. Thereupon the prisoner took a belt and hit him upon the hand, and afterwards swink• leg it round the buckle caught him in the eye.—Dr. Nichol- son, who attended prosecutor, said the latter was sufferiog from an incised wound, extending from the corner of the right eye to the bridge of the nose. Witness was afraid the prosecutor would lose the sight of the injured eye, and there was danger of inflammation. When taken into custody by Police-sergeant Smith, prisoner said "I neither cut nor wounded him." Prisoner, who had driven over from Liver- pool with other young men, and refused to give any address than "the North Kid Of Liverpool,'' was commit All to the sessions for trial, further

are perhaps able to pay for without risking a tight with a shower, or being laid under the necessity of chartering a cab. A short distance will bring them, to another store, where " daisies " of lace curtains give the en- trance a baz ear-like appearance; and the chances are that however well-lined the pocket, there is a prospect of coming out centless. Oh, the seductive influences of these charming places! Silks are placed before you as though the wand of the magician had baen at work, and these can be bought at prices quite as low as they can in England, because of their being home manufacture. Rolls of carpeting are sent spin- ning about in such profusion that you tread on beds of flower garden till yen begin to imagine you are some prince upon whom the populace are lavishing their tokens of loyal respect and admiration. These goods are of home produc- tion. Then the clouds of shirtiags that float about you in fine texture, and snowy whiteneos ! These lead you to ex- claim," Ah, here are the products of Lancashire, not to be beaten anywhere." Then your heart drops into your boots when you are told that they were woven in Manchester, New Hampshire. This was my feeling on being shown through one of these establishments, and I could not help putting to myself the question, "Is the mother of this great country to take a back seat ?'' But there is a set-off in our favour against all this. The American "helps " have not been taught, or have not learned, the most economic principles. They know not the value of waste. There would be an exodus out of Garden-street and Mark-lane, Manchester, if our dealers in droppings " knew what a " bonanza " could be picked up here. A manufacturer f tom East-Lanca- shire who was once on a visit here, remarked, on going through a cotton mill," I would not care to have any profits on goods manufactured if I might have the waste for my share." But can this condition of things be reckoned upon to last for ever? Surely not. It is, therefore, a character- istic failing on our part to be stilt cont‘nt with living in a "fool's paradise." We ought to look at things with sober earnestness if we mean to keep our industrial supremacy. Bar-parlour bounce will not serve us is our growing needs. I had forgotten to note what beautiful prints are turned out in New Hampshire. They remind me ot the "Calico Garden Party" held some time ago at our Botanical Gardens. The printers here are rapidly approaching the heels of Sunny- side, and I am afraid that in time their running will be such that we cannot afford to take the " sponge " in the

WIT AND TUMOUR. The following is told of the late Provost of Eton. One day the headmaster asked him why so few masters were coming out of chapel. " Because so few went in," was the caustic reply. If some Yankee would invent an" old bachelor's needle" he would make a fortune. The needle need not differ greatly from other ne‘.dles, except at the eye, which should be about an inch in diameter. LOOKING AllEAD.—Algy "They want six thousand pounds for the lease, Maria. It runs for eighty-nine years." Maria: "Oh, don't buy it, Algy ! Only eighty-nine years! Fancy dear baby being turned out of his house at ninety-one' and possibly infirm into the bargain! " HER APPRECIATION OF Pr.—" My dear, look down be- low," said a grandieso, as he stood on Wet-rloo Fridge with his wife, and gazing at a tug hauling a long line ot barges. " Such is life—the tug is like a man, working and toiling, while the barges, like women, are—" " I know," inter- rupted Mrs. G., acridly; "the tug does all the blowing, and the barges bear all the burden." A LONG SLEEP.—A barrister, noticing that the judge before whom he was pleading had fallen asleep, stopped short in the middle of his speech. The sudden silence awoke the judge, And counsel gravely resumed—" As I remaike I yesterday, my lord—" The puzzled judge stared in wonder, as though he half believed he had been asleep since the previous day. A new page-boy at one of the large London clubs was noticed by a member wandering about the room, evidently with a message for somebody. Member: Whom are you looking for, boy ?—Boy, scratching his head: I've forgotten the gentleman's name, sin—Member : What is he Ike ? Boy : Don't know, sir—Member: What are you doing then? —Boy: Looking for him, sir. YOUNG ONCE HIM,ELF.—" Well, John," said old man Jordan to his young friend," you have just been married I hear." "Yes, sir," he ansrered, with a spring-morning smile, "just a month age, and I want you to go up to dinner with me to-day." " Have you got a cook ?" "No." " Well, My boy, s'potse we go to a restaurant this time. You must remember I had a young wifi once myself." _ I am in New York again, because I cannot avoid it, if I mean to get along anywhere. At,4 3O I board the coasting boat, and take my ticket for Fell River, Mass. What a crowd of people are there, bound for the same port !—..and are booking state-rooms and beds as though they had to voyage to Liverpool, so eagerly were they jostling and Pushing. lam too late for the former, and must make up ray mind to rough it. Nobody strips for this class of berth, . they may take off their coat, and boots, and cram them on a small shelf at the foot,—a shelf emmething like what I have seen servant girls put placklng brushes on; bet trousers are retained fur einergsncies. A drunken passenger may dispute possession, because he has not booked; and you've got to "best" him, which recraires a little pluck. I had no trouble of this kind; but a neighbour had, and the bully got the worst of it. When the morning waa fairly awake, we found this bravo in his boots, laid flat on the baggage deck floor, with his slouched hat drawn over him for a coverlet, and muttering joint blessings on rats. I took out about four hours' sleep ; then drew aside my curteic, for a look- out. The darkies were laying the cloths for breakfast; and the barber was airing himself in his white morning gown, with as much self assertion as if the vessel was his • own. He WM on the look-out for cestomere, and was imper- tinent to those who di' not want 8124 iug. Twenty-five -cents a shave is much better remuneration than newspaper Paragraphers get. The wash I had was a delicious one, and very much a surprise to me; and this refreshing ablution, "Pt:demented by a cooling drink, prepared me to face a drizzly morning, the boat being two hours late in conse- quence of a fog that set in at sunset, and prevailed all night. I saw my friend Salisbury of the Advance waiting for me, like a rooster under a shed, where for two hours he had been -anathematising old tubs and things in general. .1 saw his jolly face, a little writhen by disappointment, long before he saw mine, which was not jolly. Some kinds of details are apt to tire people; and I do not mean to put upon patience. I was welcomed right royally, .and made to feel at home whether I would or not. After breakfast, which I hid been waiting for some time, we sal- lied into tho city. The road was not strewn with flowers, nor did the people dance in front of us, waving garlands, .and clanging cymbals. But many an open hand gripped mine and as often was I asked to take "snthin." These kindly meant invitatione had to be deolieed, otherwise "George" and I would have found ourselves in the hands of The city marshall before the day was properly on its legs. Nothing like self denial and a reasonable respect for our- selves. The day wes spent in visiting, and ended as family Parties used to end at wakes times. The hands left one of the mills in swarms to meet me; and one enthusiastic Lan- e-3411in Irishman made the observation," Misther Irving had a great reception in New York, but he couldn't shut down a Mill." Shut doses, in the Yankee sense, means shut up, aa We understand.it. After the first night I was the guest of the mayor, the Hen. Milton Reed, whom I met in Manchester three years aeo. At his residence on the hill overlooking Bowen- villa we spent several quiet evenings, looking out on the Natrangansett Bay, and fading with the brief twilight, like flowers, to an early closing. From the elder Reed 1 gleaned "quite" an amount of inform ttion concerning the history Of the States, and the characteristics of the people who in- habit them. We were mostly downstairs before the house Was astir ; and old "Christopher North," for Mr. Reed might sit for his portrait, could declaim for an hour uninterrupted by anyone who might dispute his word. But I had to leave to be present at one of the institutions of Fall River—that HOLY Timmy dinstoas v. Rue:come NEwrowstkWitiTz was a 'clam-brake." Warrington were only able to place a weak team against the very strong team brought by Bolton, who bad secured the services of three extra professionals. Warrington batted first aud totalled 67, T. Wallington and CU. Lawton batting carefully for their scores. Bolton began badly, but Connolly and Brooks altered the score by hard hitting. Connolly bit up 55, which included a six, ten fours, two threes, a two and a single. The last seven wickets were easily disposed of, the batsmen being unable to make runs from Denton and Deni- son. The,fielding, with the exception of one mistake, was smart and close throughout. Warrington went in a second time and had made 44 runs for one wicket when time was I called.

race. • But with all America's progress there is one thing she has yet to learn. England has not been built up on extrava- gance. If her nobility in past years measured their civiliea- don by their expensive habi•s, the people generally held to thrift and economy. The British taxpayer groaned at every penny added to the burden he had to bear; and the hustings cry of "Economy with Efficiency," was the out-come of much objurgation on his part. But he does not complain of expenditure that he is willing to allow may be necessary ; but by bitching the Board School system on to other state institutions he was givea cause for a 1 tile soreness thst has gradually been healed. After having fought and struggled, and paid for an imperfect education for himself, he did not feel bound to pay for the hetttr training of others quite as able to pay for their own as he in his day was. He has not yet so far overcome this feeling as not to wince when the usual precept for the modest sum of £5,000 is handed, into •the City Council Chamber, and ordered to be paid. But he has the satisfaction of knowing that this money is not ex- travagantly spent. ' Our Board School teachers are not overburdened with salaries. A young girl has to cost her parents, perhaps, more than they can afford to pay to get qualified for a position in which she cannot earn as much as can an uneducated weaver. But irk America the "school marten" 4s a bird of another plumage. After being primarily educated at the public expense, even though her parents may be well-to-do, she is "finished" by the latter; and influence has to do the rest. She is foisted upon the school authorities, and placed in a position that the English "governess' would be afraid could not be maintained. Only fancy a young " marm" who has just laid aside her skipping-rope, pocketing annually as much as one thousand dollars for thirty-nine weeks' work; the rest of the year being taken out in holidays. Yet such is the case; and the general expenses of the City of Fall River are on a par. I have before me the city treasurer's report for the year 1882, which gives the total expenditure on a city of fifty-two thousand inhabitants of 1,075,059 dollars, which Total l-071 Total .......... ....... 13 -sum has to be raised by direct taxation. The match between the Yorkshire Players and the York- shire Gentlemen was resamed in glorious weather on 'Tues- day, at Sheffield. The Gentlemen, with 123 to the bad, followed on, and utterly collapsed in their second attempt. Score:—Players, 204; Gentemen, 81 and 35,—An hour and ten minutes' play sufficed to bring the match Lancashire v. Derbyshire to a conclusion at Derby on Tuesday. Each side had completed an innings on Monday, and Derbyshire, being then in a minority of 82 runs, of course had to follow on. Their batsmen, however, made no sort of stand what- ever against Barlow and Watson's bowling. When the last wicket fell the total was bat 46, and Lancashire were conse- quently left with an easy victory by an innings, with 36 runs to spare. Score :—Lancashire, 162; Derbyshire, 80 and 54. At Canterbury on Wednesday Kent gained a brilliant vic- tory over the Australians by 96 runs, a result which was no doubt expected after the clese of Tuesday's play, and one that will do a groat deal towards restoring Kent to its old position amongst the counties. Since 1880 no county has ever been able to beat an Australian eleven, and on that , account more especially Lord Harris and his team are to be heartily congratulated. The match was won by good, genuine, all-round cricket, and, though it would be too much , to say that the better side proved successful, it is scarcely possible to give enough credit to the winning team. Score: Kent, 169 and 213; Australians, 177 and 109.—Surrey made a draw of the return match with Notts., at Kennington Oval on Wednesday, wanting 153 runs to win, with three wickets to fall when the game came to an end. At Clifton. on Thursday, in the match Gloucestershire v. Australians, Mr W G Grace, for the third time during the present season, hit an innings of over a hundred against the Colonials. He is the only English cricketer who has ever ae,ievecl the distinction t.f scorieg three three-figure innings in one season against the bowling of the Colonists, and, if his acknowledged position as the premier of English batsmen rested upon no other peformance than this, the claim might be fairly allowed.—After a plucky up-hill fight at Lords, on Thursday, the M.C.C. were beaten by Cheshire by 40 runs. The victory was greatly due to Millward, who carried out his bat for 65, the highest individual score in the match.

LEGED MEET OF a. froasH.- -At the St Helens Police Court on Tuesday, before Aldermen Cook and Nlcßryde, Polius Herrin, a young man, was charged with stealing horse, the property of Messrs Richard Evans and Co, Bay- dock, from a field belonging to them. Mr Riley appeared for the defence, and Mr W Swift prosecuted.—James Bro-pra, a labourer at Messrs Evans and Co, deposed that the horse was missed on the 30th July. He next saw it at Newton Common in the prisoner's possession. It had not been sold. —• ['he prisoner was remanded.—The prisoner was brought before Alderman Harrison on Wednesday evening, and it being stated tnat no evidence of identification of the horse as the property of the prosecutor was forthcoming, the magistrate discharged the prisoner.—On Thursday, at the Town Hall, before Alderman Harrison and Mr C J Bishop, Mr J 0 Swift, representing Messrs Evans and Co., said that certain circumstances had come to the knowledge of the Droveutors which had led them to think there might have been some mistake; that the horse, in fact, might not belong to them. div.head: VICAR OF EARLESTOWN AND
div.p: THE VICAR OF EARLESTOWN AND
HIS WASHERWOMAN.

At the Warrington County Court on Thursday, before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, judge' Walter Stacey, of 23, Lord- street, Earlestown, on bebalf of his wife Sarah Stacey. brought an action against the Rev. T. R. Matthews, vicar of Earleetown, to recover the sum of £8 12s 61 alleged to be due on account of work done. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the plaintiff, and the defendant conducted his own case. There were several Earlestown people present in court, who watched the proceedings with considerable interest, owing to the belligerent position in which the 'Vicar and his parish- ioners now stand with regard to each other.—ln opening the case Mr. Browne said that the claim was for the balance due for washing done since 1881, and also for keeping clean a school. of which the defendant was the manager, at the sum of 3s 61 per week, the claim in the latter respect amounting to £1 11s. There was also 2s a week for each meeting of a building club which the defendant undertook to pay to the plaintiff. There were 21 meetings, making for that a claim of £2 2s. The sum of £3 93 61 was doe for washing. mak- ing a total of £lO 2s 61. On that account the defendant had paid the sums of £l 103 and £2, leaving due the balance sued for, £6 12s 61.—The defenca was that the defendant had paid £6 on account of the work for which the claim was made and the remaining odd shillings were all that was owing, to which the plaintiff said that the .£l3 received had nothing to do with the present claim, and that it was paid in respect to other work than that which it was now sought to recover for.—Mr Browne said that the £6 paid was for an old debt—His Honour : It is for the defendant w prove that; have you (to defendant) nothing to show what you paid that for? Have you no receipt ?—Defendant : No, your Honour; I never got a receipt for any money paid until last May.—Mr Browne (to defendant) : You are the Vicar of Earlestown Church? Yes, you knew that before to day.—When did the plaintiff's wife filet begin to wash for you? I really cannot tell. My wife is dead, who taa4 these things in hand.—You did Day £6 on the 13th Febru- ary, 1882, and there was then £6 7s 31 owing? Not that lam aware of; I never received any bill from Sarah Stacey but the one his Honour has on the desk.—Yon do not die- pate owing the money for the school? I dispute owing anything more than 124 63, which I have never paid in money. For some time I have been subjected to annoy- ance, and this is the result of spite and so on, which is very prevalent in Earlestown jast now.-1 did not ask you about that at all. You agree that meetings were held of the building club, and did you not agree to pay 2s per meeting? Never.—Do you remember the former parson who kept it? No.—Did you not undertake to pay 2s per week to Mrs. Stacey? No.—Mr. Browne said that when the £6 was paid Mrs Stacey went to the defendant and told him that if she did not have the money she should get into trouble with her creditors, and he then gave her £6 on account of the £6 7s 31, for which he had a bill.—ln answer to the Judge, who asked the plaintiff for more definite particulars and evidence of her tranactions with the defendant, Mrs. Sticey said that she did not think that she would have had to come there, as she thought Mr. Matthews was a gentleman.—His Honour said that she had not come there to make remarks of that kind, but to give her evidence in a proper manner.—Defen- dant : I believe that from time to time small sums of money were paid to the plaintiff.—Mrs. Stacey: That was for the school, and not for the tvashing.—Defendant : I do not know that, my wife had to do with the school, and as for the meetings of the club I never promised you anything, as I did not know at the time what the building club paid.—Mrs Stacey: You said you would pay me for the time you were in he howe.—Defendant Never; the whole thing was included in 31 61 a week.—Re- ferring to the memorandums submitted to him, his Honour asked who was to check them, as no accounts appeared to have been rendered and Mrs Matthews was dead. Had the defendant any memorandum or accounts relating to the washing T—Defendaut ; No; It appears to be a good deal of guess work, and only lately taken up.—Mr. Browne: I ob- ject to that —Defendant : That lam quite aware of. Mre Stacey's claim is from 1881 clearly on her own bill; off it I paid her £3, £1 103, and £2.—His Honour hayine ex- amined the memoranda and bills handed by the plaintiff said that the first item was for doing something at the sum of 3s 61 a week, the time extending from February, 1881. to August in the same year. The next item was for washing, not for balance. from May, 1881, to August, 1882, £3 PI 61, mak- ing £lO 28 6d. It was Cetween May, 1881, and Aug. 1882, that the £6 was paid, and at that time there was owing to the plain- tiff something between £6 and DI. The .£6 was paid, no receipt was given, and no bill rendered to show what it was paid on account of. It would not do now to say that it was paid for merely a part of the account and not for the whole. If there Was anything due on the washing account it should have been put into the account then, for it was clear that the payment referred in part to what was in the bill. He thought that he should take it that the money was paid generally on account, as it was not disputed that it was paid. The difficult matter he had to determine was what it was paid on account of. It was said by the plaintiff that it was paia on account of part of the bill, and on the other hand there was nothing to show that it was paid on account of anything. Mrs. Stacey's only memorandum was merely "Received the sum of £6, 13th February, 1882," not "On account of washing," or anything else. he thought he must conclude that the £6 was paid generally on account, but it was a great pity that propet'accmnts had not been kept —Mr. Browne: These'people did not know the impotta9t difference between "balance of washing ac- count" and washing account."---His Honour: You come into court with a claim and the defendant has proved pay- ment. It is for you to prove that it was not paid generally on account by the defendant. but against s nne particular item. I think you have failed to do that, and I must give judgment for the plaintiff for 123 63.—Judgment was given accordingly, with costs.
