div.p: BITILTONWOOD CIIIIROII : SERVICE OF SONG.—A ser- vice of song, entitled "Gems from the life of John Ash- worth," was given in the Burtonwoad Church schoolroom on Saturday evening by the choir of the church. The read- ings were effectively given by Mr. E. Boardman, of St. Helens. Mr. 8.. Saunders ably conducted, and Mr. W. Seph- ton presided at the harmonium. The various musical por- tions of the service were well rendered by the choir. Mem OF BOWLS AT Intant.—An open main of bowls took place on Saturday, on the bowlieg green attached to the Ship Hotel, Earn, whoa the proprietor offered a handsome clock for the first prize. Owieg to the main not being ad- vertised, only 16 players entered, for the competition—nine being from Warrington. At the commencement of the third round only one lrlarnite—J Cordwell—was left in, but be faitly held his own, beating his opponent (D Daniels, War- rington,) in the final game by five points. DISTURBING A POLITICAL MEETING. A man named George Poole was summoned to the Warrington County Sessions, on Wednesday, to answer a charge of being drunk and disorderly at Penketh on the 28;13 July —A constable having proved the eise, the defettlant questioned him as to whether he (defendant) was not at a " politisbion " meeting, to which all were invited. and asked by what right one of the persons present caught him by the neck. Did not he say "Give us a whole bill end not belt a bill ?"—The con- stable said that the defendant was very disorderly at the tweeting.—The defendant said that he went to the po.irical gathering at Penketh, and he had not, been long on the ground when the people began speaking on the Franchise Bill. He (defendant) called out "Give us the whole bill and not half a bill," when one of the leading Liberals pushed him out, which rather excited hi.-n.—He was fined 5s and costs.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 9, 1884.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 9, 1884.
THE LORDS AND THE FRA.NCIIISE BILL.

The Chairman then pat the resolution to the meeting, and called upon those in favour to say "aye." The audi- ence responded with a great shout, followed by load cheer- ing, sad the resolution was declared carried. Dr. O'Keeffe said he had the honour to propose the fol- lowing resolution:—" That this meeting is of opinion that the house of Lords, by frequently impeding and mutilating ,useful legislation, endangers the peace and prosperity of the Un;ted Kingdom." This, he said, was a grave constitutional evil., and it was absolutely necessary that decisive measures should be taken to prevent such obstruction in the future. (Cheers.) Why is not a labouring man as worthy of his vote as a millionaire? Was not he made of the same flesh and blood? (Hear, hear, and cheers.) The speake, afterwards referred to several usefLl measures which the hereditary House bad rejected in the past, and asked what was tbe House of Lords guilty of. (A voice : " Murder.") How many did it murder by refusing to pass the Compensa- tion for Disturbance Bill in 1880. ("Thousands.") The ; speaker quoted from a book called "John Bull and his Island," written by a Frenchman, in which it was stated that the existence of the House of Lords was an insult to the common sense of the English 'nation. (Cheers.) Mr E Carey seconded the resolution. Why, might he ask, were the majorities in Layour of the Franchise Bill so large in the House of Com- mons recently l' It was because the members of the House of Commons felt that they were responsible to ;heir constituencies. _ The House of Lords had, be must _ . _... . -

GREAT OPEN AIR DEMONSTRATION AT WIDNEB• Widnes added one more page to use history of the present crisis ea the reform question on Saturday, when the work- ing men of the town assembled in their thousands to demand their rights as citizens, and to show Lord Salisbury that the indifference of the people on this qtrstion existed only in his own imagination and had no foundation in actual fact. Toe organisation of the demonstration was in the hands of a committee appointed by the Council of the Liberal Asso- ciation, and the arrangements were conceived and carried out in an admirable manner. The extensive space of land opposite the Local Board offices was chosen as the place of meeting, and it proved eminently set able for the purpose. Tbe town had been mapped out into four districts, and from each distrleL a procession started to the spot chosen.. Each procession was headed by a brass band, and the flags of Eng- land. Scotland, and Wales were borne aloft to represent that the Franchise Bill would emancipate the United Kingdom. Adorning each man's breast was a dark red shield, with a gilt border, and surmounted by symbols of the United King- dom, while in the centre were the words, "Widnes Franchise Demonstration, 1884." The processions were watched by ,considerable numbers of people, who seemed to regard them with much sympathy. The first contingent, preceded by the Star of Temperance Band, left the promenade, West Bank, about three o'clock, and, marshalled by Mr W Whitley and Mr John Jackson, walked through Mersey, Water- loo, and Victoria-roads. The second procession started from Ditton, beaded by the village brass band and proceeded by way of Farnworth and Peelhouse-lane. Mr Warne and Mr Gardiner acted as marshals. Moss Bank was the starting point for the third contingent, which, headed by the Catholic Young Men's brass bond, and marshalled by Mr J Mallon and Mr Heaney, went through Lugsdale and , Newtown. The fourth contingent was formed at Halton View, and preceded uy the Trish National Foresters' band' walked through Mill BMW and Simms Cross. Mr J W Car- tile and Mr D Wright acted as marshals. By four o'clock, the time announced for the commencement of the meeting, all the contingents had arrived on the ground, and the audience numbered nearly 4 000 persons. The digs of the four nationalities fluttered in the breeze above the heads of the audience, each set of standard bearers occupying a lorry as a point M vantage. The accommodation for the speakers and the Press was of an excellent character. On that side of the Market Hall which faces towards Widnes- road a large and suostantially constructed platform hod been erected under the directions of Mr Carey and Mr Morrison, and it was so accoustically arranged that the tones of the speaker's voice would reach the furthest limit of those pre. lent with the minimum of exertion. As Mr E K Muspratt, the president of the Liberal Aesociation, and chairman of the meeting, ascended the platform followed by the leaders of Liberal thoeght in the district, ;hey were greeted with ' prolonged cheering, and throughout all the proceedings the utmost enthusiasm was sown. Besides the Chairman, there were also on the platform Messrs S K Maspratt, Holbrook Uaskell, jour., E Carey,' R Pilkiegten (St. Helens), W Dalton, (Liverpool), T Snape (Liverpool), B R Russell (Liverpool), li Skinner (corres- pondent uf the Daily iVews), J Walton (Liverpool), Dr. O'Keeffe,J Morrison, J R Warne. J W Carlile, D Wright, J Tallow, It Mercer, 8 Sadler, J Gardiner, A Sinclair. Robinson, and W Stirrup and Flood (Warrington), and H B Seeres (secretary Widnes Liberal Association.) Seated in his carriage a short distance from the platform was Mr. , W Hartland, an earnest Liberal, and the pioneer of Wesley- aniem in the town, who, while unable to take all active part , In the proceedings, had come to Ove the meeting his coun- tenance and support. The Chairman, who was received with loud cheers on rising to open the meeting, said lettere had been received from Mr. F. H. Gessage and Mr. T. Sutton Timmis expres- sing their regret that they could not be present. A letter had also been received .from Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, senior, as follows, which was riad, and from which we mark the following extract :—The newspapers will have informed you of the resolutions which were passed. Of the Household Franchise Bill,not much need be said in its behalf, for lo ! all parties are agreed in its favour ! (Hear. hear.) Evan Lord Salisbury, who in 1863-7. left his party out of hatred to reform, now makes vehement assurances o! he s love for ` it !

charitably suppose, rejected the Bill because they did not know what the people of the country really wanted. (Hear, hear.) No daubt the measure would be revived in the Autumn session, and if the House of Lords wished to avoid the socialism which threatened Germany and Russia, and similar revolutions to those which had devastated France, they would take warning in time, and by timely concessions to those who had political power, and to th ore who had not, but who ought to have; to prevent their house from being, as Mr. Morley had said, either mended or ended. (Cheers.) Mr. E R Russell, who was cordially greeted, supported the resolution, as did Mr. J. Walton, barrister, Liverpool, and Mr. Skinner, the war correspondent of the Deftly News, and Mr. Wm. Stirrup, of Warrington, who delivered a character- istically hurnourous speech. The resolution was carried amidst loud cheers. Mr. Joslab Morrisou. in proposing a vote of thanks to those gentlemen who had come from a distance to support the meeting, obeervod that although the meeting had been organised in a great hurry, it had been an unqualified suc- cess. It was the first meeting they had had in the open-air in Widnes, but it would not be the last if the Lords went on opposing the will of the people. (Hear and cheers.) Mr. S. Robinson seconded the motion, which was carried by three cheers. Mr. Russell replied for the visitors, and in doinK se pro- posed a vote of thanks to the chairmao. Mr. Oulton seconded the motion, and it was carried with loud cheers. The Chairman, in reply, said he should like them before they parted to give three cheers for Mr. Gladstone. His request was heartily responded to, and the gathering dispersed.

" Prodigious birth of love it is to me That I must love a loathed enemy." (groans and cries of "we won't have him.') We have like- wise to thank my Lord Salisbury for having brought within the range of practical.politica, not merely the reform of the House of Commons. but the far more important subject which, but for him, might have slept for years, of the re- form of the House of Lords. (Cheers) I feel the deepest regret that I cannot' avail myself of the opportunity to speak my mind on this burning question to our friends at Widnee on Saturday next, but another opportunity will probebiy occur before long. (Cheers). The Chairman said they were assembled to show that the men of Widnes were in favour of the Franchise Bill brought in by the Government and rejected—he sold re- jected notwithstanding what Lord Salisbury had said—re- jected by the House of Lords. (A voice: "Down, with the Lords," and cheers.) They were there that day to let Sir Richard Cross and Colonel Ireland Bleckburne understand that they would not be satisfied with lip service. They did not believe them when they told them they were in favour of the Franchise Bill, for in the past they had never lifted up their voice in favour of the extension of the franchise to the heusehoiders in the counties. (A voice: "And never will; down with them.") For reasons best known to them- selves, Lord Salisbury and the House of Lords told them they were in favour of the extension of the franchise. Now, he for one, did not believe in a deathbed repentance— (cheers)—and the House of Lords was, he believed—at any rate, if it opposed the will of the people— on its deathbed. (Renewed cheering.) They were now brought face to face with the question whether the country should be governed by a Prime Minister like Mr. Gladstone —(load cheers)—elected by a large majority of those who bad at present votes, or by Lord Salisbury, who was elected by nobody. That was the question they bed to censider. There were thirty-six occasions when the House of Lords had opposed, °locked, mutilated, and obstructed Liberal legislation. (Cheers). And they must not forget that Liberal legislation in favour of Ireland was often tyevented becoming law by the House of Lords. Lord Salisbury at present seemed to be of opinion that he loved the franchise and hated Mr. Gladstone. He (the speaker) believed the latter, but he did not believe Lord Salisbury when he asserted the former. Lord &Mettle did hate Mr. Glad- I stones because the latter had endeavoured to obtain Liberal legislation for England, Ireland, and Scotland. (Loud cheers) Mr. Richard Pilkington (of St. Helens) moved the first vesolutioo, as follows :—" That . this meeting desires to ex- press its thorough confidence in Her Majesty's Government, and its hearty approval of their decision to hold an autumn session for the purpose of passing the Franchise Bill during the present Parliament." It was hardly necessary, he said, to move such a resolution to such an audience, for he felt quite sure they esteemed the Government of the da-y as much as he did, and felt that the Government of Mr. Glad- stone was a Government in which the people of England might well trust. (Cheers.) The present Government had passed and had tried to pass many measures for the benefit of the people, and.that measure they had just tried to pass. the Franchise Bill, was one of the greatest that had been I brought forward for twenty years. That measure proposed I to enfranchise two millions of people. ' As they knew it had been passed by the representative chamber of the people by majorities varying from 130 to 190, and that bill which would so benefit the whole of the country would give to Widnes 4,000 fresh electors and to St. Helens 8,000 fresh electors. (Cheers.) What were the reasons why that bill should not be pissed ? One of the reasons given was because there was no Redistribution Bill accompanying it. The Lords said that the Government ought to have dealt with redistribution at the same time. But surely it was quite clear that the Redistribution Bill would come afterwards. Was it not certain that Mr. Gladstone and his Government were pledged to the very lips to bring in a Redistribution Bill? (Hear, hear.) As to the way the reform of the House of Lords was to be made, they might well leave it to the great statesman at the head of the Government. For fifty years Mr. Gladstone had had experience cf Parliament, and they might well leave to his unerring judgment the ques- tion before them. (Cheers.) Mr Flood (of Warrrington), who was cordially received, seconded the resolution, and addressing the audience as fellew-working-men, said in rearlinx the pages of history he had scarcely ever found that the House of Lords had been the pioneers of any measure that had been for the benefit of th 3 people. (Hear, hear, and cries of "Never.") Referring to the Franchise Bill, Mr. Flood asked why should he, pos. semed of no more intelligence than those he saw around Isles, enjoy a privilege in Warrington, which they in Widnes were deprived of, altfiough only a few miles away. (Hear, hear.) It was monstrous that men who had no legitimate claim to represent the people men should step in and veto a privilege that was the birth- right of all English and Irish subjects. (Cheers.) Mr T Snape, who was received with load applause, sup- ported the resolution. He remaiked that Lord Salisbury had said that he sought by an appeal to the people through the melting booth to declare the supremacy of the nation, If be (the speaker) thought Lord Stlisbury was sincere, and that by' an appeal to the polling booth they could really get the supremacy of the people declared, he should support Lord Salisbury in the action he had taken—(hear, hear,)— but when they knew that instead of an appeal to those who bad a right to vote the appeal would be made to a very Darted part of the nation—to three million voters when it ought to be five millions—then he objected to such an peal being made. (Cheers) In Widnes a large portion of the population was composed, and rightly composed, of natives of Ireland. (Hear, hear.) He knew that maiy of them were Catholics, and he wished them to understand What these Lords had been doing in reference to Ireland and with reference to Catholics io the past and in the present. These Lords who had taken this action • upon this Bill also rejected the bill for Catholic emancipation in 1825. (Cheers.) It was these Lords who in ISSO refused to pass the Comeen- fattion for Disturbance Bill, which would have sav‘d an enormous amount of suffering amongst the poor country people, and only two weeks ago the Poor Law Guardians for Ireland Bill, which was passed by the House of Com- mons, was rejected by the House of Lords, as they had done almost every measure that pointed in the direction of aif popular rights and liberty. (Cheers.) At present the House of Lords would neither reform themselves nor allow the House of Commons to carry out its measures of reform ; but the question had been raised, and it was now not alone the Franchise Bill with which they had to deal; they had to set steadily before them the qeostior, of the reform, if not the abolition, of the House of-Lords. (Cheers.) Mr. W. Calton, of Liverpool, supported the resolutisn. I

Addresses were also delivered by the Revs G Rack,l W Vause, and T Griffin; and Mr J Withington. Ou the proposition of Mr 8 Faulkner, seconded by Mr D Bisbrown, a cordial vote of thanks was accorded to the chairman. The thanks of the meeting were also givan to all those who had in any way given their aid in carrying out the demonstration.

W Heetheringten, Wtn Norman, J IV Boyle, T Holt, 1J Jones, and T Cooke (secretary.) The Chairman, who was heartily received, delivered a speech upon the general aspects of the temperance question. At one time the arguments of total abstainers were thwarted or defied, but so great was the change which had been wrought within a few years, and so rapid the progress that had been made, that now instead of being browbeaten and called fanatics, a large majetity of the people of this country was in their favour. They had given the question of intem- perance consideration years ego, TheY 110 If Itched its effect on individual life. They saw Low it marred the pleasure and happiness of individual man, bow it affected fetniJies and through families the nation ; and they found that not only were men miserable, but as a consequence, the cures was eating like a cankerworm into the vitals of our nationel life, and as patriots they were anxious that this matter should be looked into. He thought they might con- gratulate themselves that the temperance estimate of drone- enness had been accepted, add that judges and doctors and even statesmen were now prepared to do something, and ía- stead of calling total abitainers fanatics they were rather proud to hive their acquaintance and accept their advice. (Applause.) Having quoted eminent scientific authorities upon alcohol and its effects, the chairman said if they could clearly demonstrate that drink was the cause of the greatest portion of the misery lathe countryond that on the other hand drink for ordinary purposes was no good, the only logicil outcome of these two facts was that the safest and best thing was to abstain altogether. (Hear, hear.) Tnat was the position he took up, and it was olio of the proudest boasts of his life that he had never tasted driuk—(appleuse)—and he hoped to be able to mike that boast to the end of his life. He must frankly confess that be had very little sympathy with the moderate drinker. That narrow ledge upon which they were standing was the ledge from which every drun- kard in the country had slipped, and it struck him forcibly that there were a thousand chances of their going into the vertex below to their one chance of taking a man and putting him right They must put men not on the narrow ledge, the shifting sands of moderation, but upon the firm rock of total abstinence— (applauee)—if they would establish their going. He was not there that evening for the purpose of making any politi- cal allusions, but there was no doubt that both parties of the Slate were agreed that at no distant day we were to have a reformed Parliament, and the history of the past clearly demonstrated that in a reformed Parliament domestic legislation had a prominent place. He felt confident that the reformed Parliament, coins when it may, would most certainly tackle the drink question, and he was sure they would deal with it meet effectively. Toe men who returned men to Parliament at the next election, if they voted on the new register, would speak on the question with no uncertain sound. They were told that they could not make men sober by Act of Parliament. They did not try to do that, but what they insisted upon was that they should net make j them drunk by Act of Parliament. (Applause.) With the growth of bands of hope and other temperance organisatione they had growing up a generation that would speak out in the future, and when he looked at the forces that had coins to assist them in their warfare against this monstrous evil, he could not help applying those beautiful lines of Kings- ley, when he triumphantly declares— The nlght is past, behold the sun ! The Idol falls, the lii, is done The judge is set. the doom begun. And none shall stay it.

• (Loud applause.) Mr. T. Cooke, the secretary, was called upon to reed his report. He said the objects of the society were to give re- lief in sickness, with free medical attendance and medicine, and to insure a sum of money to be ptid on the death of a member's wife, or widow, by means of a fortnightly contri- bution ; and to shield its members from the evils of intern- perinea by means of a total abstinence pledge. The order adapted itself to the wants and means of all classes in society, and enabled its members on the payment of a small weekly subscription to secure from 54 to 20e per week in sickness, and from £lOlO £5O et death; also secur- ing £lO on the death of a member's wife or widow. The first great principle of the order was that all the members must be total abstainers, so that the; would observe that absolute sobriety was the basis of their common insurance and association. (Hear, hear.) They were moreover an association of temperance meu, stimulated, encouraged, and improved by their intercourse. (Hear, hear.) The order was again an org tnisation for the saving of the young and the rescuimg of the aged from the blandishments and curse of drink and its surroundings. The conception of two tem- perance men in New York that a temperance provident society would best provide for the contingencies of a workman's life and rescue him from the temptation of the public-house had been realiz d beyond expection ; for after 40 years' losses by death, by removals, by temptations sanctioned by law and sustained by society, their order could boast of mow brave souls who dared to be sober. (Applause.) That which was born in Division-street, New York, was rapidly wafted over every state of the union to Canada, and to one own shores, then away to the Australian Continents, to all the British Settlements in Africa, te Germany, to Norway, so that they could scarcely go anywhere where the Sons of Temperance were not to be found. (Applause.) 1... et the homes of our coantry be castles of sobriety, love, purity, and fidelity, and our nation need fear no foes without or within, for these were a nation's surest bulwarks,-.-(Ap- plause.)—for what in this world destroyed wealth snd lum- piness equal to the liquor traffic. Therefore these 100 000 members of theirs were called upon to be more than mere contributers to their own funeral fund. It was theirs to be examples at home, teachers in the workshop, brave men before temptation, and herees in society. He pointed out that the order's funds could not be touched for Cases of sickness or death brought on by drunkeness, which, of course, materially lessens the number of cases for sick al- lowance, and made the average yearly death rate seven in every thousand as compared with ten per thousand in non- temperance societies. 8n greatly had the principles of the order commended themselves, that since its establishment in England 28 years ago, it had grown to Ito present magnitude. During the p tst year the progress Had been unparalelled, 27 new lodges having been instituted, and 20 juvenile sections and 3,730 new members initiated into the order, and £4,072 IN ld increase in the funds of the society. The increase in the Runcorn district had been 130 in membership, and £lOO in funds. After referring to the fact that the society was like an assurance corporation, be pointed out that during the last year they had paid in sick claims alone £12.507 15e 91, and in death claims £2,442 10s. and given £212 34 81 away to deserving members in distress. Tbere were now 20,000 members and £60,000. They had proved by their statistics that the members of the Sons of Temperance lived former, that they had aboat ball the sickness of drink- ing provident societies, and that they were financially soun- der. The Sons of Temperance was a long life and good health society, and in a sound financial position, and no society better managed. Then it those working-men present wanted rood health, happy homes. pleasenter existence, sweeter lives, length of daye, a less amount of physic, cof- fins and plaster, they should become Sons of Tem- perance. He concluded by advising 'those present to keep clear of the publichouse, sign the pledge and come and enrol themselves as members of the Sons of Temper- ance. (Applause).

div.head: EARLESTOWN. ' NEWTON COMMISSIONERS.. MONTHLY MEETING.
div.p: EARLESTOWN. ' NEWTON COMMISSIONERS.. MONTHLY MEETING.
The monthly meeting of the Newton Improvement Com- missioners was held at the Town Hall, Newton, on Monday _

F J E Pardey, James Fairslough, Thomas Hunt, T J Gillespie, James W Emmett, BB Glover, Thomas Forster, James E Worsley (law, clerk), and R Brierley (surveyor).—The minutes of the last meeting were read and confirmed. ELECTION OF CILEIRMEN.—Mr Emmett said he believed

the first business of that meeting was to elect a chairman for the ensuing year.—Mr Worsley : That is so.—Mr Emmett remarked that he had very great pleasure in proposing that Mr Gooth be re-elected chairman. He had discharged his duties to his (Mr rrnmetes) entire satisfaction, and he was sore to the entire satisfaction of the Commissioners, and be hoped,to the satisfaction of the ratepayers as well.—Mr Gil- lespie bad great pleasure in seconding the motion. They all knew Mr Gooch well and what he did he did thoroughly. He did not know there was ahy other man who could, do it more thoroughly or more to their approba- tion than he (Mr Gooch) did. (Hear, hear.)—Mr Forster and Mr Pardey also supported the Motion, which was unani- mously carried.—The Chairman thanked them for the henour they bad again conferred upon him. He added that it bad always been a pleasure to him to it at that Board, because they always worked so harmoniously and well toge- ther. He was quite aura they all had the interests of the township at heart; and he thought that was the only way of carrying- out the duties of the. Board. Ho hoped they would continue to work harmoniously together and though little differences might arise from time to time he hoped they would get on smoothly. THE PROCEEDINGS OF THE SCHOOL ATTENDANCE CONI•
MITTRE —With reference to a matter discussed at the last

meetinv, Mr Emmett asked if the law clerk had received any answer to his letter to the Education Department with regtv-d to the School Attendance Committee.—Mr. Worsley stated that he had subnsitted a question to the Education Department as instructed, and he had received an answer to
the eff-ct that they had no authority to decide it. (Laugh- -- - - -

ter )-11r. Gillespie said be would like to know what the question wa4, as he was not present at the previous meet- Worsley said the question was whether the min- ntPs of the School Attendance Committee selected out of a

Locil Board required confirmation by the Local Board out of which the committee was taken.—Mr. Pardey said they never had been confirmed previously. They bad simply been read at the Board meeting for the intormstion r.l the public.—Mr. Emmett asked if theft; was any obj-ction to have the minutes confirmed at a regular any meeting. He did not see any objection to it himself, because it would let the ratepayers see what the School Attendance Corn- mittee were doing. It was only fair that the ratepayers should know what was going on.—The Chairman said it did seem that the proceedings should be made pablic.—Mr. Pardey said it was not a question of publishing the proceed- ings, but whether the resolutions come to by the School At- tendance Committee should be final or not. Hai the minutes to be confirmed or rejected at the pleasure of another Board? It had always been thought sufficient hitherto to read the minutes.—Tbe Chairman thought the thing might remain aa it was at present.—Mr. Pardey said the minutes of one School Attendance Committee were confirmed at the next meeting.—Mr. Stone said every member of the Board was on the School Attendance Committee and he did not think it necessary that the minutes should be confirmed.—

Mr. Gillespie said it would not make any difference to the ratepayers if the minutes were confirmed or not. The pre- sent system appeared to work well and he did not see there was any necessity for altering it. It might lead to some difficulty in future.—The chairman: I think so.—Mr.

Emmett stated that his object was to let the ratepayers know what the School Attendance Committee was really doing. He scarcely thought that the ratepayers knew from the minutes what was really being done.—Mr. Pardey. Raid Mr. Emmett's object cnuld be met if he (Mr. Emmett) would move at the next meeting of the committee that the re- porters should be admitted. He would have no objection to that —The Chairman thought if the minutes were pro- perly written out they gave as much information to the public as was really required.—Mr. Emmett : What is the object of the minutes being read at all if they are not to be discussed or confirmed ?—Mr. Pardey : To let the public know what has been done —Mr. Emmett said he would have pleasure in moving at the next meeting of the committee that the reporters be admitted HIGHWAY. AND SAATARY COMMITTEE. - A meeting of Highways, Public Works, and Sanitary Committee was held on the 21st July, at which letters were read from Mr Worthington and Mr Biddle, representing the London and North-Western Railway Company respecting the discharge of sewage into their canal, west of Earlestown. Messrs
Gooch, Fairclough, and the Surveyor were deputed to call upon Mr Worthington respecting the arrangements . .

Made by him and the committee, to convey the sewage under the canal into tanks to be built on the company's land between the canal and the brook, The com- mittee recommended that the law clerk be instructed to write to Mr Legh's agent calling upon him to remove the Pest and wire fence on the north side of Newton Common- road, it being an encroachment upon the public road as advised by the law clerk, nder section ItB. 3rd George IV, cip 1211 and subsequent acts. The committee recommen- ded that the roads and paths within the cemetery be asphalted instead of macadamised, the approach road to the ledge gates to be mac idamiseC, as originally provided for, the extra cost being estimated at about £65. It was ordered that a cheOus for £lOO be drawn in favour of Mr Cunliffe on his contract at the cemetery, the same being certified by the Surveyor. ,Plans for the alteration of closets to cottages in Fairclough-street. for Mr Thomas Cunliffe and for additional bedrooms to Mr Wm Burdis' house, Park- road were submitted and approved. Ihe sanitary officers were directed to see to the effective cleaning of night soil from the streets and to the application and free use of disin- fectants during its removal. --- Oa the motion of Mr Stone, rescinded by Mr Emmett, the minutes were confirmed.

GAS MATTERS.T/Ild LIGHTING OF LAMPS.—At A meeting of the Gas and Water Committee, held on the 21st. ult., the carbonizing account for the past month which was presented showed fuel used 75 tons 5 cwt.; gas made 784,81D0 cubic feet, averaging 10,030 feet per ton, of fuel used.—Mr. Brierley suumitted a statement which be had prepared by an order of the House of Commons, hating reference to the cost and working of the gas works, which was approved and ordered to be sent to the Board of Trade.—After the minutes
L AT EST
NEWS.

The Socialist, Steelmacher, was hanged at Vienna at five o'clock on Friday morning, without confessing. When play concluded at Clifton yesterday the Austra. Hans had scored 295 for the loss of nine wickets.
On inquiry yesterday afternoon it was stated that the condition of the Bishop of Claughton remains about the same.
The German Government has declined to entertain Por- tugal's proposal of a European Conference to consider the Congo question.

- - The d.eath penalty on Michael Tansey, who was sentenced to be executed at Galwarnext Monday, has been commuted to penal servitude for life. At a mass meeting of colliers on strike held at Netherton, near Dudley, yesterday. it was stated that several additional employers .had conceded the men the old rate of wages._

Cornwall, Pillar, Johnson, Little, Surgeon-major Fer- nandez, Captain Kirwan, Fowler, and Considine, arraigned at Dublin Commission on Friday for the unnatural crimes, pleaded not guilty to all the counts, and were informed they would be tried on the 19th.

The Central News understands that, as Lord Northbrook has been strongly adivsed to take at least some w;eeks rest and change of air before proceeding to Egypt, the dinner to which the Narthbrook Club had invited his lordship, and which had been fixed for the thirteenth inst., has been aban- doned.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
A NEW SCHEME PROPOSED.

A meeting of the Provisional Committee of the Manches- ter Ship Canal scheme was held on Tuesday, at the offices, Marke,street,. Manchester, this being the first meeting since the rejection of the bill by the Select Committee of the House of Commons. The meeting was one of the largest ever held since the formation of ttfe committee. Mr Hanle AdarraOnt chairman of the committee, presided, and arnnst those present were Mr John Rvlancis, the Mayor of Salford (Mr Alderman Makinson), Mr Mackie (Warrington), Mr Hilton Greaves (Oldham), Mr Alderman Husband, Mr Thos. Bradford, Mr Henry Boddington, jag., Mr Reuben Spencer, Mr A E Sin ton, gton Mr .1 E Platt (Oldham), Mr J Leigh (Stockport), Mr Marshall Stevens (Liverpool), Mr W John- stone (Liverpool), Mr William Fletcher, Mr H C Piogstone, Mr J U Fielding, Mr John Walthew (Stockport), Mr Rind. James, Mr James Johnstone, and the legal adviser's and officers of the committee.

The Chairman reviewed at considerable length the present pisition of the proiect, and referred to certain alternative schemes which had been previously under the consideration of the Provisional Committee He also called attention to the following extracts from the proceedings before the Com- mittee of the House of COMM3OB, to show that if the Com- mittee decided to adopt an alternative scheme, avoiding the estuary works, such a scheme would not meet with any op- position from the Corporation of Liverpool or from the Mersey Docks and Harbour Bo.rd. On the 30th of July Sir William Forwood was examined before the Committee on behalf of the opposition by the Liverpool Town Council, and in his evidence said :

To show the absolute bona fries of what I have said. sPelk- log on behalf of the Oo poration of Liverpool, I have no obie::- lion whatever to this scheme being passed by this Oorninittee as far as Ituncom. and if the promoters would bring In a bill next yesr carrying out their estusry works. as they can carry them out, without Interference with the estuary either along the northern or south-r-i shores, we will not. upon pri oponse that bill next year. I earl say nothing stronger to show the entire bona fides of Liverpool. _ . "

Mr. Aspinall. QC., addressing the Committee on behalf of the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, said : During Clir William Forwud's evidence he offered a ple Ige— I don't ,emember tne ex id t w irds. I represent the Dock and lam authorised in the stronge,t po4sible sense up m be- h if of the Dock Board t r&ttfy that offer of tlir William For- wood in the preci,e words li, wh ch he mada it. Fir wnat it is w. rth time tffer is tnerefore before you both on behetif of the Corporation of Liverpool and on behaif of the Kersey Dozka and liarb,mr Baard.

On the motion of Mr. John Ryland& seconded by Mr, Hilton Oreaves, and supported by Mr. jamts Platt, the Mayor of Salford, Mr. MaCkin, and Mr. Walthew, the follow- ing.res-lution was unanimously adopted:—" That this Com- mittee, notwithstanding the rejection of the bill lately before the House of Commons, is of opinion that the movement to connect Manchester.with the sea by a chip canal should be continued and prosecuted to a successful issue; and further, that the concessions made by the opposition warrant the con- sideration of an alternative scheme, avoiding the estuary, which will secure a satisfactory canal. This Commitee is also of opinion that a tneeting of subscribers as well as a public meeting should be summoned at an early date to re-1 ceive the report from the Provisional Committee and to test the feeling of the district as to further operations." Although the Committee are thus considering alternative schemes, it is not because they think their plan for dealing with the eetuare was not the right one. They think the river, being the natural waterway, should 'have been im- proved. The proper authorities having, however, de&ded against them, they are compelled•to consider alternative schemes, their object being to obtain a ship canallrom Man- chester to the sea. With this view surVeys and examina- tions of the routes suggested have been at once taken. The meeting, having passed a hearts vote of thanks to Mr Adamson for his zealous and unwearied labours in the promotion of the scheme, was adjourned to Friday. The employetts of Messrs John Fletcher and Sons, Eagle Foundry, Booth-street, Salford, held a meeting on Wednes- day, at which the following resoldtion was unanimously adopted: "That we express to the Provisional Committee of the Manchester Ship Canal our great satisfaction at see- ing that it is their intention to prosecute to a successful issue the movement to connect Manchester with the sea by ship canal." It was also resolved to contribute one day's wages in support of the movement. At a meeting of the Collyhurst Conservative Club, held on Tuesday evening, the following resolution was passed unanimously :—" That this meeting deeply regrets the de- cision of the Select Committee of the House of Commons in rejecting the Manchester Ship Canal Bill." At a meeting of the Liverpool City Council, held on Wednesday, Alderman A B Forwood congratulated the town upon the success of the opposition raised to the Manchester Ship Cinal Bill by the Corporation and Mersey Hock Board, and sald that if Manchester people would only approach Liverpool they would he glad to receive them and discuss some means of cheapening the communication between the two cities, so as to'clo away with the extortionate charges of the rail way companies, _ _ _ _ .

_ aThe Salford Town Council on Wednesday unanimously adopted a resolution declaring their opinion that the failure of the House of Commons Committee to pass the Ship Canal Bill is a great calamity which must retard the return of prosperity to the cotton districts, and expressing satisfaction that the promoters intend to persevere with the enterprise, and a hope that their efforts may be crowned with ultimate success.

A conference took place on Thursday afternoon, at the Manchester Town Hall, between the promoters of the Man- chester Ship Canal and several members of the special Ship Canal Sub-committee of the Manchester Corporation, in regard to the recent action of the Committee of the House of Commons. Mr Adamson. on behalf a the promoters, submitted their case to the members of the Committee present, but no resolution was proposed, it being considered desirable that the conference should be further adjourned, in order to allow a full attendance.

Since the rejection of the Ship Canal Bill the Committee have received many letters from all Darts of the country. encouraging them to persevere in their design to connect Manchester with the sea by means of a ship canal, ind so during the last few days promises of material support have come in very freely. A deputation of fourteen members of the Provisional Committee surveyed the Lancashire side of the Mersey es- tuary (from Garston, to Rtincorn), with a view to an alter- native scheme, on Wednesday. The Cheshire side of the es- tuary will also be closely surveyed.

FIRE AT BIIRTONWOOD.—On Thursday morning a fire broke out on the premises of Mr Warburton. at Burtonwood, the fl taws being discovered in a shed used for the storage of hay. A mealenger at once proceeded to Warrington. and the fire brigade lost no time in reaching the tire, which was quialy put nut. SPECIAL SERMONS AT GLAZEBROON.—The Primitive Metho- dist Sandy School anniverstry sermons were preached on Sunday, by Mr Joh ftBOl3,Gl azebrook, both afternoon and even- ing. The chapel was crowded at both services. Appropriate hymns were sung by the children. The collections amounted to MI. On Monday evening there was a tea meeting, which was well attended.

had been confirmed, Mr, Pardey drew attention to the fact that on a recent dark night the large lamp in the centre of High-street near the Oak Tree was left unlighted. Be thought it was purely an oversight —Mr. Stone supported Mr. Pardey's remarks, and added that any person who did not know of the lamp being there might easily have driven straight against it.—Mr. Gillespie: It seems of very little use putting down lamps unless they are lighted.—The Chairman: None of the lamps are supposed to be lighted now, but I think they should be lit on dark nights.—Mr Stone thought the lamps might be left lighted all the night on dark nights.—Mr. Glover: Cannot the surveyor give an explanation 7—Mr. Brierley : The lamps are all extinguished from May fair to August fair. It has always been so since we had the gas works.—Mr. Stone expressed tne opinion that the order was very good and all right so far as it related to ordinary lamps, but he thought it was desirable that. lamps in the middle of the road should be lighted on dark nights.—Mr Emmett thought such lamps might be lighted a little to show that there were lamps in the middle of the road.—Mr Pardey moved that the large lamps in the middle of the road be sufficiently lighted at all times during the night to show there were such lamps —Mr Gillespie seconded 'the motion, which was adopted. FINANCES —At a meeting of the Finance Committee, held on the 21st ult., accounts amounting to .£789 4s lid were , ex .mined and ordered to be paid.—The minutes were passed.

SCHOOL A TTENDANCE —At a meeting of the School Attendance Committee, on Its 21st ult., the School Attend- ance Officer read his report, stating that since the last meet- ing most of the schools bad been closed for the midsummer holidays, therefore he had nothing special to refer to. It was ordered that the Clerk be instructed to write to the Overseers of the Poor urging immediate payment of the precept issued by that committee and due on the 315t.1114y last.

RE APPOINTMENT or. MEDICAL OFFICER—The Chair- man said be had very great pleasure in proposing the re- appointment of Dr. Watkins as medical officer of health for the di3trict for the ensuing year on the same terms as he now held the office.—Mr Gillespie seconded the motion, which was supported by Mr Einmett and adopted. THE PROPOSED SEWERAGE SCHEME —The Chairm n remarked that the next business was the proposed sewerage works.—Mr. Pardey observed that be had better retire &can the room during the consideratinn of that question. There was one thing he would like to mcntion, however, before he did so. He wished to ask if it had really been decided to have a road to the sewerage works not only through the road to the cemetery, but actually through a portion of the ceme- tery itself. If that was so be must, as a Commissiener, express his very sincere regret that that decision had been come to. He thought they would find that the public too would come to the same conclusion in time. He could not move an amendment, as be was leaving the room, but he must express his feelings on the matter.—The Chairman said that that resolution was come to after a great deal of consideration and discussion. It was very much upon the ground that the amount of cartage along the road would be so small that it would not be any detriment to it, and that the cost of putting in a new road and the severance of others would be an expense which they did not feel justified in entering upon at the present time. The proposed road would last for a great number of years, and when the time did arrive for a new road to be made they could get one con- structed.—Mr. Pardey said they might not be in a position to get the land then—there might be some difficulty. He could not agree with the suggestion that the cartage would be confined to some three or four carts a week. He would not, however, oppose it, but he could not allow the proposal to pass without expressing great regret at what bad been done.--(Mr. Pardey thereupon left the room)—Mr. Gillespie asked the surveyor what amount of cartage there was likely te be along the road.— Mr. Brierley did not think there would be very much. They would require the refuse at present gathered for the cemetery for some years, and then the farmer adjoining had made application for any . other they might not use.—Mr. Gillespie: Will any night , soil or anything of that sort pass along this road P—Mr. . Brierley : Oh no, that is out of it. allogether.—Mr. Guise- pie did not think there would be any difficulty in securing any piece of land they might require for a new road in ; future years —M. Worsley (law clerk) afterwards stated that at a previous naee: ing he was instructed to suggest to Mr. Pardey the name of Mr. Voisey, late borough engineer of Warrington, as the valuer of the land required tor the sewer- age works, but Mr. Pardey bad written stating that be could not agree to the proposal. He (Mr. Pardey). however, had no obj=ction to any of the following gentlemen: John • White, Warrington; John Pierpoint, ‘Varrington ; Mr. Gar- ' lick, Preston; Mr. Cross, Manchester; Mr. Kellett, Man- chester ; and Mr. Thompson, Manchester.—After some die- : cussion Mr. Gillespie moved that a committee consisting of ' the chairman of each committee see Mr. Pardey and try to arrange with him what price had to be paid for the land re- quired; and failing that arrangement that Mr. Voisey be appointed valuer for the Commissioners, and that it be left to Mr. Pardey to appoint whom he thought fit to act on his behalf.—Mr. Emmett seconded the motion, which was ' carried.

TOULON, FRIDAY, 10 AM. —There was one deith from cholera in the Bon Rencontrr Hospital list night. A NEW CANDIDATE FOR THE AMERICAN PRESIDENCY.

NEW YORK, THunsne.Y.,—General Butler announced his intention to accept the nomination as candidate for the Pre- sidency, offered to him by the " Greenbackers," the 1 tbour- ing men, and the anti-monopolists, and will state his rea- eons for so doing after the publication of Governor Cleve- land's letter accepting the Democratic nomination for the Presidency.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS. The House met at 4 o'clock.

MISCELLANEOUS —The Lord CHANCELLOR, replying to A question, said that by order of the Council it was not in- cumbent on judges to have the proclamation against vice read at the asiizes.—Several bills were read a third time, in- cluding the Corruptyractices Act (Vuuicipal Elections) Earl KIMBERLEY, replying to a question, said the map showing the boundaries of Afghanistan was progressing Earl GRANVILLE refused to lay on the table now papers re lating to negotiations for Commercial treaties with Turkey and Janan.
The House then adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The House met at four o'clock.

QuEsnows.—Lord FITZMAIIRICE, replying to Mr Arthur Moor, said if the Board of Freda thought further information than it possessed with regard to the sale cf oleomargarine and hutterine in the United States. in Holland, and other coun- tries was required, Earl Granville would take steps to obtain further information.—Lord Fazmanificg intimated that Lord Dufferin bad telegraphed that the Porte had informed him that there would be no objection to ships nassin in transit from and to the Black Sea through the Dardanelles.
The Appropriation Bill was brought in and read the first time.

THE INDIAN Bupoar.—Mr. K. Caoss then made the In diau Budget statement. He entered at length into the in- come and expenditure for the last two years, and also that for 1884-5, and on the whole he considered the financial prospect satisfactory and encouraging. The estimites for 1884-5 gave a surplus of .£319,000, the revenue for opium being put down at £6,241,00C which was a million below the average revenue that had been received from that source for the last five years. Mr. ARNOLD moved a resolution to relieve Jodie from the Consular charges on the Persian Gulf, the Tigris, and the Euphrates, and to place British trade in western Asia in the hands of those completely responsible to the home Government.— Lord FITZMATIRICE declined to accept the resolution which was negatived without a divi- sion,

EXTRAORDINARY ASSAIILT."-A. vanman named John Carter was charged at the Warrington/Borough Court, yes- terday, with beating a little boy named Mark Harold Holt, on the let met, at Latchford.—Mr P Davies prosecuted, and said that it seemed that that day week the defendant was driving along Knutsford-road, and the complainant wes walking on the footpath going to school. Without any reason that they could make out \ the defendant struck the complainant with his whip round the neck, taking the skin off his neck and chin. Defendant kept his bold of the whip, and the boy was dragged some distance on the road.—The defendant said that some boys were on the road, and one pushed the other in the way If the van, whereupon he "scotched" complainant with the whip to correct him. He luct no intention to bust him.—The Bench fined the defen- dant Ss and costs, which was paid,

FATAL ACCIDENT AT TIIII COTTAGE HOSPETAL.—Nri W T Husband, deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Feathers Inn. Croppers Hill, St. Helens, on Thursd3y- at noon. touching the death of John Diyies, 30. a toick'ayers- in the employ of Mr Harrison, builder, who died at the cot- tage Hospital on Monday from injurie• received by 3 fall at the Cottage Hospital on the previous Friday.—Miss For • wood, matron at the Cottage Hospital, deaosA that de- ceased was admitted into the hospital Cu Friday, sulTtring from broken ribs and internal injuries. He told her that he was engaged on the new wing of the hospital when he slipped and fell. He could not account for his fall. He was attended by Dr. Gaskell up tO his death, which occurred early on Sundae morning. Ann DaVbri, 44, Talbot-street, deposed that the deceased was her husband. He died at the Cottage Hospital,and his body was afterwards removed to 69, Eccles- , ton-street, where his mother lived. He was 30 years of'ne• He was in good health, and quite sober when ho went to work on the previous Friday morning.—The Deputy Coroner, on behalf of himself and the jury desired to express their sympathy with the witness in her bereayement.—John- a bricklayer residing in Boundary-road, St. Helene,.: said he was working at the new wing of the cottage hos- pital on Friday, next to the deceaaell, who was quite sober,- Deceased was standing on the scaffold, about 24 feet frotn,, the floor. He had his hand on a corner brick, which gave way, and be fell with it from the sciffold to the ground. - He was p;cked up by two meal and carried into the hospital. George Hart, a labourer residing at Parr, said he was an inmate of the Cottage Hospital on the day of the accident. He saw the deceased fall be the manner described —The• jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."
